Bugaboo architecture

AcceptedPhase 3 of 5·2026-10-04

How Bugaboo is built: the big decisions, the parts and how they work together, how it runs when sold or served, the technology underneath, and the checks that keep the code true to this design. Feature IDs (like SEC-04) refer to the feature list.

How to give feedbackUse this page's comment button. Mention the section number shown next to each heading (for example §7.2), or select text and comment on it. Tapping a section number copies it, ready to paste into your comment.

Goals and constraints

Quality goals

Ranked. When two goals conflict, the higher one wins, and the trade-off is recorded in a decision record (ADR).

RankGoalWhat it means for the architecture
1Security, secure by defaultOne authorization path for every way in (UI, API, search, MCP, assistant, exports, notifications). Deny by default. Hidden data never leaves the server, not even as a count or an error-message difference.
2UXPlain, fast, works for people less technical than average. Common actions feel under 100 ms; the server sends only what a screen shows.
3AI integrationThe assistant and outside AI apps (MCP) act as the person, with that person's permissions, through the same code as the UI. AI proposes; people decide.
4Software and design architectureSSOT, DRY and ODR are mandatory. Clear module boundaries, testable core, generated code instead of copied code.
5Feature completenessThe feature list, with no architectural dead ends for later features.
6Ease of installationOne binary, an embedded database, a setup wizard.

Across all of them: privacy by design (GDPR) and EU product law (CRA, AI Act, Data Act, NIS2) are constraints, not features. See compliance.md.

Constraints

Technology

  • Server: Rust, latest stable (1.97 at time of writing), edition 2024. unsafe is forbidden unless an ADR allows it.
  • Browser app: TypeScript 7 (the native compiler) and React 19.
  • Exact versions: see Tech stack. Versions are pinned through lockfiles and updated on purpose.

Platforms

  • Server: Windows 10/11 and Windows Server 2022+ (x64, ARM64); Linux (x64, ARM64, any distribution, static build); WSL 2 uses the Linux build.
  • Browsers: the last two versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari, on desktop and phone.

Data and scale

  • Databases: SQLite, built in, by default; PostgreSQL 16 or newer for larger installations.
  • Scale target for 1.0: about 500 people, 1 million issues and 200 people working at the same time on one installation, on a 4-core server with 8 GB of memory.
  • One organization per installation. Projects separate teams inside it.

Distribution

  • Bugaboo may be sold (the customer runs it) or served (we run it). Both must work from the same code (DIST-01; review: checked at every milestone review).
  • No telemetry and no outside requests unless an administrator configures them (mail, AI provider, single sign-on, update check).

Licenses of third-party parts

The license of Bugaboo itself is not decided. Every part we ship must therefore allow both proprietary and open-source distribution (DEP-LICENSES):

Allowed in the shipped binaryNot allowed
MIT, Apache-2.0 (also with LLVM exception), BSD-2/3-Clause, ISC, Zlib, Unicode-3.0, MIT-0, 0BSD, CC0, Unlicense, BSL-1.0, CDLA-Permissive-2.0 (data), OFL-1.1 (fonts), MPL-2.0 (file-level, unmodified)GPL, AGPL, LGPL (static linking), SSPL, BUSL, "non-commercial" licenses

The exact allow list lives in deny.toml (the single source) and is enforced by DEP-LICENSES (coding-standards §5).

People and process

  • Implementation is done by AI agents in milestones, guided by these documents. Everything an agent needs must be written down (review: checked at every milestone review), and every rule that can be checked by a machine is checked by a hook.

NeighborDirectionTrustNotes
People (browser)inUntrusted input, authenticated identityEverything they send is validated and checked by the policy engine.
AI apps (MCP)inAuthenticated, scoped; output untrustedAct as the person who connected them; scopes can only narrow permissions.
AI provideroutUntrusted outputReceives only fields the person may read and that are not excluded from AI. Off by default.
Mail serveroutTrusted transportNotification content is filtered by the recipient's permissions.
Company sign-in (OIDC)out/inTrusted identity sourceGroup claims can map to Bugaboo groups.
Webhook receiversoutUntrustedPayloads signed (HMAC); each webhook runs as an agent of the organization with its own role (ADR-0029).
Control planeinTrusted operator, no customer dataServed model only. Emergency data access needs the customer's approval (DIST-03).

Trust boundaries

  1. Browser ↔ server: the browser is never trusted. The UI is a normal API client (principle 3); the server re-checks everything.
  2. Server ↔ AI provider: prompts carry only permitted data; answers are treated like text from a stranger. They may propose changes, never make them.
  3. Issue and document content: written by people, so it is untrusted in every place it is shown or sent: sanitized for the browser, fenced for the assistant, escaped for e-mail.
  4. Operator ↔ customer data (served): our staff and the control plane sit outside the customer's data. Access is an exception with approval and a log entry.

Solution strategy

The few big decisions that shape everything else. Each links to its decision record.

#DecisionWhyADR
1A modular monolith in one binary, with a pure domain core and adapters around itEasiest to install, secure (one process, one boundary), fast; modules keep it maintainable0001
2Tokio + axum + rustls for the serverMature, fast, memory-safe TLS, no OpenSSL to install0002
3SQLite by default, PostgreSQL optional, through sqlx and one query builder; the database schema is defined once, in RustZero-setup install and a path to scale, without writing everything twice0003
4One policy engine; data leaves the domain only as Authorized<T>; searches get permission rules compiled into their SQLMakes bypassing authorization a compile error, not a code-review hope0004
5Our own search language, one Rust crate, also compiled to WebAssembly for the browserSimple and Advanced search share one parsed form; the editor behaves exactly like the server0005
6Own fields stored in a typed value tableFast filtering and sorting on both databases, permissions per field0006
7An append-only event log with an outbox is the single source for history, notifications, webhooks, the security log, search indexing and live updatesOne write, many consumers; nothing can change without leaving a trace0007
8API first: the OpenAPI description is generated from the Rust code, and the TypeScript client from thatAPI types exist once (ODR); the UI can't use what the API doesn't offer0008
9React 19 + Vite + TanStack Router/Query + React Aria Components in the browserType-safe URLs, one cache for server data, accessible building blocks0009
10Design tokens as the only source of style, turned into CSS variables; one theme file with the rules of every componentFour themes and the theme editor from one source; customization can't inject code0010
11One Markdown renderer (Rust), used by the server and, via WebAssembly, by the editor previewWhat you preview is exactly what others see, sanitized the same way0011
12The same binary is sold and served; served means one isolated instance per customer plus a control planeNo second product to maintain; strong isolation; keeps "one organization per installation"0012
13AI through one provider interface and one tool registry, shared by the assistant and MCP; AI never decides about peopleSame rules for both ways in; AI Act high-risk uses designed out0013
14One check runner (cargo xtask) called by Git hooks, Claude Code hooks and CI; Biome and ast-grep for TypeScript and pattern rulesChecks are defined once and behave the same everywhere0014
15Personal-data marks in the data model drive export, removal, deletion rules and the record of processingGDPR can't be forgotten by a new feature0015
16Full-text search inside the database (SQLite FTS5, PostgreSQL text search)Permission rules apply in the same SQL query; no second index to secure0016
17Background jobs in the databaseNo message broker to install; works on both databases0017
18One settings registry defines every setting once: storage, defaults, permissions, API and the settings dialogs"Everything configurable in the UI" without hand-building hundreds of forms0018

What we deliberately don't do

  • No microservices, no message broker, no separate search server, no cache server. Each would add installation steps and attack surface for a scale we don't need.
  • No plugins that run third-party code inside the server. Integrations use the API, webhooks and MCP.
  • No server-side rendering framework. The server serves a static app and a JSON API; this keeps the security boundary simple and the CSP strict.

Dependency rules (checked by cargo xtask check only ARCH-DEPS)

  1. bb-core, bb-searchlang and bb-markdown do no I/O and depend on no other Bugaboo crate except bb-core (markdown not even that; bb-searchlang does, for the rules of an Issue ID and of a short name, which are defined once in bb-core and which the server reads the same way; bb-core and bb-policy use bb-macros for derives at compile time only), so they compile to WebAssembly.
  2. bb-app knows ports (traits) only. It never imports bb-store, bb-files, bb-ai or bb-notify. Tests run use cases against in-memory fakes.
  3. Only bb-policy can create Authorized<T>. Its constructor is private to the crate.
  4. Only bb-api and bb-mcp speak HTTP. Only bb-server wires adapters to ports, and from M2 WP-06 on also the developer program bb-sample; the developer program bb-load-check (M3 WP-10) depends on bb-store to read the database of a load run, and wires no use case (cargo xtask check only ARCH-HTTP-EDGE).
  5. The browser app talks to the server only through @bugaboo/api-client (cargo xtask check only ARCH-WEB-API), and has no hand-written types for what the server sends (LINT-API-TYPES).
  6. A crate may name itself as a dev-dependency to switch on its own testing feature for its integration tests (bb-api does, for Options::for_tests); that is no edge between two crates (cargo xtask check only ARCH-DEPS). The same feature is on for every crate in a build of the whole workspace (cargo build --workspace), because cargo unifies the features that any member asks for; the shipped program is built with cargo build -p bb-server (cargo xtask build), which leaves the test hooks out.
  7. Only bb-sample may switch on the feature dataset of bb-store (the one write that only the large dataset needs, Transaction::set_issue_counter), in any kind of dependency; the program that ships and every test are built without it (cargo xtask check only ARCH-DEPS).

The core modules

bb-core

Newtype IDs (IssueId, ProjectId, …, all UUIDv7 inside, readable keys like WEB-142 outside), field types and values, domain entities, domain events, and the error code catalogue (one Rust enum; becomes OpenAPI, the TypeScript union and message keys). Entities carry personal-data marks (ADR-0015). It also holds the settings registry (ADR-0018: every setting is declared once, in settings/), the message keys generated from messages/en.json as Rust constants and functions (UX-07), and the entity list behind the generated personal-data page docs/privacy/personal-data.md. Its wording module chooses the words of a change and of a notification once (message keys and the words of values; the region-dependent writing of days, moments and numbers for e-mail), so the server and the browser (through bb-wasm) say the same (ADR-0033, amendment of M4 WP-13). The HTTP layer (bb-api) and the binary (bb-server) use bb-core directly for error codes and message text.

bb-policy

  • Permission catalogue (one Rust enum with plain-language descriptions as message keys) and the starting roles (one definition, used once to make editable copies and for Reset to the starting permissions), as ADR-0025 decides.
  • Evaluation: given an actor (and an access key's choice) and a place, computes the effective permission set, the field mask (hidden / can see / can change per field, per issue type later) and the Who sees people levels, from roles, groups and assignments on the project tree with No access (§7, Authorization model). No I/O: the assignments come in through a port of bb-app. Cached per request.
  • PersonRef: resolves every person shown for the viewer, the kind of people information and the place (ADR-0022). Check access: the decision with its reasons as data.
  • Visibility: project tree, issues (Evaluation::sees_issue: See issues, or an issue the person reported), restricted issues, documents.
  • Search predicates: turns the actor's visibility into query-builder expressions that bb-store adds to every query.
  • Authorized<T>: the only way data leaves the domain. It carries the field mask, so projections drop hidden fields automatically. A view is masked by #[derive(Masked)]: every member says whether it holds a field of the catalogue, a view inside the view or nothing hidden, so a hidden field of a nested view never leaves (SEC-04, M2-F21).

bb-searchlang

Lexer, parser, syntax tree, canonical printer, checker and suggestions. Knows nothing about databases or permissions: the caller passes the readable fields (the fields this person may read, not to be mixed up with the field catalogue of bb-core), so a hidden field fails exactly like an unknown one. Simple search (filter buttons) edits the same syntax tree. The final grammar, the limits and the canonical text are in §7, Search language. It depends on bb-core for the rules of an Issue ID and of a short name. The tree and the readable fields cross into the browser module as JSON, which the feature browser (only the module turns it on) reads with a reader that is written from the Rust types (cargo xtask gen search-reader): deriving Deserialize made the module bigger than its budget, and a reader written by hand would be a second definition of the tree. The test vectors (vectors.rs) are what the browser's unit tests run the module on.

bb-wasm and bb-wasm-search

Two modules, one way: each has its own crate (the bindings only pass calls through to the pure crates, they hold no rule), its own package in web/packages/ that loads it when its feature first opens, and its own budget in tools/checks/perf-bundle.toml (PERF-BUNDLE, by the name of the file without the hash). A list should not fetch the module of Markdown, nor an editor the search language. cargo xtask wasm builds both (the list MODULES in xtask/src/wasm.rs).

bb-app — use cases by feature

Built so far (M0 to M4): auth (signing in), people (people and groups), roles (roles and who has which role), access (field permissions, Who sees people, Check access, the starting roles), projects, settings, issues (issues, types, IDs, the trash), fields (own fields and their choices), relations (relations, sub-issues, kinds of relation), tags (tags, labels, groups of labels), comments (comments, mentions), follow, history (the history read from the events), editing (edit locks, drafts, the check of versions, the structured conflict), layouts (the issue page and the new-issue form), many_changes (changing many issues, with the run that goes on in the background), notifications (the reader of the outbox that tells people, their e-mail, handles and the confirming of an address; M4), jobs (the queue as the use cases see it, and what each kind of job does), first_start (what a new server makes before anyone signs in), workflows (the judge's inputs, the editor, Publish with its preview and the check that no issue is stranded; M4), offers (where issue types and groups of labels are offered, and what a person may know of them; M4), files (uploads in parts, attachments with the trash and Undo, signed downloads, previews and the daily clean-up; M4), preview, status. Planned: releases, search, boards, timeline, calendar, relation_map, time (timers, time entries, working hours, rules), documents, assistant, privacy, themes, admin.

search (M5 WP-04) holds what a person may ask a search about: readable_fields builds the fields the checker of bb-searchlang gets, once per request, from the field definitions, the levels of the person's roles and Who sees people. A field counts only when it is readable in every project the search looks at (SearchScope; a project the person does not see is resource.not-found), so a hidden field is as unknown as one that does not exist; a field that holds people (Field::person_kind, FieldType::people_kind) also needs the level Names. A word belongs to one field for everyone (ADR-0005 amendment M5, decision 9): the words of the catalogue (Field::search_word) and of the fields every issue has (IssueField) are reserved, and between own fields the first in their order keeps a word, decided before the rights of the person. Choices are names as shown, each once by the one rule of the same name (names::same_name, also in the checker): the issue types the person may know that reach a place the search looks at and the statuses of the workflows in force there (Ctx::workflows_reaching, which project_statuses uses too); the built-in lists (priority, status group) are English words of the language (search_word), not catalogue text. search, search_count and search_groups run a text: the fields first, then the text read and checked (every mistake is answered before anything else), then the names turned into what they stand for for this person (names.rs: statuses, types, choices, people and groups, each by the one rule of the same name), then the sight of the person limited to the same places the fields were judged for, and last the store port SearchStore, which bb-store implements with the compiler (bb-store/src/search): one statement with the sight first, the filter, the order with the ID last and the keyset after the last issue of the page before. A cursor holds nothing but the ID of that issue: the store reads its place in the order itself, so no title, name or value is ever written into a cursor (the API seals it for the person and the search). A row that points to an issue (a parent, an issue in an own field) counts only when the person reads that issue; the values of an own field count only in the projects it reaches. A group is named by identity (an ID or a word), and the use case shows a person as the viewer may see them. The one visibility predicate is bb-store/src/sight.rs. Counts and groups are made from the same condition. A search is stopped after 2 seconds (statement_timeout on PostgreSQL, a progress handler on SQLite) and answers search.too-slow; each person may run 60 a minute (Limits::check_search).

Every use case has the same shape:

pub async fn change_status(
    ctx: &Ctx,               // actor, request id, clock, ports
    cmd: ChangeStatus,       // validated input
) -> Result<Authorized<IssueView>, AppError>
  1. Ask bb-policy whether the actor may do it.
  2. Load, change and validate inside one transaction.
  3. Append domain events (same transaction). A command use case writes only through the ChangeStore port (record_change), which bb-store implements; a use case whose input type ends in Query only reads. Enforced by: ARCH-EVENTS.
  4. Return the result through Authorized<T>.

bb-store

sqlx connection pools, migrations (defined once with the query builder, run on both databases), repositories implementing bb-app ports, the search compiler (search/: the checked tree + the sight of the person → one statement; values are bound, names arrive resolved to IDs and keys, text is compared by its bytes with COLLATE "C" on PostgreSQL so both databases order alike, and the 2-second limit is statement_timeout on PostgreSQL and a progress handler on SQLite), full-text search adapters, the event log and outbox, the job queue tables, the security log (hash chain), stored secrets (envelope encryption) and setting values. It is the only crate that touches a database; it takes the time and the IDs from its caller and gets no clock of its own. Enforced by: ARCH-SQL-EDGE (no other crate may depend on a database library, and no SQL text is built with format!), DATA-MARKS (every table belongs to an entity with personal-data marks), ARCH-SETTINGS (setting values are read and written only in settings.rs).

bb-app also holds the real clock and secure random source (context::SystemClock, context::SystemIds), because bb-core does no I/O; bb-server passes them to the use cases and the store.

bb-testing

Test-support crate, used only as a dev dependency ([dev-dependencies]) and never shipped (ARCH-DEPS fails on any other kind of dependency on it). each_database runs one async test body against every database named in BB_TEST_DATABASES (sqlite, postgres; default sqlite), each with a brand-new empty database that is removed afterwards (also when the test panics), hands the body a typed pool (Pool::Sqlite or Pool::Postgres), and records what ran for ARCH-DB-PARITY. It depends on bb-dev-words only, which names the databases and the variables. How it is wired to cargo xtask db and cargo xtask ci is in testing.

bb-files

The file adapter (ADR-0032): it implements the port FileStore of bb-app and keeps the bytes in the files/ folder of the data folder. An upload is put together part by part; a finished file is stored once under the SHA-256 of its content (DiskFiles); the real type is read from the content (sniff), never from the name. A preview is made by the program itself, started as a child process (bugaboo preview) with an empty environment, the bytes on standard input, no path and limits on memory, pixels, input size and time (preview); a file that cannot be previewed just has none. The server never serves the folder: a file leaves only through a signed link that bb-app judges again at every use. A virus scan (ATT-05) and a second storage (S3-compatible, ATT-06) are not built; the port has room for both.

  • May depend on: bb-app (the port), bb-core. Nothing depends on it except bb-server, and bb-sample with its feature testing.
  • In the layout and the diagram: ARCH-MAP-SYNC and ARCH-DEPS read the repository layout and the module map above, which list the crate and its edges.

bb-notify

The delivery adapter for e-mail (NTF-02, ADR-0033): it implements the port Mailer of bb-app over SMTP with lettre. Every e-mail is plain text and nothing else (no HTML, no picture, no attachment), a subject is one line, and what the crate logs is a class of failure and never the answer of the mail server, which can repeat an address (DATA-LOGS). Webhooks are planned for the same crate and not built.

  • May depend on: bb-app (the port), bb-core. Nothing depends on it except bb-server.
  • In the layout and the diagram: ARCH-MAP-SYNC and ARCH-DEPS read the repository layout and the module map above, which list the crate and its edges.

bb-jobs

The loop that runs the background jobs (ADR-0017): a worker that, every two seconds, takes the jobs that are due and does them as long as there are some. It owns nothing else. The queue, the lease and the retries are the store's behind the port JobStore; which use case does the work of which kind of job, what is a permanent failure that goes to the dead-letter list at once, and what a job that died does to the work people can see (a change to many issues ends as failed) are bb-app's (Ctx::run_due_jobs, jobs.rs). The server starts the loop and stops it.

  • May depend on: bb-app. Nothing depends on it except bb-server.
  • In the layout and the diagram: ARCH-MAP-SYNC and ARCH-DEPS read the repository layout and the module map above, which list the crate and its edges.

bb-api

axum router; extractors that turn a session cookie, access key or OAuth token into an actor; CSRF and origin checks; security headers and CSP; rate limits (limits); the one cookie module (cookies); ?fields= projections; cursor pagination; ETags; problem+json errors (errors: ApiError, ApiJson); the one route table (permissions::ROUTES: what each route needs, whether its answer may be kept, is never stored or is a secret; it writes the marks x-permission, x-never-stored and x-secret, and it decides which changes are open without a CSRF token); OpenAPI generation from the handlers' #[utoipa::path] descriptions (openapi, served at /api/v1/openapi.json, printed by bugaboo openapi, written to web/packages/api-client/openapi.json by cargo xtask gen api); the embedded static app.

bb-api-words

The words of the API description that more than one program needs, written once: the marks bb-api puts on a route (x-permission, x-never-stored, x-secret, x-long-text), the words of a change that overwrites nothing unseen (version, lock_token, the schema of the conflict), the words of a paged list (fields, cursor, limit, include, items, next_cursor, truncated), the four words for a route that needs no single permission of the catalogue (public, signed-in, own-account, by-record), and the actor and answer names of the permission matrix (SEC-MATRIX). It has no dependencies and does no work, so bb-api (writes the words), the server tests (read them) and xtask (its checks read the generated description) can import it. The table that says which route gets which mark is bb-api's permissions::ROUTES.

bb-dev-words

The words that the developer tools, the tests and xtask share, written once: the databases Bugaboo runs on (DatabaseKind: sqlite, postgres) and the variables that tell the test harness what to do (BB_TEST_DATABASES, BB_TEST_POSTGRES_URL, BB_DB_PARITY_FILE), the passwords and the address of the sign-in tests (accounts), and the schema of tools/dev/sample.json (sample::Layout), which says where the sample organization is made and what its files, groups, projects and roles are called. It does no work and no input or output, and depends on bb-core (for the message catalogue), serde and serde_json only, so bb-testing, bb-sample, xtask and the tests of bb-app and bb-server can import it without pulling in the store or the use cases.

bb-ai and bb-mcp

One tool registry (search issues, get issue, create, change status, comment, log time, …). Each tool maps to a bb-app use case, so permissions and validation are identical. bb-mcp exposes the registry to outside AI apps; the assistant uses the same registry but returns proposals for writes instead of running them.

bb-sample

The sample-organization generator (architecture §11): a library and a small program that cargo xtask dataset sample runs as a process, so xtask does not link the store or the use cases (it imports only bb-api-words, bb-core, bb-dev-words and bb-policy, for the names its checks hold the code against). It makes the organization through the same use cases the API calls, deterministic from a seed, on SQLite and PostgreSQL. It is a developer tool: not linked into bugaboo until Try it out (OPS-12), and never shipped before then.

  • May depend on: bb-app, bb-store, bb-core, bb-policy, bb-auth, bb-dev-words, bb-searchlang (the dump of the sample data reads a whole project with the empty search, which only the sample program builds, so the app crate has no search without a person), and bb-files with its feature testing (M4 WP-10: the sample stores its files in the data folder and makes their previews in its own process; the program that would be the child of a preview is not this one), and bb-testing as a dev dependency only. Nothing depends on it except, from OPS-12 on, bb-server.
  • It wires an adapter: like bb-server, it builds the store and hands it to the use cases, so dependency rule 4 names it as the second crate that may wire adapters to ports; ARCH-HTTP-EDGE's list of wiring crates (bb-server, bb-sample, bb-load-check) is in xtask/src/checks/arch_http_edge.rs.
  • In the layout and the diagram: ARCH-MAP-SYNC and ARCH-DEPS read the repository layout and the module map above, which list the crate and its edges.

bb-load-check

The invariants after a run of many people at once (architecture §11, TEST-CONCURRENT), written once. Two things end in it: the invariants test of the server (test_concurrent_invariants_hold_after_a_run, on both databases, in memory) and cargo xtask load (the Node driver writes its book, a JSON file of what each person kept, was refused and read, and xtask runs the small program bb-load-check on that book and the database of the run). Both call the same function, check, which reads the database through bb-store and judges it against the book in judge.rs, the only file in the repository that says what must hold. It is a separate crate so that xtask does not link the store (it runs the program as a process, as it runs bb-sample), and so that bb-server can use it in its tests without the program depending on test code.

  • May depend on: bb-app (the name of the member of a comment event), bb-store, bb-core. bb-server uses it in [dev-dependencies] only; nothing else depends on it.
  • In the layout and the diagram: ARCH-MAP-SYNC and ARCH-DEPS read the repository layout and the module map above, which list the crate and its edges.

Browser app (web/app)

web/app/src/
├── routes/              TanStack Router routes in code (guest, signed-in and administrator
│                        layouts decide who may open what); URL search params are typed state
├── features/            shell (sidebar, top bar, phone bar, quick search, frames), sign-in, sign-up,
│                        invitation, setup, account (sign-in and security, where you're signed in),
│                        admin (invitations, status), home;
│                        M2: settings (the generic settings form), my-settings (appearance, region,
│                        start page, shortcuts, access keys), projects, people (people, groups),
│                        roles (roles and who has which role), access (field permissions,
│                        who sees people, check access);
│                        later: issues, search, board, timeline, calendar, relation-map,
│                        documents, time, dashboards, notifications, assistant
├── shared/              api client, session, errors, formatting (Intl), page title and focus,
│                        the shortcut registry, the helpers for instant changes
└── main.tsx
  • Server data lives only in the TanStack Query cache, fetched through the generated client, keyed by generated query keys.
  • Forms get their validation rules from the server's exported schema; the server still decides.
  • Components come from @bugaboo/ui, built on React Aria Components; a component carries no style and no class name: it puts data-part, data-variant and data-state on its elements (partOf) and the rules of design/theme.kdl do the rest, compiled into one static style sheet (ADR-0026). The content security policy allows no inline styles, so React Aria's one injected style element is replaced by a base rule of the theme file (the element is declared in index.html).
  • Who is signed in is read once with GET /api/v1/auth/me; a 401 anywhere (a session that ended, a wrong CSRF token) takes the person to the sign-in page with the reason in the address, and the guest layout does not send a signed-in person away while a reason is shown.
  • The frame (features/shell) lays out three sizes from the bp-* tokens: a sidebar on a computer (1280 px and wider), a menu that slides in on a tablet, a bottom bar and one screen at a time on a phone. places.ts is the one list of the screens that exist (menus, the trail at the top, quick search and the topics of the settings frames read it), so nothing is shown that does not exist. Other features add to the shell through registries (addSidebarSection for the project tree, addQuickSearchSource for search results). Which item is open lives in the address (typed search parameters), so it can be shared and Back closes it.
  • Shortcuts are defined once in shared/shortcuts.ts (ID, default keys, words, where they work, the visible button that does the same). One engine handles sequences such as g h and stays silent while a text field has the focus; a person's own keys come from one source: the server when somebody is signed in (stored as one validated value), this browser before sign-in.
  • Instant changes: useOptimisticMutation shows a change in the query cache at once, goes back with a plain message when the server refuses, and reports Saving…, Saved or Not saved yet; skeletons appear only after 0.3 s; Undo is on offer for 10 seconds. Undo is sent on the version that the person's own change made, so it is refused, not written over, when someone else changed the value since.
  • Appearance (the mode Match my device, Always light or Always dark, one light and one dark theme, spacing, text size, motion) is one AppearanceSource. The source is the person's settings on the server once the person is signed in (they follow the person to every browser and are gone from the browser after sign-out), and this device's choice before sign-in. The browser keeps one copy for the first frame, which sign-out removes. Region (time zone, date and number format, first day of the week) reads from the same answer, and shared/format.ts writes times and numbers by it.
  • One home for what several screens share (M2C): the choices and defaults of the settings and the page sizes of the lists are written by cargo xtask gen api from the Rust code (setting-keys.generated.ts, paging.generated.ts in @bugaboo/api-client) and read by the app, never typed again. Every list of pages goes through shared/paged.ts (usePaged, linesFrom, typed fields); the keys of the query cache are in shared/query-keys.ts and nowhere else, and the browser tests take the size of a part of an upload and of a megabyte from the generated files.generated.ts. Enforced by: ARCH-WEB-KEYS; the pages of a project (path, name, tab, permission, title) are the table in shared/project-pages.ts; a person shown by name is picked by namedPerson and named by shared/person.ts; what the browser keeps is read and written only through @bugaboo/ui storage.ts, whose storageKey lists every key. A search box with choices is the SearchPicker of @bugaboo/ui; a page that waits for one answer is a QueryGate (features/shell). The components of @bugaboo/ui take one prop that names a look (tone, look, from, kind, size; the words are in props.ts), not a flag per look. The browser tests reach the API through the typed client (e2e/support/api.ts), open pages by paths.ts, and take their windows from web/tooling/viewports.ts.
  • Rules the checks keep: feature folders are reached only through their index.ts and shared code and packages never import features or the app (ARCH-WEB-FEATURES); all text comes from the catalog (TXT-LITERAL); no color is written out (STY-TOKENS), no size or duration either (LINT-CSS), and no style, class name or CSS file of a component exists (THEME-ONLY); every address in paths.ts is opened by the accessibility suite in the four themes on a computer and a phone (TEST-A11Y).
  • Heavy features (timeline, relation map, document editor, workflow editor, theme editor, WebAssembly) are split into separate chunks and loaded when first opened.

Runtime

How the parts work together in the most important situations.

Reading an issue

sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant A as bb-api
  participant U as bb-app
  participant P as bb-policy
  participant S as bb-store
  B->>A: GET /api/v1/issues/WEB-142?fields=title,status,priority
  A->>A: session → actor (or 404-style error)
  A->>U: get_issue(actor, WEB-142, fields)
  U->>P: may actor view WEB-142?
  P-->>U: yes + field mask
  U->>S: load issue (only requested ∩ visible fields)
  S-->>U: row
  U-->>A: Authorized<IssueView>
  A-->>B: 200 JSON + ETag (hidden fields never serialized)

If the actor may not see the issue, the answer is the same "not found" as for an issue that doesn't exist (SEC-MATRIX).

Searching

sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser (Simple or Advanced search)
  participant A as bb-api
  participant Q as bb-searchlang
  participant P as bb-policy
  participant S as bb-store
  B->>A: search text or syntax tree
  A->>P: readable fields of the actor
  A->>Q: parse + check against catalogue
  Q-->>A: syntax tree, or "There is no field called …"
  A->>P: visibility predicates (projects, restricted issues)
  A->>S: compile tree + predicates → one SQL query
  S-->>A: page of rows + next cursor
  A-->>B: rows (only requested ∩ visible fields)
  • Sorting, grouping and totals are only allowed on readable fields.
  • Every query has a time limit, a page-size cap and a complexity limit.
  • The browser runs the same parser (WebAssembly) for instant feedback; the server's answer is the one that counts.

Changing something

sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant A as bb-api
  participant U as bb-app
  participant P as bb-policy
  participant S as bb-store
  participant O as Outbox consumers
  B->>A: POST change status (version in the body)
  A->>U: change_status(actor, cmd)
  U->>P: may actor make this status change? (who can do it, only if …)
  U->>S: BEGIN · check version · apply · "must be filled in" rules
  U->>S: append domain event (+ outbox row) · COMMIT
  U-->>A: Authorized<IssueView>
  A-->>B: 200 (or 409 "Ben changed this a moment ago")
  S-->>O: outbox → history, notifications, webhooks, security log, search index, live updates
  • Optimistic locking: every entity has a version, and every change sends the version it read in its body (version, ARCH-VERSIONED). A stale version gives the plain-language conflict message and, with it, who changed the record, when, which fields and the values now (ADR-0019 amendment M3); the browser writes the sentence from them.
  • "Then automatically …" actions run as part of the same use case, as the same actor.
  • Consumers filter by the receiver's permissions before sending anything (e-mail, webhook, live update).

The assistant proposes, the person decides

sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant U as bb-app assistant
  participant C as Context builder
  participant L as AI provider
  B->>U: "Summarize WEB-142"
  U->>C: collect context as the actor
  C->>C: drop hidden fields and fields excluded from AI · fence untrusted text
  U->>L: prompt + tool list (read tools run, write tools return proposals)
  L-->>U: answer + proposed change (priority → Critical)
  U-->>B: answer (labelled AI) + proposal card
  B->>U: Apply
  U->>U: normal change_status / update path as the actor, marked "via assistant"

Outside AI apps (MCP) use the same tools through bb-mcp. Their token is the actor's identity narrowed by its scopes; write tools act directly only if the person granted write scope.

Editing long text (edit locks, ADR-0019)

sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Ana's browser
  participant S as Server
  participant B as Ben's browser
  A->>S: first keystroke in Description → take lock (POST /edit-locks)
  S-->>A: lock token (60 s lease)
  loop every 15 s while editing
    A->>S: heartbeat (renews lease) + private draft; the answer carries the notes of others
  end
  B->>S: open WEB-142
  S-->>B: "Ana is editing the description" (read-only for Ben)
  A->>S: save (text + lock token + base version)
  S-->>A: saved, new version → "Saved"
  S-->>S: lock released
  Note over A,S: If heartbeats stop (tab closed, network lost), the lease runs out and the lock frees itself.<br/>A save with an expired or taken-over token is refused; Ana's text stays as her draft with "Compare and save".
  • Short values use only the version check (no lock).
  • One mechanism for any record: a lock and a draft are about one part of a record named by its kind and ID (EntityRef), so issues, comments and documents use the same routes (/edit-locks, /drafts). A kind of record says where it sits, which version it has and what a person needs to change it by implementing EditableRecords; the kinds bb-app keeps itself (project, issue, comment, layout, field, label, tag, …) are built in, and a program adds none of them: EditableRecords is for the kinds a later package brings. The lease and the heartbeat are the state of an open editor and write no domain event; Edit anyway, Ask … to finish and an administrator's release are facts others can learn from, so they are commands with an event, and the release is also in the security log. Expired lock rows are deleted when the next lock is taken; a draft is kept 30 days after its last change and deleted by the job editing.purge-drafts (and ignored when older). Enforced by: TEST-EDIT-LOCKS.
  • Notes at the next heartbeat: Ask … to finish and Edit anyway leave a note for the person who was editing; the heartbeat hands it over once. The heartbeat keeps the text so far as the person's draft also when the lock is gone, and a refused save keeps its text as the draft: nothing typed is dropped. Enforced by: TEST-EDIT-LOCKS.
  • Saving long text goes through Ctx::save_text: inside the change that writes the record it checks the lock token, runs the write (which checks the version) and lets go of the lock and the draft; a refusal is edit.lock-lost, edit.taken-over or the structured edit.version-changed. Enforced by: ARCH-VERSIONED, TEST-EDIT-LOCKS.
  • Confirmed saves: the browser shows changes at once as Saving…, then Saved when the server confirms, or a plain explanation (conflict, lock lost, offline) that keeps the person's text.
  • Checking versions: every 30 s and on focus, the browser asks (POST /versions/check, up to 50 records) for the current versions of what's on screen; a newer version by someone else shows "Ben changed this after you".

Working hours

  1. Start work day creates a work-day record for today (person, start time, time zone).
  2. Breaks and the end are added the same way, or typed in later.
  3. The working-time rules of the organization's preset are checked after every change. Broken rules become warnings stored with the day; nothing is blocked.
  4. Changing a day in the past requires a reason. The event log keeps the old value; the person is notified if someone else changed it.
  5. A daily job deletes work days older than the keep-and-delete rule allows.

Removing a person (GDPR)

  1. An admin chooses Remove a person. bb-app::privacy builds a plan from the personal-data marks: what will be deleted now, what will be anonymized, what must be kept by law and until when (DATA-MARKS; legal keep periods: review (compliance.md lists them)).
  2. The admin confirms. A background job runs the plan in steps; each step is idempotent and logged.
  3. The person's name becomes Former user K7Q2 everywhere (a tombstone record replaces the user). Records under a legal hold are deleted by the normal deletion schedule.

Live updates (built last)

The outbox feeds a small in-memory hub. Each open browser tab holds one Server-Sent Events connection and subscribes to what is on screen. Every event is checked against the subscriber's permissions, then sent as a small "this changed" note; the browser refetches only what it shows.

Deployment

The same binary runs in both models (DIST-01).

Sold: the customer runs it (self-hosted)

flowchart LR
  subgraph host["Customer's server — Windows, Linux or WSL"]
    bin["bugaboo<br/>(Windows service or systemd)"]
    subgraph data["Data folder"]
      db[("bugaboo.db<br/>SQLite")]
      fl[("files/")]
      key["keys/master.key"]
      bk[("backups/")]
      cfg["bugaboo.toml<br/>(start-up settings only)"]
    end
  end
  pg[("PostgreSQL<br/>(optional)")]
  s3[("S3-compatible storage<br/>(optional)")]
  users(["People"]) -- HTTPS --> bin
  bin --> data
  bin -.-> pg
  bin -.-> s3
  • Install: download, bugaboo setup (data folder, port, HTTPS), bugaboo service install, then the browser setup with the setup code. User pages: userDocs/install/.
  • Start-up settings (address, port, data folder, certificates, database URL) live in bugaboo.toml or environment variables. Everything else is in the database and changed in the UI.
  • HTTPS (SEC-10): built-in TLS (rustls with the ring provider) with a generated certificate, a provided certificate, or ACME (V1). Plain HTTP is allowed only on this computer (127.0.0.1, ::1) or behind explicitly named proxies. Enforced by: the start-up settings check (tests sec_10_… in crates/bb-server) and SEC-HEADERS for HSTS.
  • Master key: generated on first start, stored outside the database, readable only by the service account. It encrypts stored secrets and backups.
  • Upgrades: replace the binary; on start, Bugaboo makes a backup, then runs migrations. If a migration fails, it restores the backup and stops with a plain explanation of how to go back to the previous version.
  • Also offered: container image (non-root, read-only file system except the data volume), winget/MSI, .deb/.rpm.

Start-up settings (OPS-10)

Read when the server starts, strongest first: command line, environment variable, bugaboo.toml, built-in default. Each setting has the same name everywhere; its variable is BUGABOO_ plus the name in capitals. Wrong values stop the start with a plain sentence (messages config.*).

SettingMeaningDefault
addressIP address to listen on127.0.0.1
portPort to listen onnone; the start stops without one (ADR-0023)
data_dirThe data folderbugaboo-data next to the program
database_urlsqlite:… or postgres://…; empty means the built-in SQLite file in the data folderempty
tls_modeself-signed, files or offself-signed
tls_cert, tls_keyCertificate chain and private key (PEM), with tls_mode = "files"none
tls_namesExtra host names or addresses for the generated certificatenone
trusted_proxiesAddresses of proxies that add HTTPS; with tls_mode = "off" only they may connectnone
log_levelerror, warn, info or debuginfo
max_connectionsMost connections open at once1024
header_timeout_secondsTime allowed for a client to send the headers of a request30
rate_limit_per_minuteAPI requests one client network may make per minute600
sign_in_attempts_per_minuteSign-in attempts per minute, for one client network and for one account10
access_key_requests_per_minuteRequests per minute that come with one access key300
searches_per_minuteSearches per person and minute, with a session or a key (SEC-17)60
mail_batch_secondsSeconds that changes to one issue wait for each other before one e-mail goes, at least 1 and at most 86400 (one day, refused at start-up beyond that); a short time is for tests and demos300

tls_mode = "off" on an address that is not this computer is refused unless trusted_proxies is set. The settings file can be named with --config or BUGABOO_CONFIG; without a name bugaboo.toml next to the program is read if it exists. Defaults are relative to the program's folder, not the current folder (a Windows service starts in System32); relative paths inside the file are relative to the file. With tls_mode = "files" on Linux, a key file that group or others can read is reported as a warning. A --database-url with a password in it (bugaboo setup and the commands that look after the stored data take the option; serve has none) prints a warning, because other people on the computer can read the command line. The warning of the stored-data commands names the settings file and the variable BUGABOO_DATABASE_URL as the safe places; the warning of setup, which saves the address in the settings file, says so and says to answer the setup question or use the variable next time. Neither repeats the address. A password with an unencoded / or # is not recognised (M2 follow-up). Enforced by: review (the tests ops_10_… and sec_10_… in crates/bb-server cover it; no catalogue check yet).

Commands (OPS-03)

CommandWhat it does
bugaboo serveRuns the server. The setup code of a fresh installation is printed to the console, or written to setup-code.txt in the data folder when the output is not a terminal.
bugaboo preview <image or pdf>Not for people: the server starts it as a child process to make the preview of one file (ADR-0032). The file comes on the standard input, the preview leaves on the standard output as a PNG, and the exit code says why there is none. The child limits its own memory before it reads a byte, gets an empty environment and the folder files/previews/work/ as its working folder. It is hidden from the help.
bugaboo setupAsks for the data folder, address, port (suggestion 8443, checked to be free), HTTPS, public address and database, checks the answers with the same code that reads the settings at start, and writes bugaboo.toml. --non-interactive asks nothing; --overwrite replaces an existing file.
bugaboo service install / uninstallWindows: a service named Bugaboo that runs as the virtual account NT SERVICE\Bugaboo (no password), started with the computer, stopping on the service manager's stop and shutdown messages. Linux (systemd, also WSL 2 with systemd): the user bugaboo (no password, no shell, no home folder), bugaboo.service in the folder for units that an administrator installs, as systemd names it (systemd-path systemd-system-conf, else pkg-config; the folder and the nologin shell are used only when root owns them alone and nobody else can write to them), that runs serve --config <the settings file in place>; the settings file keeps its place and becomes root:bugaboo, mode 640; the unit may write only to the data folder. Installing takes over only what Bugaboo made (the data folder itself, its known files and its own sub-folders, never chown -R over the folder as a whole; every chown uses -h, and -R uses -P, so a link is changed itself and never what it points to; a link is no known file, and a link in place of a sub-folder refuses the install) and refuses a folder that is not empty and holds none of what only Bugaboo makes (keys/master.key, the built-in database, or a layout of all its sub-folders, all empty), on Windows too. One more folder is taken over, but only with the flag --take-over-data-folder: a folder whose only content is the person's own files in tls/ (a certificate put there before the first start; the other sub-folders may be there but empty; no folder or link inside tls/, on Linux no file with more than one name; an entry that cannot be read refuses the folder). The refusal of such a folder names the flag; any other content is refused with or without it (follow-up M1-F66, test ops_03_a_data_folder_with_own_certificates_is_taken_over_only_with_the_flag). On Linux the settings file is refused when it is a link, when it lies inside the data folder (both are compared by their real paths, so .. and links do not hide it), or when the folder that holds it does not belong to root or can be changed by the group or by everybody. A data folder that is a link is planned and written into the unit with its real path (chown -h would change the link and not the folder), and the install says so. Both need administrator rights and keep the data when removed. The steps of the Linux install are a list that is built first and run second, so tests check it without root.
bugaboo security-log verifyChecks the security log chain, the checkpoint and the anchor file, and prints the head (place and hash). A log with entries and no anchor is reported as a warning. An anchor file that reaches further than the database (the database lacks the newest entries) is reported as an error that says what to check: a restore from an older backup, or lost writes.
bugaboo rotate-keyMakes a new master key and re-encrypts the stored secrets with it.
bugaboo keys export <folder>Copies the key files to a folder that only its owner can open (Linux: others who can open it make the command refuse). Each copy is made in a folder of its own (a new folder under a random name, never one that existed) that only the account can enter, made private itself (mode 0600, or on Windows an access list for the owner and the administrators), filled, and then moved into place without replacing anything (a hard link, which fails when the copy exists; on a drive without hard links, such as a FAT32 or exFAT stick or some network drives, the copy is made new in the target instead, which fails the same way, and on such a drive there is no access list to keep); a copy that exists is never replaced, a write that fails leaves nothing behind, and a run that meets an old copy removes what it made.

security-log verify, rotate-key and keys export refuse to run, with the command to use instead, when the account that runs them is not the owner of the data folder (Linux, found from the owner of /proc/self) or cannot read and change the files in keys/: a run from the wrong account would leave files that the service cannot read. On Windows the account of a service has no password, so there is no tested way yet to start the command as it (follow-up M1-F57).

The service installers are covered by tests of the plan and the texts only: starting a real service needs administrator rights and a service manager that the test machines do not give (follow-up M1-F57).

Data folder

bugaboo.db   the built-in database (made by the store)
files/       attachments: uploads/ (files on their way), content/ (finished files, by the SHA-256 of the content), previews/ (the small pictures; previews/work/ is the working folder of the preview child)
keys/        the master key and other secrets
backups/     backups
tls/         the generated certificate and its key
setup-code.txt   the setup code of a server without a console (dead once an account exists; deleted by the change that makes the first administrator, and again at the next start)

Folders that Bugaboo creates are readable by their owner only: mode 0700 on Linux, and on Windows an access list that grants only the account running Bugaboo. Key and certificate files are written with mode 0600 on Linux. keys/ and tls/ are checked on every start and made private again if someone loosened them (Windows: the access list is reset to the running account, found by its SID, not its name). Certificate and key are written as new files and renamed into place (key first, certificate second), and a key that does not belong to the certificate is replaced. A self-signed certificate is valid for one year and renewed when less than 30 days are left at start-up, or when tls_names changes. While the server runs (follow-up M1-F03) a timer looks at the certificate every hour: a generated certificate with under 30 days left is renewed, and an own certificate (tls_mode = "files") is read again and used when its files hold another one. The new certificate is swapped into the settings of the listener, so connections that start from then on get it and nothing restarts; open connections keep the one they started with. Files that cannot be used (half a copy, a key of another certificate) are reported in the log and the old certificate keeps serving until the next look. The status page shows the end of the certificate it serves now. The rest of an existing folder is only looked at (follow-up M1-F65): at every start Bugaboo checks the data folder itself, the database file (and the files SQLite keeps next to it), files/, backups/ and the setup code file, and reports what other accounts on this computer can open, in the log and on the console, and the status page shows it with the same words. Too open means: on Linux a group or world permission bit is set; on Windows the access list gives something to everybody, to all users or to all signed-in accounts. A part whose rights cannot be read (the system tool fails or its answer cannot be understood) is reported as unknown, never as private. The status page looks on a thread of its own and keeps the answer for a minute. A folder that a person made or moved keeps its rights, because making it private could lock out the account that backs it up (the backup command is OPS-06, M9). The built-in database file is made with mode 0600 before SQLite opens it, so a default install reports nothing. Enforced by: tests sec_16_… and sec_10_… (sec_10_a_certificate_near_its_end_is_renewed_without_a_restart with a clock that is moved on, sec_10_an_own_certificate_that_changed_is_served_after_the_next_look, ops_08_the_status_shows_the_end_of_the_certificate_it_serves_now; sec_16_a_too_open_data_folder_is_reported_at_start and its Windows form, sec_16_the_status_page_shows_what_of_the_data_folder_is_too_open).

One file per system (OPS-01, DIST-01)

cargo xtask build builds the browser app and then the release program with the browser app inside (rust-embed); --target builds for another system. Windows x64 is built on the development PC. Static Linux programs (x86_64-unknown-linux-musl, aarch64-unknown-linux-musl) are built by cargo xtask ci on Linux machines, which the CI workflow runs once the repository is on GitHub. Windows ARM64 waits for the MSVC ARM64 tools (follow-up M1-F01). The program has no edition or model switch: differences between self-hosted and hosted come from the settings above only.

Served: we run it (hosted by Bugaboo)

flowchart TB
  subgraph eu["EU data centre"]
    cp["Control plane<br/>set-up · updates · backups · health<br/>(no customer data)"]
    subgraph c1["Customer A — isolated"]
      a1["bugaboo instance"]
      adb[("database A")]
      afl[("files A<br/>own key")]
    end
    subgraph c2["Customer B — isolated"]
      b1["bugaboo instance"]
      bdb[("database B")]
      bfl[("files B<br/>own key")]
    end
    edge["HTTPS entry<br/>a.bugaboo.example · b.bugaboo.example"]
  end
  edge --> a1 & b1
  a1 --> adb & afl
  b1 --> bdb & bfl
  cp -- "operator API<br/>(no data access)" --> a1 & b1
  • One isolated instance per customer: own process/container, own PostgreSQL database, own file bucket with its own encryption key, own web address. No database or file store is shared between customers (DIST-02).
  • Control plane is a separate service: it creates instances, rolls out updates, runs and checks backups, and watches health. It has an operator API on each instance that can do maintenance but cannot read customer data.
  • Emergency access (DIST-03): an operator requests access; the customer's administrator approves in their own Bugaboo; access is time-limited and every action appears in the customer's security log.
  • Data location: EU only; the sub-processor list and data-location statement come from the control plane's configuration (DIST-05).
  • Switching: a customer can export everything and import it into a self-hosted installation, and the other way round (DIST-06).

Releases

flowchart LR
  src["Tagged commit"] --> ci["CI: cargo xtask check all"]
  ci --> build["Build matrix<br/>windows-x64 · windows-arm64<br/>linux-x64-musl · linux-arm64-musl"]
  build --> sbom["SBOM (CycloneDX + SPDX)<br/>third-party notices"]
  sbom --> sign["Sign binaries, SBOM, checksums"]
  sign --> pub["Publish: release page,<br/>update feed, technical file"]
  • Every release has: binaries, checksums, signatures, SBOM, third-party notices, release notes, known issues, and its support period (COMP).
  • Security fixes can ship as patch releases on supported versions.
  • The served model receives the same signed release; the control plane verifies the signature before rollout.

Cross-cutting concepts

Security

Sign-in and sessions

  • Passwords: Argon2id (OWASP parameters: 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, 1 lane), checked against a bundled list of breached passwords (a plain sorted list searched on this computer, so no network call is made; it is not a k-anonymity range file, M1-F48). A wrong password and an unknown e-mail get the same answer and the same timing.
  • Passkeys: WebAuthn (webauthn-rs), as a second step or on their own. Two-step codes: TOTP with backup codes (stored hashed).
  • Company sign-in: OIDC with PKCE; group claims map to Bugaboo groups.
  • Sessions: random 256-bit secrets, stored as a hash (SHA-256 with its own domain, so the hash of a session secret is never taken for one of an invitation); cookie __Host-bb_session (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax) that lives as long as a session may (the setting security.session-absolute-hours, default 24 hours). A session is pending after the password when the person has a second step (it can do nothing but finish it, for at most five minutes) and active after. A person who needs a second step and has none (the organization asks it of everybody with security.two-step-required, or any role they hold anywhere, through their own rows or a group's, has the switch of ADR-0025, decision 7) can only set one up: the question is asked at every request, so it counts from the next request, also in a session that was open before; every use case that is not part of setting up a code app or a passkey answers auth.second-step-required (403), GET /auth/me answers that the setup is required with no permission, and the next request after the code app is confirmed or the passkey is added is an ordinary one. Enforced by: the tests auth_03_* in crates/bb-server/src/tests/sign_in/second_step_by_role.rs and bb-store. A 401 for a session that has ended (the cookie belongs to no session, or it ran out) also makes the browser forget both cookies and what it cached (Clear-Site-Data: "cache", M2-F06); a session that is only waiting for its second step is not ended and is left alone. Enforced by: the tests m2_f06_* in crates/bb-server/src/tests/sign_in/session_ended.rs. A new secret is made at sign-in, when the second step is done, and when the password is changed (which also ends all other sessions), so a secret that was known earlier opens nothing. A session ends after the idle time (security.session-idle-minutes, default 30) or the absolute time; a session is marked as used at most once a minute; sessions nobody can use are removed inside every sign-in. Signing in from a browser that still has the cookie of an old session ends that old session, and a password alone shows nothing about the person (no name, address or administrator flag) until the second step is done. The two times are bounded settings (idle 5 minutes to 24 hours, absolute 1 hour to 30 days): a value outside is refused when it is stored and cut to the bounds when it is read. Where you're signed in lists the sessions (browser and system names, never the User-Agent text, and the shortened network) and ends any of them or all of them. The list holds at most 50 sessions and says when it was cut (truncated). Enforced by: the tests sec_12_* in crates/bb-server/src/tests/sign_in/sessions.rs (sign-out, list, end, end everywhere, idle and absolute timeouts, new secrets, password change, the old session of the browser), perf_02_the_list_of_sessions_has_a_cap_and_says_when_it_cut, sec_12_a_password_alone_shows_nothing_about_the_person_until_the_second_step_is_done, auth_01_the_session_times_have_bounds_and_values_are_cut_to_them in bb-core, and sec_12_only_sessions_nobody_can_use_are_purged in bb-store.
  • How signing in is built: the mechanisms (passwords, tokens, CSRF token, TOTP, passkeys) are in bb-auth and do no I/O. The use cases are async fns in bb-app::auth; each takes the context Ctx (store, clock, hasher, passkeys, CSRF key, limit on failed tries, client network and browser) and an input type, depends on storage only through the port AuthStore (which is made of ports by job: accounts, sessions, the second step, invitations and access keys, next to the policy, project and settings ports; a read that is also needed inside a change is written once, queries!), and writes only through ChangeStore::record_change, so every change comes with its event and is undone together with it. A check inside a change (a code used twice, an invitation taken first) stops the change with AuthStore::aborted, which rolls back everything including the event. Adding a way to sign in (the code app, a passkey) asks for the password again, so a stolen session cannot add one. Waiting passkey challenges have a pool for each kind of ceremony (adding, second step, anonymous sign-in) and a cap for each network, so anonymous sign-in starts cannot keep the second step or an addition from starting. AuthApi lists the use cases once, with the store erased, so bb-api holds Arc<dyn AuthApi> and never names an adapter. bb-store implements the port (AuthStorage; tables from migration 2, every column with its personal-data mark), bb-api has the routes below /api/v1/auth (src/api/auth*.rs), and bb-server/src/wiring.rs builds it all at start. Enforced by: ARCH-DEPS, ARCH-EVENTS, ARCH-HTTP-EDGE, DATA-MARKS, and the flow tests in crates/bb-server/src/tests/sign_in/, which run every flow on both databases.
  • Setting up the first administrator (AUTH-09): at every start the server makes a new setup code when no administrator exists and prints it to the console only (never to the log file); only its hash is stored, and a new start replaces it. The code works once: it is used up in the same change that makes the administrator, setup is closed for good afterwards, and wrong codes count against the limit on failed tries. Enforced by: the tests auth_09_* in crates/bb-server/src/tests/sign_in/setup_and_password.rs.
  • The public address: the start-up setting public_url is the origin people type in the browser. Passkeys are tied to its host name; a server that listens on this computer only uses localhost and its port when the setting is missing, any other address needs the setting, a server behind trusted proxies needs it too (people reach it through the address of the proxy), and an address without a host name (an IP address) turns passkeys off. Enforced by: the tests auth_02_* in crates/bb-server/src/config.rs and auth_02_without_a_host_name_in_the_public_address_passkeys_are_off.
  • CSRF: three layers. (1) SameSite cookies. (2) An origin check, already in the API: every request below /api that is not GET, HEAD or OPTIONS must carry an Origin equal to the server's own origin or, when the browser sent no Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin. The own origin is the scheme plus the authority the browser asked for: the authority of the request address when there is one (HTTP/2 has no Host header), else Host; the scheme is https when the connection is TLS or when a trusted proxy says so (X-Forwarded-Proto, same trust rule as the client address: only from a listed proxy, only the last entry), else http; with neither the request is refused (fail closed) with the error request.wrong-origin (403, problem+json). Enforced by: the tests sec_06_* in crates/bb-api (cross-site, null, missing headers, same-origin, scheme, authority without Host) and the TLS + HTTP/2 test sec_06_over_tls_and_http2_the_origin_check_uses_the_authority_and_the_scheme. (3) A session-bound token: the value is derived on the server from the session (an HMAC of the session ID with a CSRF key), delivered in the page-readable cookie __Host-bb_csrf at sign-in and renewed with every new session ID; the server compares the x-csrf-token header with the value derived for the request's session in constant time, and refuses unsafe methods without a valid token with problem+json. The generated client reads the cookie and sends the header on every change. Layer 3 is the middleware csrf_check in crates/bb-api/src/api/auth.rs and covers every change below /api (a route added later is protected without anyone remembering): a change without a session cookie is answered with auth.not-signed-in (401), one with a session cookie and without the right token with request.wrong-token (403). Only the routes of people who have no session yet are left out: the routes that are public and change something in the route table permissions::ROUTES (setup, sign-in, sign-up, passkey sign-in, the invitation link; permissions::csrf_exempt reads them from the table, so there is no second list); they carry no secret a forged request could use and the origin check protects them. A request that comes with an access key (Authorization: Bearer bb_...) and no session cookie is left out of layers 2 and 3 as well: it has no cookie for a forged request to ride on, and a page of another website cannot send that header (there is no CORS; sec_06_a_page_of_another_website_cannot_send_a_key); with a session cookie a request is judged as a browser's, key or not. Enforced by: SEC-COOKIES (the cookie table) and the tests sec_12_a_change_needs_the_token_of_its_own_session, sec_12_every_route_that_changes_something_checks_the_token_except_signing_in_and_up (goes through every route of the API description) and sec_12_every_session_has_its_own_secret_and_its_own_csrf_token, and the TLS + HTTP/2 test sec_12_over_tls_and_http2_a_person_sets_up_signs_out_and_signs_in_again.
  • Cookies: only strictly necessary ones (the session and the CSRF token), so no consent banner is needed (COMP-13, PRIV-01). One module, crates/bb-api/src/cookies.rs, holds the table and is the only code that sets a cookie. Every name starts with __Host-, so browsers insist on Secure, Path=/ and no Domain; the module adds HttpOnly where script has no business reading the cookie. cargo xtask gen api writes the list "Cookies we use" to userDocs/cookies.md from the same table. Enforced by: SEC-COOKIES (reads the table; finds Set-Cookie, cookie libraries and document.cookie writes anywhere else).
  • Access keys (scripts, apps; AUTH-07): bb_ + a public prefix of 8 symbols + _ + a 256-bit secret in 52 symbols of the alphabet of codes (bb-auth, access_key.rs); only the hash of the secret is stored (SHA-256 in its own domain, found by the hash, so an unknown key and a wrong secret are the same lookup); the key is shown once, in an answer marked as a secret (never stored, never compressed). Making a key asks for the password again (a stolen session cannot make a key that outlives it); every key runs out (90 days unless the person picks another date, never later than the organization's longest time: the settings auth.access-key-default-days and auth.access-key-longest-days, at most 365; a key ends at a moment, so the form shows the region day of now plus the default, the latest day is the region day of now plus the longest time, a picked day is sent as the end of that day or the longest time from now if that comes first, and the server cuts a moment at most five minutes past the longest time to it and refuses a later one with request.invalid: expiry in access_keys.rs, expiry-day.ts in the form); the last use is kept to the minute. A script sends Authorization: Bearer bb_…; the use case takes the key where it takes a session (Ctx::actor), and the actor is the owner with the key's narrowing: at every request the owner's evaluation is narrowed by the key's choice and projects (Ctx::evaluation_of, which Ctx::require uses), so a key never holds more than its owner and follows the owner losing a role at once. An expired, a deleted, an unknown and a malformed key get the same answer (auth.not-signed-in); guessing is limited per network like failed passwords: the key is looked up first and only a lookup that fails reserves a try of the network (reserve_network), so a key that works never touches the counter and is never turned away by it, while a guess from a network over its limit is answered with 429. A key follows its owner's two-step requirement: while the owner is asked for a second step it is refused with auth.second-step-required (M2-F46). A key is judged before the body or the address of the request is read on the routes of the person's own sign-in data (require_session), so a key gets the same answer whatever it sent; the public prefix of a key as presented has to be the stored one, a clash of two public prefixes is retried once with a new secret, and a key that was used this minute writes nothing. A key that keeps See status reads GET /api/v1/admin/status (see_server_status, through the actor path; /auth/me stays session only). No key holds a permission of NOT_FOR_KEYS (Invite people, Manage people, Manage groups, Manage roles, Decide who has which role, Decide what roles see, Change organization settings, and since M3 and M4 Take over text someone else is editing (Edit anyway), Manage issue types, kinds of relation and layouts, Create, change and retire fields, Manage labels and tags and Manage workflows; twelve in all, as in the list in the code): narrowing removes them whatever the choice, so inviting people, changing roles, changing the settings of the organization, taking over editing and changing how issues are described stay in the app (every use case that judges a permission goes through the actor, so the settings of WP-07 are covered as soon as they evaluate through it) (bb-policy, catalogue.rs, owner decision of 2026-10-06). Sign out everywhere deletes the person's keys (each one logged); a password change leaves them. No key reaches the owner's own sign-in data (password, second step, passkeys, sessions, keys): those use cases start at Ctx::active/Ctx::session, which turn a key away with auth.access-key-not-allowed and write it into the security log, so a route cannot forget it. A request that comes with a key and no session cookie needs no Origin and no CSRF token (there is no cookie for a forged request to ride on, and a page of another website cannot send the header: no CORS), is counted against the key as well as the network (access_key_requests_per_minute, default 300, per key), and its changes are recorded with the channel API. Making a key, deleting a key and a key that is turned away are in the security log (access_key.created, access_key.deleted, access_key.refused: the person and the key by ID; a refused key names nobody and shows the shortened network only, never the secret or the prefix). The routes of a person's own keys are /api/v1/access-keys (list, make, delete), /access-keys/rules (the default and the longest time, the single permissions with their topics) and /access-keys/project-choices (the projects the person may know, by short name, a page at a time); they declare own-account and take a session only. The form of My settings › Access keys (web/app/src/features/my-settings/access-keys) is made from them, and a person whose session must set up a second step is taken to the screen Set up your second step (features/sign-in). Enforced by: the tests auth_07_*, sec_14_* and sec_15_* in crates/bb-server/src/tests/sign_in/access_keys.rs and access_keys_http.rs, the Playwright tests auth_07_* and auth_03_* (web/app/e2e/access-keys.spec.ts, second-step-required.spec.ts, and the accessibility suite), the property test auth_07_a_key_can_do_only_what_its_owner_can_and_its_scopes_allow in bb-app, and SEC-SECRETS (the rule bugaboo-access-key of .gitleaks.toml).
  • MCP: OAuth 2.1 authorization server inside Bugaboo (authorization code + PKCE, dynamic client registration with an admin allow list), short-lived access tokens, refresh token rotation, consent screen per app.

Browser protections

  • Content Security Policy: default-src 'self'; scripts and styles only from our own origin, no inline code, no eval (only 'wasm-unsafe-eval', which lets the browser start the WebAssembly module of the Markdown preview, ADR-0011); frame-ancestors 'none'; require-trusted-types-for 'script' with the one policy bugaboo-markdown, the only place that sets HTML from a string (SEC-RICHTEXT); images from our origin and data: only (outside images only if an admin allows the host).
  • Other headers: HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, COOP/CORP, a tight Permissions-Policy, Referrer-Policy: same-origin.
  • One header layer wraps the whole router, so pages, files, API answers, errors and 404s carry the same set. Enforced by: SEC-HEADERS (the check holds the one header table in headers.rs against the requirement: every required header is set, the policy lets no injected or foreign code run) and the integration tests, which read the table and assert the full set on a page, an asset, an API error and a 404.
  • HSTS is sent only when browsers reach us over HTTPS (here, or at a trusted proxy), and never with includeSubDomains (Bugaboo does not own the other names of its host). Lifetime: one day with a certificate Bugaboo made itself, so a person who trusts that certificate on localhost does not pin every other local tool to HTTPS; one year with a provided certificate or behind a trusted proxy. Enforced by: SEC-HEADERS (no includeSubDomains) and the tests sec_11_hsts_….
  • Compression (decision M2-Q2, 2026-10-05): Brotli or gzip, as the browser asks, for the text files of the app (from 256 bytes) and for JSON answers (application/json, application/problem+json) bigger than 1 KiB (JSON_COMPRESS_ABOVE_BYTES in bb-api router.rs, the one definition). Never for an answer that hands out a secret, whatever its size: a compressed answer that mixes a secret with text an attacker chooses can leak the secret (BREACH). The secret answers are the ones the cache rules mark (Performance, Cache rules in one place: a route the route table declares Secret, marked x-secret, or any answer that sets a cookie), and the compression skips every answer that carries that mark or a Set-Cookie header, so a route added later is covered by declaring its answer in the route table. Any other type that is not text (images, fonts, archives, other kinds of JSON) is left as it is. Enforced by: the tests sec_11_json_answers_are_compressed_above_1_kib_only, sec_11_json_answers_above_1_kib_are_compressed_and_smaller_ones_are_not, sec_11_an_answer_that_hands_out_a_secret_is_never_compressed_however_big, sec_11_files_keep_their_rules, perf_03_no_route_that_hands_out_a_secret_is_compressed (every route of the API description, with a big answer: the routes declared Secret are not compressed, all others are) and perf_03_a_big_answer_that_sets_a_cookie_is_never_compressed_whatever_the_route; review decides when a new content type needs the same care.
  • Slow and many clients: a client has 30 seconds (setting header_timeout_seconds) to send the headers of a request, which also ends idle keep-alive connections; HTTP/2 connections are pinged at the same interval. At most 1024 connections (setting max_connections) and 256 TLS handshakes run at once. Every API request has 30 seconds to finish, which also stops a request body that arrives too slowly (M1-F06). Enforced by: the tests sec_10_…slowly… and sec_10_no_more_connections….
  • Client address: the address of the connection is used, with IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:a.b.c.d) always treated as IPv4. X-Forwarded-For is believed only from a listed trusted proxy, and supports exactly one trusted hop: the last entry of the last header line is what the proxy itself saw; earlier entries are what the client claimed and are ignored. Enforced by: the tests sec_10_forwarded_for_… and sec_10_mapped_….
  • User content is rendered by one Markdown renderer with an allow list (ADR-0011). Attachments are downloaded, never rendered inline unless they are images or PDFs converted to safe previews.

Secrets and keys

  • A master key (outside the database) encrypts a key per secret (envelope encryption, XChaCha20-Poly1305). Secrets: mail password, AI keys, OIDC client secrets, webhook signing keys.
  • Where the keys live: keys/master.key (the master keys) and keys/log.key (the log key of the security log) in the data folder, which the server makes owner-only. master.key has one line per key, <id> <64 hex digits>, oldest first; the newest key wraps new secrets. log.key is one key that never changes, so a rotation does not touch the security log. The files are made on the first start only, replaced atomically (and the folder flushed) on a change, and on Unix refused when anybody but its owner can read them. Keys are read through and held in Zeroizing buffers and never show in Debug output. Enforced by: the key and secret tests of bb-store (SEC-16).
  • A missing key file is never replaced silently.
