The keys are made only when the database holds neither secrets nor a security log; otherwise Database::open_keys refuses with the catalogue message server.keys-missing ("Restore them from your backup"), because new keys could never read what the old ones protected. Enforced by: the test sec_16_missing_keys_stop_the_start_when_the_database_needs_them.
  • Stored form: each secret has its own random 256-bit key; the value is encrypted with it (24-byte random nonce), and that key is wrapped by the master key (own nonce). The ID of the master key is stored with the secret, and the secret's name (and the key ID) are authenticated data, so a row copied to another name or changed in any byte does not decrypt. Enforced by: the key and secret tests of bb-store.
  • Key rotation is a CLI command and an admin action (Database::rotate_master_key): add a key to the file, wrap every secret's key again with it in one transaction (values are not touched), and only then drop old keys that nothing uses. A stop half way leaves a state that still decrypts. Old keys decrypt, new keys encrypt. A running server follows a rotation made by the command line: the key ring looks at the modification time and size of master.key whenever it is asked for a key and reads the file again when it changed, so it never encrypts with a retired key; a write that was in flight while a key was retired is done again. Each secret is re-wrapped only if its row is still the one that was read (compare on the old wrapped key), so on PostgreSQL a secret replaced during the rotation is not overwritten with an old copy. Rotation is a rare administrator action; run it while no secret is being changed. Enforced by: the rotation tests of bb-store.
  • Backups are encrypted with a backup key derived from the master key, or with a separate key the admin keeps.

Limits and abuse

  • Rate limits per IP and per account on sign-in, search, API and MCP; slow-down after failures, never a permanent lock that an attacker could trigger. Only failed tries are limited, and a try is counted before it is checked (M1-F27). A wrong password, a wrong code of the second step, a wrong password asked again before a sensitive change and a wrong setup code each reserve a slot of their account (the lower-case address, or the person after the password step) and of the client network when the try starts, and the slot counts as a failure from that moment, so many requests at the same time are not many guesses: no more than the allowance get through to be checked. A success gives the slot back (the account is cleared, the network gets its one try back), so signing in again and again never uses anything up. After the allowance (sign_in_failures_per_minute, default 10) a key waits for the rest of its window, also with the right password. Every window that ends with at least one failure makes the next one twice as long, up to 15 minutes, so pacing the tries just under the allowance does not help; a success (for the account) or a quiet time of 15 minutes ends the growth, and a key is never locked for good. The keys of a network are shared by many people and keep a window of a minute: they limit a flood and never grow. The wrong codes of the second step are counted under the key of the person, which only a finished second step clears; typing the password again before a sensitive change and confirming the code app have keys of their own, so a password that is right somewhere else does not reset the guesses at a code. A try that fails because the server failed (the database, the passkey library) gives its slot back, because it says nothing about the account; a request that was dropped stays counted. The sign-in cap and the failure keys use one size of network (IPv4 /24, IPv6 /48, the shortened address of the security log). Wrong codes of one half-finished sign-in are also counted without a window: after 10 the half-finished sign-in is ended and second_step.given_up is written to the security log, so whoever has the password starts again from the password. Wrong setup codes are counted per network, so nobody far away can lock the person at the console out. The counters are keyed hashes in memory; the failure that uses up an allowance is written to the security log once (sign_in.limited), so a flood does not fill the log. Enforced by: the tests sec_14_parallel_wrong_tries_at_one_account_get_no_more_than_the_allowance, sec_14_parallel_wrong_codes_at_one_half_finished_sign_in_get_no_more_than_the_allowance, sec_14_parallel_wrong_passwords_before_a_sensitive_change_get_no_more_than_the_allowance, sec_14_a_success_gives_the_try_back_also_when_tries_run_at_the_same_time, sec_14_only_failed_tries_count_and_a_success_clears_them, sec_14_ten_wrong_codes_end_the_half_finished_sign_in_and_are_written_down, auth_09_wrong_setup_codes_are_counted_per_network_not_for_everybody and sec_14_failures_of_one_network_are_limited_whatever_the_account in crates/bb-server/src/tests/, sec_14_only_a_finished_second_step_clears_the_wrong_codes_of_a_person, sec_14_a_failure_of_the_server_does_not_use_up_the_tries_of_a_person, sec_14_a_failure_of_the_server_does_not_use_up_the_tries_at_sign_in_and_before_a_change, sec_14_a_failure_of_the_server_does_not_use_up_the_tries_at_setup, and the tests sec_14_* in crates/bb-api/src/failures.rs (the growing wait also when paced, a network that does not grow, a full table) and sec_14_the_sign_in_cap_counts_per_network_in_the_size_the_failure_keys_use in crates/bb-api/src/limits.rs.
  • Rate limits (SEC-14) are counted per minute, in memory, per client network (an IPv4 address, an IPv6 /64; the canonical client address from above, never the raw header): all /api requests (setting rate_limit_per_minute, default 600) and sign-in attempts (setting sign_in_attempts_per_minute, default 60, a generous cap against floods) per client network (every try) and, as described above, failed tries (setting sign_in_failures_per_minute, default 10) per account, person and network, where the key is kept only as a keyed hash. Going over a limit answers 429 with Retry-After and the message error.rate-limit.exceeded; nothing is locked for longer than the minute. The limiter is Bugaboo's own fixed window instead of tower_governor: it needs no other dependency, reads the canonical client address that the logging layer works out, and gives sign-in the per-account hook that a one-key-per-layer limiter does not. When a table is full, expired counters go first (swept at most once per second, so a flood cannot make every request scan the table) and counters still running are never dropped; new clients then share one overflow counter in the general window, and are refused in the sign-in windows (fail closed). This is a trade-off accepted on purpose: while a table is full (100,000 clients within one minute), newcomers share one general bucket and new sign-in keys wait for the rest of the window; a per-network aggregate is M1-F35. Enforced by: review, backed by the tests sec_14_* in crates/bb-api (unit tests of the windows, integration tests for the 429 and for the client address).
  • Access keys have a limit of their own (SEC-14): a request that comes with a key counts against the key (the hash of what was presented, in memory, a window of a minute; access_key_requests_per_minute, default 300) besides the client network, so one script that runs wild uses up its own key and nobody else's; things that start like a key and are none share one counter, so they cannot use up the limit of a key that exists. Enforced by: the test sec_14_a_key_has_its_own_limit.
  • Search limits (SEC-17, M5-Q10): a search runs for at most 2 seconds (then search.too-slow, which asks to narrow it), has at most 50 filters (in (a, b) counts as many as it has values), within N steps at most 5, sort by at most 5 keys, a text of at most 4 096 bytes (ADR-0005, amendment M5), at most 10 different words in one contains (MAX_CONTAINS_WORDS, each word is another lookup in the text index), a word of contains that ends in * with at least 2 letters before it (MIN_PREFIX_CHARS, so one letter cannot match nearly every word; ADR-0016, amendment M5), and pages of at most 100; each person may run 60 searches a minute (Quick search counts one search per pause in typing). Every number is a named constant or a bounded setting in one place. Enforced by: the tests of M5 WP-02 and WP-04.
  • Request size limits; upload limits per project. API request bodies are limited to 1 MiB unless a route sets its own limit; a bigger body answers request.too-large. Enforced by: review, backed by the test sec_14_a_body_up_to_the_limit_is_read_and_a_bigger_one_is_refused_as_problem_json.

Authorization model

The decisions are ADR-0004 (one policy engine, Authorized<T>), ADR-0022 (Who sees people) and ADR-0025 (roles, groups and assignments on the project tree). This section is what bb-policy builds.

flowchart LR
  actor["Actor<br/>person · access key · AI app for a person ·<br/>agent (ADR-0029)"]
  groups["Groups"]
  assign["Who has which role<br/>person or group · role or No access ·<br/>whole organization, only this project,<br/>or this project and its sub-projects"]
  roles["Roles<br/>(permissions, field levels,<br/>Who sees people, two-step switch)"]
  fieldp["Field mask<br/>Hidden · Can see · Can change"]
  people["PersonRef<br/>name · role · Someone · Former user"]
  vis["Visibility groups<br/>restricted issues and documents (V1)"]
  scopes["Access key choice and projects<br/>(only narrow)"]
  actor --> groups --> assign
  actor --> assign
  assign --> roles --> fieldp
  roles --> people
  actor --> vis
  actor --> scopes

The permission catalogue

One enum, Permission in bb-policy. The four tables of this section and the next one that carry a GENERATED comment (the catalogue and, for the starting roles, their permissions, field levels and Who sees people levels) are written from that code by cargo xtask gen roles; DOC-GENERATED fails when one differs, so they are never edited by hand. The key is also the value of x-permission in the API description; the sentence is the message permission.<key>; the topic is the message permission-topic.<topic>. Counts says where a permission counts (ADR-0025, decision 1); Kind is what an access key's choice keeps (decision 8). Routes that need no single catalogue permission declare public, signed-in, own-account or by-record; the last is for the routes of edit locks and drafts, which work on any record by its kind and ID: what a person needs to change a record depends on its kind (for a project Change the project's name, short name and settings, for an issue Change issues), so the route lets in whoever is signed in, or comes with an access key, and the use case judges the record. A permission that no route asks for yet, because a use case judges it and its screen and routes come later, is named in tools/checks/permission-exemptions.toml with a reason that names the follow-up; the entry must go when a route asks for the permission. Enforced by: ARCH-PERMS (every operation of the API description has x-permission with a key of the catalogue or one of the four words; every permission is asked by a route or named in the file; every permission and topic has its message).

  • A project permission given for the whole organization counts in every project; given on a project, in the project (and its sub-projects when the row says so).
  • The rows for the whole organization, and a role's own field and people levels, are changed only with Decide who has which role or Decide what roles see from a row for the whole organization.
  • Moving a project takes Move projects at the old and at the new parent; a project at the top level counts as inside the organization, so moving to or from the top takes the permission for the whole organization. Making a top-level project takes Create projects; a sub-project takes Create sub-projects at its parent. Renaming a project takes Change project settings; changing its short name takes that and also the right to create projects where the project sits (Create projects at the top level, Create sub-projects at the parent), because a short name that is taken is told only to people who may create projects there (owner decision of 2026-10-06: keep). A move shows its preview first (who gains or loses access or changes role, which fields and kinds of people information change for whom: the difference of two evaluations, bb_policy::preview_move) and is refused when somebody could take away a No access that applies to them after it and could not before (ADR-0025, decision 6; M2-F23). Changing a project's short name takes Change project settings and the right to create projects where the project sits, because only those people may be told that a short name is taken.
  • Later milestones add their permissions to the enum (issues M3, time M6, documents M11), each with its topic, sentence, kind and starting values. Enforced by: ARCH-PERMS (a permission without a route or a message fails).

Assignments

An assignment is one row of Who has which role:

PartValues
Whoa person, or a group
Whata role, or No access
Where it countsWhole organization (rows in Organization settings), Only this project, This project and its sub-projects (rows on a project); No access always covers This project and its sub-projects

A person or group can have several roles on one project, never a role and No access there. In the API the place is named applies_to with the values organization, project and project-and-sub-projects (glossary: Where it counts).

Evaluation

For an actor and a place (the organization, or a project and its parents), from one port call that loads the actor's groups and the rows of the place and its parents:

  1. Default deny: nobody signed in reaches only public routes; a signed-in person without an applicable row can do nothing and sees no project (SEC-01).
  2. Applicable rows: the actor's own rows and their groups' rows for the whole organization; rows on a parent project with This project and its sub-projects; rows on the project itself.
  3. Rank: the depth of the row's project (the whole organization lowest, a top-level project 1, its sub-projects 2, …), and at equal depth the person's own row above a group's row.
  4. No access: the highest-ranked No access row removes every role row of equal or lower rank. Roles from higher up, roles of the person's groups on the same project and other groups' roles on the same project are removed; a role given lower down, or to the person directly where a group has No access, stays. Decide who has which role from a removed row is kept when the row is strictly above the No access (a parent project or the whole organization), so nobody is locked out by a project below them; from a row at the depth of a No access that removes it, it is not (ADR-0025, decision 6).
  5. Permissions: the union of the remaining roles' permissions that count at this place (organization permissions only at the organization and only from rows for the whole organization).
  6. Narrowing: for an access key, keep only the permissions of the key's kinds (or the picked permissions), and nothing outside the key's projects and their sub-projects; a key with projects gets nothing for the whole organization.
  7. Field mask: for each field of the catalogue and each remaining role, the level set for that role on the nearest of the project and its parents, else the role's own level; the mask is the highest of these (Hidden < Can see < Can change), at most Can see for a See only key.
  8. Who sees people: for each kind, the level set for each remaining role the same way; the viewer's level is the most open (Names > Role only > Hidden).
  9. Visibility (restricted issues SEC-05, V1): an issue is visible if the actor sees its project and (it isn't restricted or the actor is in one of its visibility groups).

The evaluation is cached for the request and never longer (review: the cache lives in the request context; tests sec_03_a_role_taken_away_counts_from_the_next_request, auth_07_a_key_follows_its_owner_losing_a_role_at_once).

The field catalogue

Declared once in bb-core (fields): key, name (message issue-field.<key>), the thing it belongs to, and the kind of people information when it holds a person. Own fields join in M3 (CF-06) through one key type, FieldKey: either a built-in field of this catalogue or an own field (FieldKey::Own(FieldId)), so levels, masks, the field-permission page, history and fields= name both the same way and no list of own fields is written twice. A new own field starts Can see for every role that sees the project and Can change for Team member and above; whoever makes it can change that at once. Levels per issue type use the lookup of ADR-0027.

KeyNameBelongs toHolds a person

A person in a field is shown only when the field is visible (mask) and then as its kind says (PersonRef).

Kinds of people information

Declared once in bb-core (people_kinds), each with its name (message people-kind.<key>): assigned-to, reported-by, last-changed-by, authors (comment and history authors), editing ("… is editing"), followers, time-entries, mentions, pictures (pictures of people: shown only where the kind of the place also gives Names), and project-members (member lists of a project, M2-Q3). The starting levels are in the table above; a new role starts with Hidden everywhere (default deny).

People who manage see names (M2-Q3): in Organization settings, Who has which role and Check access, a viewer who holds Manage people, Manage groups, Manage roles or Decide who has which role at that place sees names; anybody else sees the people in these screens by the kind Project members. E-mail addresses are never part of a PersonRef: only the person and holders of Manage people see them (ARCH-PERSON-REF finds others).

How PersonRef resolves

Every person in an answer is a PersonRef, resolved by bb-policy for the viewer, the kind and the place (ADR-0022). Enforced by: ARCH-PERSON-REF.

  1. The viewer themselves: their name.
  2. A removed person (PRIV-04, M9): with Names, the label Former user plus a random code (Former user K7Q2): four characters of Crockford Base32 from the secure random source, drawn again on a clash and longer when four run short, unique among removed people, made when the person is removed and stored with the tombstone, never made from the person's ID or a counter (PRIV-13); with Role only or Hidden, Someone.
  3. Anybody else by the viewer's level: Names → the name (and the ID, for links); Role only → the label of their first role at that place in the order of roles ("Someone (Team member)"), or Someone when they have none there; Hidden → Someone.
PersonRef = { shown: "name",    id: UserId, name: String }
          | { shown: "role",    role: String }          // the screen says "a {role}"
          | { shown: "someone" }
          | { shown: "former",  label: String }         // "K7Q2"; the screen says "Former user {label}"

A role label and Someone carry no ID, so a browser cannot tell two hidden people apart or follow one through the answers. A viewer who cannot see names for a kind cannot search, sort, group or filter by it (SEC-06, from M5 on).

The answer of Check access

A query use case (bb-app, WP-05) answers for a person and a place; the screen (WP-12) turns each reason into a sentence with message keys check-access.reason.<kind>. The checker holds Check access at that place; names follow the rule above.

CheckAccess = { person: PersonRef, place: Organization | ProjectRef,
                permissions: [{ permission, allowed: bool, reasons: [Reason] }],  // every permission that counts there
                fields:      [{ field, level, reasons: [Reason] }],
                people:      [{ kind, level, reasons: [Reason] }] }

Reason = { kind: "role",          role: NamedRef, through: Person | NamedRef, on: Place, applies_to, inherited: bool }
       | { kind: "no-access",     through: Person | NamedRef, on: Place }        // the row that removed the roles
       | { kind: "kept-above",    role: NamedRef, through: Person | NamedRef, on: Place }  // decide-roles kept over No access
       | { kind: "not-given",     roles: [NamedRef] }                              // the roles they have here; empty: none
       | { kind: "organization-only", role: NamedRef, on: Place }                  // counts only for the whole organization
       | { kind: "level",         role: NamedRef, level, set_on: Place | "role" }  // a field or people level and where it was set
Place  = "organization" | ProjectRef | "hidden"                                    // "hidden": a project the checker cannot see

Example: "Yes. Ana is in the group Backend, which has the role Team member in ACME. Website is inside ACME, so the role applies here too." comes from role with through: Backend, on: ACME, inherited: true. The decision always equals the engine's, and the reasons are enough to reach it (property test sec_03_check_access_explains_every_result_with_the_chain_of_reasons).

No counts that leak (PRIV-13)

  • No answer holds a number that counts things which include something the viewer cannot see: lists page with next_cursor and never answer a total; Used by counts only what the viewer can see; the project tree shows no counts of sub-projects or members; a member list that is Hidden for the viewer is left out with its number. Enforced by: ARCH-NO-COUNTERS (a total, count or similar property, or a whole number whose description says it counts, needs an entry in tools/checks/counter-exemptions.toml that says why the number holds only what the viewer can see; an entry that matches no property fails), and the tests priv_13_no_project_answer_holds_a_count and priv_13_used_by_counts_only_what_the_viewer_may_see.
  • No identifier counts up: people, groups, roles, projects, assignments and access keys have random IDs; Former user labels and access-key prefixes are random. Enforced by: ARCH-NO-COUNTERS (product code with a counting column or sequence, or a number made by adding one to a count, fails; only the folders named in the same file, the counting issue IDs of M3 and labels nobody sees, may).

Enforcement points

  • Every use case asks bb-policy first. Every result passes through Authorized<T>, which applies the field mask during serialization. The API answers a view only through answer_authorized or a page made by Page::of_authorized; the steps of signing in and the caller's own sign-in data, which hold nothing of anybody else, are the exceptions, each named with its reason in tools/checks/api-out-exemptions.toml. Enforced by: ARCH-AUTHZ-ONLY, ARCH-API-OUT (a handler that answers through answer(…) or axum::Json without an entry fails; an entry that nothing needs fails).
  • Every search gets the visibility predicate compiled into its SQL; the readable fields given to the checker contain only the fields the person may read (M5).
  • History, notifications, webhooks, exports, assistant context and live updates apply the receiver's mask and PersonRef (each in its milestone, with its SEC-MATRIX column).
  • Tests: a generated matrix (actors × routes, roles × fields × levels, roles × kinds × levels; the record names the entry point of each route, api today, and later entry points add theirs; what the server sends on its own has delivery lines, one for each starting role as the recipient and each of the entry points notifications and e-mail, which say whether the recipient heard and what of the changed field and its author they were shown, and the check holds them against the tables of the starting roles; the routes of issues and issue types are rows like any other, and their example requests make the issue a person has not reported) runs on every build. The route rows run the example request of every route of the API description (crates/bb-server/src/tests/matrix/examples.rs, one row per route, added in the change that adds the route) for nobody signed in, a person without a role, each starting role for the whole organization, a project lead on the parent project, a project lead on a sibling project only, No access on the project (and a lead above a No access) and, with the access keys of WP-09, a key that may only see and a key for another project; each answer is allowed or refused, and a refusal of what the person may not know about is resource.not-found, as for a project that does not exist. A route may answer a person without the permission with what they may see only when the table says so (the list of projects). The matrix writes what it covered to tools/checks/sec-matrix-record.txt and fails when the file differs; the check holds the file and the table against the API description. The rows of fields and of kinds of people information are tests of the engine (bb-policy, tests/engine/matrix.rs). Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX.

Data model

erDiagram
  PROJECT ||--o{ PROJECT : "contains"
  PROJECT ||--o{ ISSUE : has
  ISSUE ||--o{ ISSUE : "sub-issue of"
  ISSUE ||--o{ RELATION : from
  ISSUE ||--o{ RELATION : to
  RELATION }o--|| RELATION_KIND : "is a"
  ISSUE ||--o{ FIELD_VALUE : has
  FIELD ||--o{ FIELD_VALUE : defines
  ISSUE ||--o{ COMMENT : has
  ISSUE ||--o{ TIME_ENTRY : "booked on"
  PERSON ||--o{ TIME_ENTRY : books
  PERSON ||--o{ WORK_DAY : records
  WORK_DAY ||--o{ BREAK : has
  PROJECT ||--o{ FOLDER : has
  FOLDER ||--o{ DOCUMENT : has
  DOCUMENT ||--o{ DOCUMENT_VERSION : has
  BLOB ||--o{ ATTACHMENT : "stored as"
  BLOB ||--o{ DOCUMENT_VERSION : "file content"
  EVENT }o--|| PERSON : "caused by"
  • IDs: UUIDv7 everywhere internally; readable issue IDs per project, counting (WEB-142) or random (WEB-K7Q2X), with redirects from old IDs (ADR-0021); short names for projects.
  • Own fields (ADR-0006): one field_value table with typed columns (text, number, date, reference) and indexes per type; used by issues, time entries, work days, documents, releases and projects.
  • Relations: one table for every kind, including timeline dependencies; sub-issues use a parent column, shown as part of on the map.
  • Files: content-addressed blobs (SHA-256), referenced by attachments and document versions; deleted when nothing references them and no keep rule applies.
  • Time: all timestamps in UTC; each work day stores the person's time zone so "day" means their day.
  • Versions: every changeable entity has a version number for optimistic locking.
  • Advisory locks (the order): a check that a program makes before it writes (a name is free, a limit is not reached, an issue still has a status) holds a lock from the check to the end of the change. A change that takes more than one lock takes them in this order and no other: the migration lock, then Policy, TagsAndLabels, Workflows, IssueCodes (one per project), and then the rest by their numbers (IssueParents, IssueRelations, Handles, Uploads, IssueFiles); LockClass in bb-store is the one home of the classes and of the order. Two changes that take two locks in different orders can wait for each other (more so behind a change that takes the Workflows lock alone, which waits for every shared holder and is waited for by every new one). SQLite takes no advisory lock (its single writer already serializes), so a wrong order would show only as a PostgreSQL deadlock under load; every transaction therefore records the highest class it took, on both databases, and in debug and test builds refuses a lower one with an error. The SQL of a lock is written in one file (db.rs), so no lock passes the guard unseen. A rule that rests on a program check under a lock (the unique names of types and groups, the limits of a place, since the offer table has no unique key) is part of this order. Enforced by: ARCH-LOCK-ORDER.
  • Edit locks: edit_lock rows (what, who, session, token, expires at) for long text and admin editors; private drafts in edit_draft; both deleted when no longer needed (ADR-0019).
  • Deleted items move to the trash (soft delete with a deletion date), then are removed by the keep-and-delete job.

Events, history and the outbox (ADR-0007)

Every change appends a domain event in the same transaction: who (actor), how (UI, API, MCP, assistant), what (entity, field changes before → after), why (reason, when required). The outbox delivers events to consumers that run after commit:

ConsumerUses events to …
Historyshow the change log (filtered by the reader's field mask)
Notificationsnotify followers and mentioned people (filtered per recipient)
Webhookssend signed payloads (filtered by the permissions of the agent it runs as)
Security logappend hash-chained entries for security-relevant events
Full-text indexupdate search text (inside the same database)
Live updatestell open screens that something changed (built last)

Consumers are idempotent and resume from their last position after a restart.

In bb-store: Database::record_change is the only way to write domain data: it runs the change, appends the event and the outbox entry, and commits all three or none. Outbox positions are handed out from a counter row that the change transaction locks until it commits, so positions become visible in order and a consumer that has seen position 7 cannot miss a 6 that commits later (the price: changes commit one after the other). Each consumer stores the last position it finished (outbox_done). Enforced by: the event tests of bb-store; ARCH-EVENTS (a command use case in bb-app must write through the ChangeStore port, whose method record_change bb-store implements); ARCH-SQL-EDGE (no other crate may write to the database).

Background jobs (ADR-0017) are rows in the job table. A worker leases due jobs with one UPDATE … RETURNING statement (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on PostgreSQL); a lease that runs out puts the job back, every start counts as an attempt, failures wait 30 seconds doubled each time (at most an hour), and after the last attempt the job goes to the dead-letter list (at once when the failure is permanent: a refusal can never succeed, so it is not started five times), and the use case that owns the work then ends it in a state people can read (a change to many issues ends as failed, with what it did so far). A dead job stays on the list; the store can give it a fresh start (requeue_dead_job), but no command or screen calls that yet (M3-F150). A kind of job is named area.what-it-does: lowercase words joined by hyphens, one variant of the enum bb_app::jobs::JobKind, which also says which kinds come back every day (is_daily). Enforced by: the job tests of bb-store and the tests of the dead job in bb-app.

The security log (SEC-15) is append-only. Each entry stores the HMAC-SHA256 (under the log key, keys/log.key) of the previous entry's hash and all its own fields in a length-prefixed encoding. Because the key is not in the database, somebody who can only change the database (SQL injection, a stolen copy) cannot change an entry and hash the rest of the chain again; somebody who also holds the host's key files can, and that is outside what the log protects against. After every append, one line seq hash signature goes to an append-only anchor file outside the database (logs/security-head.log, owner-only). verify_security_log reads one consistent snapshot (no write lock) and reports the first entry that does not verify (a gap, a broken link, changed content, a missing or forged checkpoint, an anchor line with a wrong signature) and whether the database reaches the newest anchored entry with the same hash (cut off or replaced ends are Truncated); a log whose anchor file is missing verifies but says it is not anchored. After the keep period, whole blocks of 1000 entries are deleted from the start; before deleting, the job verifies those blocks from the previous checkpoint and that the first kept entry points to the last deleted hash, in the same transaction, and refuses otherwise. A checkpoint is left: place, hash and time of the deletion, signed with the log key, so the remaining entries still verify. The newest entry is never deleted. Network addresses are stored shortened (IPv4 /24, IPv6 /48). Enforced by: the hash-chain property tests (sec_15_any_changed_row_breaks_the_chain, sec_15_a_rewritten_tail_without_the_key_does_not_verify) and the security-log tests of bb-store.

Storage types: every whole number is a BIGINT, every moment is microseconds since 1970 in a BIGINT, IDs are 16-byte blobs and JSON is text, so both databases hand back the same Rust types. SQLite runs in WAL mode with foreign keys on, a busy timeout and synchronous=FULL (a committed change survives a power cut; the cost is one more disk flush per commit than NORMAL), and every write transaction starts with BEGIN IMMEDIATE (one writer at a time). Migrations record a checksum of their steps and take the write lock (SQLite) or an advisory lock (PostgreSQL), reading the record again inside the transaction, so two processes starting together cannot apply one migration twice; a changed, renamed or unknown applied migration stops the start. Migrations given out to packages that are built at the same time must not depend on each other, because a database can get them in either order. PostgreSQL pools are sized to the number of processors. Every table is the home of an entity with personal-data marks. Enforced by: DATA-MARKS (tables), DATA-MIGRATIONS and ARCH-DB-PARITY (the migrations test and every repository test run on both databases).

Privacy engineering (ADR-0015)

  • Every stored field is marked in the entity definition: personal data or not, category (contact, employee time, content, technical), and the legal basis note. Unmarked fields fail the build.
  • The marks generate: Download my data, the Remove a person plan, keep-and-delete jobs, the record of processing, and the data-flow map.
  • Logs hold IDs, never names or e-mail addresses; IP addresses are kept 7 days by default.
  • Former users: a removed person becomes a tombstone (Former user K7Q2); references stay valid, personal data is gone.
  • Legal holds: working hours stay until their keep period ends, even after a person is removed.

Search language (ADR-0005)

One grammar, written once in Rust (bb-searchlang) and used by the server and, as its own WebAssembly module (bb-wasm-search), by the browser. The words are English and the same in every language of the app, so a shared search works for everyone. A field is written as on screen in one word, in lower camel case (assignedTo, statusGroup); the caller passes the readable fields (the fields this person may read), and a field outside them is as unknown as one that does not exist.

search      = [ or ] [ sort ]
or          = and { "or" and }
and         = unary { "and" unary }
unary       = "not" unary | "(" or ")" | filter
filter      = helper | field test
helper      = "contains" text | "under" id | "blocks" id | "blocked" "by" id
            | "connected" "to" id [ "within" count ( "step" | "steps" ) ]
test        = "is" [ "not" ] value | "is" [ "not" ] "empty"
            | ( "<" | ">" | "<=" | ">=" ) value
            | "in" "(" value { "," value } ")" | "in" "last" count unit
            | "contains" text | "member" "of" text | "within" short-name
value       = word | quoted | number | day | id | "me" | time
time        = "today" | "yesterday" | "this week" | "last week" | "this month"
sort        = "sort" "by" key { "," key }
key         = field [ [ "," ] direction ]
direction   = "highest first" | "lowest first" | "newest first" | "oldest first" | "A to Z" | "Z to A"
field       = word | quoted
unit        = "day" | "days" | "week" | "weeks" | "month" | "months"
  • Words. A word is letters, digits and the underscore, starting with a letter. A number is 12, -3 or 1.25, at most 15 digits. A day is written 2026-10-25; a day that the calendar does not have is a mistake. An id is an Issue ID of either kind (WEB-142, WEB-K7Q2X, ADR-0021), read by the rules of bb-core that the server reads it with (a lower case web-142 is read and written WEB-142); a short name is the capital letters of a project (WEB, 2 to 10). A value is read by its field when the fields are given (parse_with, which the server and the browser use before they check): an ID is read only where an issue is expected (issue fields, under, blocks, blocked by, connected to), so parent is web-142 is parent is WEB-142, while tag is re-test stays the text re-test (written in quotes). Without the fields (parse) nothing says what a field holds, and a word written like an ID is read as one. A short name is read in any case like an ID (within web) and written in capitals; a word of the language is a short name only in capitals (within and is a mistake). A quoted text is in double quotes; \" and \ are the only escapes. A count is a whole number of 1 or more.
  • Words of the language (and, or, not, is, in, contains, empty, member, of, within, last, this, today, yesterday, me, sort, by, under, blocks, blocked, connected, to, the units, step, steps, first and the four directions) are read in any case and written in lower case. A field that is one of them is written in quotes. A value is written in quotes only when it would be read as the language: and, or, not, is, in, contains, empty, member, within, last, this, today, yesterday, me and sort. A status Blocked and a priority highest need no quotes. The word of an own field is made from its name by one rule (own_field_word): Story points is storyPoints; a name that cannot be one word stays as it is and is written in quotes.
  • Words in the texts. contains "crash on save" on its own finds the issues that have all of these words somewhere in the title, the description, the comments or the names of the files, each word in any of them; title contains and description contains look in that one text, and <own field> contains in one long text of the issues (ADR-0016, amendment M5). A person for whom the title or the description is not readable has no contains on its own: the checker tells it as a field that is not there and the suggestions do not offer it (ReadableFields::allows_bare_contains).
  • Helpers. project within WEB is a project and everything below it, assignedTo member of "Backend" a group, under WEB-7 the sub-issues, blocks WEB-1 and blocked by WEB-1 the two ends of a relation, connected to WEB-7 within 3 steps any chain of relations (as far as the limit allows without within). Time words stay relative in the tree; the server turns them into moments in the zone of the person's region.
  • Person fields. A value of a person field is read as a name: assignedTo is WEB-1 asks for a person named WEB-1, not for an Issue ID, and assignedTo is 5 is refused.
  • The tree. Every node has the bytes it covers, so the browser can mark a word. and and or are lists of at least two items with no same kind directly inside: (a and b) and c is a and b and c. A text is a plain word, a number, a day or an ID by how it is written, so a text value that looks like one is quoted ("404").
  • Canonical text. The printer writes one spelling of each word, one space between words, quotes only where needed, brackets only where the meaning needs them (or inside and, and or or inside not), contains and member of always with quotes, sort by with commas as in sort by priority, highest first, dueDate, oldest first, and the unit and step in the singular for one. parse(print(tree)) has the words of the tree for every tree (Search::same_words: the places in the text do not count; the property test of TEST-SEARCH-ROUNDTRIP) and print(parse(text)) is the canonical text of any accepted text. The canonical form is one form: it flattens and inside and and or inside or and writes a number in its shortest form (1.50 is 1.5), so a text and its canonical text are the same search, not the same characters. A tree that the browser gives back as JSON is held to the same rules, and the module only gives its canonical text when the language reads that text back as the same tree. The canonical text is what the address, the API and a saved search carry; the tree never crosses the wire.
  • Limits (named once, limits.rs): at most 50 filters (in (a, b) counts as many as it has values), within N steps at most 5, at most 5 keys in sort by, brackets and not at most 32 deep, and a text of at most 4 096 bytes, which is checked before anything is read of it. After the limit of filters nothing is looked at.
  • Mistakes have the bytes they stand on, a message key search.mistake.* with the words for its placeholders, and what may be meant (the closest field or choice). The parser stops at its first mistake; the checker returns all of them. The message texts are in the catalog; no sentence is written in Rust or TypeScript.
  • Suggestions for a text and a cursor: the fields, the operators a field allows, the choices of its list, me and the time words, and the words of the language that may come next. What only the server knows comes back as a request of its kind (ask people, groups, projects or issues starting with what is typed), which the search bar sends to the server.
  • In the browser. bb-wasm-search takes and gives JSON (the text, the tree, the readable fields, the mistakes, the suggestions) with byte offsets; @bugaboo/wasm-search loads it when a search bar first opens and turns the offsets into positions in the string. Its types are generated from the Rust types (cargo xtask gen search-types), and the vectors of texts, canonical texts, mistakes and suggestions come from the same code (cargo xtask gen search-vectors); the unit tests of the browser run the module on them.

Settings and configuration (ADR-0018)

  • Start-up settings (address, port, data folder, database URL, certificates): bugaboo.toml or environment variables, written by the setup wizard.
  • Everything else comes from one settings registry: each setting is defined once (key, type, default, levels — organization / project / person — who may change it, help text key). The registry drives storage, the API and the settings dialogs, so a new setting appears in the UI without hand-written forms.
  • In code: settings are declared in crates/bb-core/src/settings/catalog.rs and nowhere else, and are read through their typed handle (settings::APPEARANCE_MODE). A setting key written as text elsewhere, in Rust or in the browser app, is a way around the registry and is found (not in generated files, in migrations, or as the argument of a message lookup: messages and settings are separate namespaces, and appearance.larger-text is both); the browser app names a setting through the generated constants of @bugaboo/api-client (settingKeys), and a migration may name the keys of its time. Enforced by: ARCH-SETTINGS.
  • What the registry knows: key, name and explanation (message keys), type, bounds or list limits, a format for text (a fixed list of choices with the words for each, a time zone, the address of a page of the app, the keys of shortcuts), the levels, who may change it (changed_by) and whether it can be locked. One check of a value (SettingDefinition::accepts) is used by the store and the use cases. Settings that exist only for tests (feature test-settings of bb-core) cover the project level while no real setting is set on a project.
  • Layers (CFG-06): the value that counts is the default, then the organization's, then the nearest project up the tree that sets it, then the person's own; a value the organization locked wins over every lower layer and lower layers are refused with setting.locked (decided inside the change, so a lock made at the same moment is seen). Reset to default takes the value of one layer away and leaves the others. Every answer says where the value comes from (default, organization, from ACME, your own) and whether it is locked. One function, Layers::resolve, decides; the store, the use cases and the tests use it.
  • Who may change what (ADR-0025, decision 14): the organization's layer needs Change organization settings; a project's layer Change project settings in that project (a setting only administrators change also needs the organization's permission); a person's own layer is theirs alone and only for a setting each person changes. Every change writes its event, and a setting of the topics security and auth also a security-log entry. Enforced by: the tests cfg_06_only_administrators_change_organization_values_and_each_person_only_their_own and cfg_06_a_change_of_a_setting_that_touches_security_is_in_the_security_log, ARCH-EVENTS and ARCH-PERMS.
  • A person's own values are stored for that person (their own table, person_setting, so the person is a column with a personal-data mark), are never kept by the browser or a cache (x-never-stored), and are gone with the person. The routes are one set for every setting: /settings, /projects/{id}/settings and /me/settings, and the browser draws any topic from them with one generic form.

User interface

  • Server data: only in the TanStack Query cache. URL: the search, the presentation and the open issue live in typed URL parameters, so every screen is shareable.
  • Lean requests: each screen asks for the fields its layout shows (?fields=); lists use cursor pagination and are virtualized.
  • Text: every user-facing string is a key in messages/en.json (ICU message format), typed via generated keys. The hooks reject literal text in components. The browser catalog is split into parts (ADR-0028): the first page loads shared, and the entry of each feature imports its own part, so the texts of a lazy area arrive with its chunk; t() of a text whose part is not loaded fails. Enforced by: TXT-CATALOG, DOC-GENERATED.
  • Text in Rust: the server uses the constants and functions generated into bb_core::message (SERVER_NOT_FOUND, server_port_busy(port)), whose placeholders are typed arguments; a key that does not exist does not compile. Keys that nothing uses are found. Enforced by: TXT-CATALOG.
  • Styles: one theme file (design/theme.kdl): tokens per theme and mode, and the rules of every component as part rules that use token variables only; one generated style sheet; no inline styles and no class names (CSP, THEME-ONLY).
  • Accessibility: React Aria Components for focus, keyboard and screen-reader behavior; axe checks in CI.

Errors

  • One ErrorCode enum in bb-core (for example issue.not_found, issue.version_conflict, search.unknown_field). The message of a code is made from its text, never written next to it: error.<area>.<name> with - for _ (auth.wrong-credentials is error.auth.wrong-credentials). The same rule gives permission.<key>, permission-topic.<topic>, starting-role.<key>, people-kind.<key>, issue-field.<key>, field-level.<word> and people-level.<word> (words! with messages, bb-core). A made key that is not in the message catalog stops the build (bb-core, tests/message_keys.rs), for any enum that is declared with messages. Enforced by: the build itself, ARCH-ERRORS and ARCH-PERMS (they read the enums and hold the keys to the rules of errors and permissions), and TXT-CATALOG (a made key counts as used, so a key nothing makes is found).
  • The API answers with application/problem+json: type, title, status, code, message_key, params, the request_id (the same as the x-request-id header) and, for a field.* refusal, the field it is about (the word of a built-in field or the ID of an own field; only a field the person may fill in is named), so the browser shows the refusal at that field. Handlers take their input through ApiJson, ApiQuery and ApiPath, whose rejections are problem+json, and return an ApiError made from an ErrorCode; a failure below /api that still has no problem body (any layer) is turned into one by its status: the status, the title and the message key come from the table, and a cause inside the server goes to the log (ApiError::internal), never into the answer. Every route in the OpenAPI document lists the standard answers 429, 500 and 503. Enforced by: ARCH-ERRORS (finds error answers built from a text written in the code, handlers that use axum::Json, Query, Path or Form as extractors instead of the wrappers, and compares the generated API description with the table).
  • The Display texts of error types such as TlsError are English in code and reach only the log or the terminal; a person reads catalogue messages. Enforced by: ARCH-ERRORS (an error answer cannot be made from a text).
  • A stale version has an answer of its own (edit.version-changed, ADR-0019 amendment M3): the problem body also holds conflict with the version the record has now, who changed it last (a PersonRef for the reader, of the kind Last changed by), when, which fields, and the values those fields have now. The values are left out for a field the reader's role hides. A use case only answers AppError::Stale (the record, where it sits, who asks); AuthApi makes the Conflict from the last event of the record in one place, and bb-api writes it into the answer and documents it as the 409 of every route that takes a version, so a route carries it without code of its own. The browser writes the sentence from it ("Not saved: Ben changed Priority to Critical 2 minutes ago."): the message itself has no placeholder. Enforced by: ARCH-VERSIONED (a route that takes a version documents the conflict), TEST-EDIT-LOCKS (iss_17_a_stale_version_answers_who_changed_what).
  • The TypeScript client gets the codes as a union type; the UI shows the message from the catalog.
  • An error message in the catalog has no placeholder, so an error cannot carry a name or number the person may not see; anything hidden answers with resource.not-found, exactly as if it did not exist. Enforced by: ARCH-ERRORS.

Observability

  • Structured JSON logs (tracing, one object per line on standard error) with random request IDs. One line per request holds the request ID, method, route pattern, status, duration and the client network cut short (IPv4 /24, IPv6 /48); never the path as typed, the query, headers, bodies, names, e-mail addresses or free text. Enforced by: DATA-LOGS.
  • Health endpoints: /health/live answers while the process runs; /health/ready also checks the data folder (and the database once the store exists) and answers 503 when something is missing; both are sent with Cache-Control: no-store; optional Prometheus metrics, off by default and protected.
  • The admin Status page shows version, database, disk, jobs, backups and certificate expiry.

Performance

  • Per-request caches for permission evaluation; Brotli and gzip compression (see Compression under Browser protections).
  • Lean lists (PERF-02): every list takes fields, cursor and limit, written once in bb-api (lean.rs, paging.rs, seal.rs). fields names what the screen shows; the answer schema lists every field that can be asked for, and the route names a small default, never everything (one table of fields per route, each marked as default or not). A field that does not exist and one the person may not read are refused alike with request.unknown-field (SEC-06). A page holds at most the page size of bb-core (paging, the one definition for the use cases and for the API description) and every page answers next_cursor: the cursor of the next page, null on the last. Enforced by: ARCH-LEAN (the parameters, the maximum of limit and next_cursor in the API description), backed by the tests perf_02_a_list_answers_only_the_fields_asked_for, perf_02_a_list_refuses_an_unknown_field_like_a_hidden_one and perf_02_every_page_answers_next_cursor_and_the_last_one_answers_null.
  • Cursors: a cursor is opaque text: the position of the last item (sort key and ID) with a tag made by HMAC-SHA256 under a random key that is made when the server starts and kept in memory only, and bound to the list it was made for. A cursor that was changed, cut, made up, taken from another list or made before a restart answers request.bad-cursor, whatever is inside it. A cursor holds only a position: every filter and every permission comes from the request, every time. A cursor is readable (the seal is a checksum, not a lock), so it never carries a value the person may not see: its position is made of the last item of the page, which the person has just been shown, never of something a page looked at and left out (a project they may not know about, a person they may not see). A page that stops after looking at many hidden items continues past them with a number of whole stretches that were looked at (the project list of the access-key form: NAME, NAME+500 or +500), which says no more than that the page ended early and there is more. Enforced by: the test auth_07_the_cursor_of_the_projects_for_a_key_holds_no_name_of_a_project_hidden_from_the_person, and review for every other list (each list says in its use case what its position is made of; the lists of invitations and of a person's own keys use the last item they return); the tests perf_02_paging_walks_every_item_once_and_refuses_a_changed_cursor and perf_02_a_cursor_that_is_cut_empty_made_up_or_for_another_list_is_refused, and review (that no route puts a filter or a permission into a cursor).
  • Who asks comes before what is asked: a list judges the person (401, 403) before its query (400), so a person who cannot list learns nothing about its fields or cursors. Enforced by: the test perf_02_a_list_judges_who_asks_before_it_judges_the_query.
  • References, not embedded objects: a list item names a related thing by its ID, or by a reference schema whose name ends in Ref (PersonRef); it embeds the thing only when the route declares the query parameter include with the closed set of names that may be embedded, and declares include only when it embeds. Enforced by: ARCH-LEAN (an embedded object without include, and include without an embedded object), and review (whether a property is "another resource" is a judgment).
  • ETags and 304 (PERF-03): a read that holds no personal data gets a weak ETag, a tag made with the seal of this server run from the final answer body after masking, so two people with different rights never share a tag for different text; If-None-Match with the current tag answers 304 without a body. Every GET documents the ETag header and the 304 answer, except the routes marked x-never-stored. Enforced by: ARCH-LEAN, backed by the test perf_03_every_get_answers_an_etag_and_304_on_a_match, which runs over every GET route of the API description.
  • Cache rules in one place: bb-api (etag.rs) sets them for every answer below /api, from the route table permissions::ROUTES (the same table puts x-permission, x-never-stored and x-secret into the API description; no handler writes a mark by hand) and from the answer itself. A read is Cache-Control: private, no-cache (kept, asked again every time). An answer with personal data (a GET route marked x-never-stored: who is signed in, the sessions, the invitations, the second step, the state of the server, the projects a person sees and one project, which differ with what the person may see) is no-store with no ETag. An answer that hands out a secret (a route the route table declares Secret, marked x-secret, or any answer that sets a cookie) is no-store, has no ETag and is marked as a secret answer, which the compression never touches (Compression under Browser protections). Every other answer, errors included, is no-store; an answer too big to tag is passed on whole as no-store. An answer that clears the session cookie also sends Clear-Site-Data: "cache". A new route has a row in the table with the kind of its answer (Ordinary, NeverStored or Secret), so nobody forgets to decide. Enforced by: the tests perf_03_only_a_read_is_never_stored_and_every_read_is_ordinary_or_never_stored, perf_03_a_route_whose_answer_has_a_field_named_like_a_secret_is_declared_a_secret, perf_03_answers_with_a_secret_are_not_stored_or_compressed, perf_03_no_route_that_hands_out_a_secret_is_compressed, perf_03_answers_with_personal_data_are_never_stored_for_anybody and sec_12_signing_out_clears_what_the_browser_cached.
  • Files of the app: named by their content hash and sent public, max-age=31536000, immutable; the start page and other files are no-cache. The manifest the build leaves for the checks is neither in the binary nor served. Enforced by: the tests perf_03_files_with_a_content_hash_are_kept_forever_and_api_answers_are_asked_again and perf_04_what_the_build_leaves_for_the_checks_is_not_served.
  • Compression quality: one number, in tools/dev/compression.json, read by the server and by the budget check, so the check measures what a browser receives. Enforced by: the tests perf_04_the_server_compresses_with_the_quality_the_budget_is_measured_with and the_budget_is_measured_with_the_quality_the_server_compresses_with (xtask).
  • First page budget (PERF-04): the JavaScript the first route loads (the entry and what it imports at once, read from the Vite manifest) stays within the budget in tools/checks/perf-bundle.toml, the only place the number is written. The WebAssembly modules of the build have a budget of their own in the same file, measured with the same Brotli quality (follow-up M2-F03), because every browser that opens a preview or an editor fetches them. Enforced by: PERF-BUNDLE.
  • SQLite: WAL mode, one writer task with a queue, many readers. PostgreSQL: a pool sized to CPU count. SQLite chooses between indexes by the size of its tables, which it knows from statistics: migration 23 runs ANALYZE issue, and a connection that closes runs PRAGMA optimize with a short look at each table (OPTIMIZE_ANALYSIS_LIMIT in db.rs), so it never holds the write lock long. Without the statistics it reads a whole project through the index of the project and sorts it, where the index of the creation gives the newest page at once (2.9 s against 2 ms on 1 M issues).
  • A dataset generator (cargo xtask dataset large --issues 1000000, architecture §11) feeds the nightly benchmarks (cargo xtask nightly); the budgets of PERF-01 are written once, in tools/checks/perf-bench.toml, and a scenario over its budget fails the run (PERF-BENCH).

AI (ADR-0013)

  • Providers: one trait; adapters for Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible endpoints (which cover local models) and a test fake.
  • Context builder: reads as the actor, drops hidden and AI-excluded fields, wraps people's text in clearly fenced "untrusted content" blocks.
  • Tool registry: shared with MCP. In the assistant, write tools return proposals; nothing changes without Apply.
  • Output: rendered by the Markdown renderer with remote images and auto-links disabled; marked Written with the assistant when saved.
  • Hard rules (AI Act): no tools that rank, evaluate or assign people; no access to working hours; no mood analysis. These tools don't exist, so they can't be called.
  • Limits: per-person and organization budgets; each call logged with metadata (who, tool, size, cost), not content, unless an admin enables content logging for troubleshooting.

Risks

Prompt injection through issue textMediumUntrusted-content fencing, proposals instead of writes, no remote content in output, AI off by default
EU law uncertainty (CRA category, AI Act details, NIS2 in Germany)MediumBuild for the strict reading; legal review before first release (compliance.md)
Working-time law details differ by country and changeLowRules are data (presets), not code
SQLite write contention at the upper end of the scaleLowSingle writer queue, short transactions; PostgreSQL for large installations
Agent-written code drifts from these documentsMediumHooks for every checkable rule; architecture-doc check; reviews per milestone

Technical debt we accept on purpose

  • No real-time co-editing in 1.0. Instead: edit locks with heartbeats for long text, drafts that are never lost, and confirmed saves (ADR-0019).
  • Live updates come last; until then, screens refresh on focus and after own changes.
  • The served model's control plane starts minimal (scripts plus the operator API) and grows when there are customers.

Architecture checks

The architecture is only true if the code follows it. AI agents write most of the code, so every rule that a machine can check is checked, by many small checks rather than one big one (ADR-0020).

How it works

flowchart LR
  cat["tools/checks/catalog.toml<br/>every check, once"]
  xt["cargo xtask check …<br/>implements every entry"]
  edit["Claude Code hook<br/>after each file edit"]
  commit["lefthook<br/>commit · push"]
  ci["CI<br/>all · nightly · release"]
  cat --> xt
  edit --> xt
  commit --> xt
  ci --> xt
  • One catalogue, one runner. Each check has an ID (for example ARCH-AUTHZ-ONLY), a plain title, the rule it enforces, the tool, when it runs and which files trigger it. People, agents and CI all run the same code.
  • Small and fast. A check runs only when its files change, and the selected checks run side by side, as many at once as the machine has cores (several read the whole repository, so one after the other they grow with the code). Edit-time checks take under 3 seconds per file and commit-time checks under 10 seconds on a quiet PC, so nobody is tempted to skip them.
  • Explains itself. A failing check prints one sentence: what's wrong, which rule, and where it's written down.

Groups of checks

GroupGuards
FMTFormatting: rustfmt, oxfmt (TypeScript, JSON, CSS), taplo (TOML), rumdl (Markdown)
LINTLinting: clippy, oxlint with type-aware tsgolint (TypeScript 7), stylelint, tsc type check, typos, lychee, actionlint
TXT / STYPlain words and design: no literal UI text, message catalog complete, glossary "don't say" words, tokens only, theme contrast
ARCHThe structure in this document: allowed crate dependencies, pure crates, WebAssembly build, Authorized<T> only from the policy engine, only safe types leave the API, HTTP and SQL only at the edges, events for every change, versions and edit-lock tokens on change endpoints, lean list endpoints, permissions declared, settings via the registry, AI tools only from the registry, browser uses only the API client, module map matches the code, docs change with boundaries, no unsafe, both databases tested
SECSecrets, private details of the owner, dangerous patterns, the permission matrix, security headers, known vulnerabilities
DATAPersonal-data marks, no personal data in logs, one schema source
DEP / DOCThird-party register, licenses, unused dependencies, SBOM, generated files up to date, decision records name their checks
PERF / TESTBundle and WebAssembly budgets, query counts, benchmarks, accessibility, search round trip, edit locks
METAThe checks themselves (next section)

The full list, generated from the catalogue, follows this chapter.

Checks that guard the checks

Adding a rule should be easy, and forgetting part of it impossible. The META checks make sure that:

  1. Catalogue and implementation match (META-CATALOG): no check without an entry, no entry without a check.
  2. Every check is tested (META-FIXTURES): each has a "bad" example that must fail and a "good" example that must pass, in tools/checks/fixtures/<ID>/.
  3. Nothing is unchecked (META-COVERAGE): every file type in the repository is covered by a formatter or linter. Adding the first .sql, .yaml or .py file fails until a check covers it. This is the hook that asks for new hooks. Generated files need no check of their own; the few other exceptions are listed with a reason in tools/checks/coverage-exemptions.toml.
  4. New modules are declared first (META-NEW-MODULE): a new crate, package or top-level folder needs a module-map entry and dependency rules.
  5. Every rule is traceable (META-RULE-TRACE): each "must" in the coding standards, decision records and these chapters names its check ID or says review with a reason.
  6. Callers agree (META-WIRING): lefthook, the Claude Code hooks and CI call only xtask, with the same lists.
  7. Suppressions are visible (META-SUPPRESS): every allow, oxlint-disable, ast-grep ignore or "not affected" vulnerability statement needs a reason and an issue ID, and the total can't grow unnoticed. The file types searched are listed in xtask/src/checks/meta_suppress.rs.
  8. Checks stay fast (META-SPEED). The 3 and 10 seconds hold on a quiet PC. Several builds often run at once, and wall-clock time alone would then fail a fast check, so the check times a fixed reference workload (a few small processes plus some file and CPU work, like a typical check) right before, during and right after each measurement. The budget is a multiple of that reference: the quiet-PC budget times how much longer the reference took than on a quiet PC (the load factor, never below 1 and never above 20). Each timing is taken up to 3 times and the best attempt counts, which drops one-off spikes. A check that is slow by itself is slow in every attempt and still fails. The failure names the measured time, the allowed time, the reference time and the load factor, so a human can tell real slowness from load. The numbers (budgets, quiet reference, attempts, ceiling) are defined once, in xtask/src/checks/meta_speed.rs.

Adding a rule

  1. Write the rule where it belongs (coding standards, a decision record, or a chapter here), with Enforced by: <ID>.
  2. Add the entry to tools/checks/catalog.toml.
  3. Implement it in xtask/src/checks/.
  4. Add the bad and good examples.

The META checks fail until all four steps are done.
