Database tests

Every repository test runs against SQLite and PostgreSQL (ADR-0003). Nothing is installed machine-wide (ADR-0024).

  • PostgreSQL 18.6 is a pinned tool in tools/dev/tools.toml. On Windows cargo xtask setup downloads the official binaries (checksum checked) into .tools/postgresql/. On Linux it uses the system PostgreSQL (on the PATH, or in the folder that pg_config --bindir names, as on GitHub's Ubuntu runners; no folder of the system is written down, and libpq-dev is the version of the installed server) and explains how to install it when missing.
  • cargo xtask db start | stop | reset | url manages a throwaway cluster in .tools/pg-data/. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, on the port postgres from tools/dev/ports.json (strict: a busy port is an error). Its random password lives in .tools/pg-password, never in the repository; on Windows the file is protected only by the inherited permissions of your user profile, on Unix it is readable by its owner only. All work folders share port 47240 (ADR-0023), so only one cargo xtask ci or db start runs at a time on a machine. db url prints the connection URL for tools of your own.
  • cargo xtask db run -- <command> starts the cluster if needed, runs the command with BB_TEST_DATABASES=sqlite,postgres, BB_TEST_POSTGRES_URL and BB_DB_PARITY_FILE set, stops the cluster again if it started it (also after an error), and then checks the parity record against ARCH-DB-PARITY and DATA-MIGRATIONS. Before the run it deletes the old record and any bbtest_* databases left behind by killed test programs; after a failure it deletes the record again, so an old or partial record never decides anything. cargo xtask ci runs the Rust tests this way.
  • Writing a test: bb_testing::each_database("name", async |db| { … }).await runs the body once per selected database. The body gets a typed pool (db.pool() is Pool::Sqlite or Pool::Postgres; tests/example_repository.rs in bb-testing shows the pattern). Each run gets an empty database of its own (a temporary file for SQLite, a freshly created and afterwards dropped database for PostgreSQL), so tests never see each other's data. Without BB_TEST_DATABASES, plain cargo test runs SQLite only.
  • The record target/db-parity.txt has one line per finished run (<database> <test name>). ARCH-DB-PARITY fails when a test ran on one database but not the other, or when a database did not run at all. DATA-MIGRATIONS additionally forbids .sql migration files and, once bb-store has migrations, wants its migrations test in the record for both databases. Both rules on the record run only inside cargo xtask db run, right after the tests; check all never reads a record left on disk (it can be from an older state of the code). There, ARCH-DB-PARITY checks that cargo xtask ci runs the Rust tests through db run, and DATA-MIGRATIONS checks for .sql files.

Enforced by: ARCH-DB-PARITY, DATA-MIGRATIONS.

Sample organization

A realistic, fully fictional organization used for development, end-to-end tests, demos and the optional "try it out" mode (OPS-12). Generated by cargo xtask dataset sample, deterministic from a seed (default 42), into SQLite or PostgreSQL. The people and the organization take a few seconds; the 10,000 issues with their comments take about six minutes (see Issues of the sample below), which is why --check and cargo xtask dev --sample make a smaller one.

Making it and using it

cargo xtask dataset sample [--seed N] [--database sqlite|postgres] [--issues N] [--out <folder>] [--check] runs the bb-sample program (crate bb-sample, architecture §4) as a process, so xtask does not link the store or the use cases. The program makes the organization through the same use cases the API calls: the first administrator with the setup code, everybody else as that administrator by invitation, so every change has its event and its security log entry and nothing is written to the database by hand. It is deterministic from the seed (default 42) with its own random source; it never reads the clock, because every date comes from one start moment that xtask passes in (now; a fixed moment for --check). The people and the organization take a few seconds on SQLite; the issues take minutes (see Issues of the sample).

  • Names: the folders the sample is made in, the names of its files and the environment variable of the PostgreSQL address are written once, in tools/dev/sample.json; xtask, the bb-sample program and the end-to-end tests all read that file.
  • What it makes in <out> (default target/sample, target/sample-postgres on PostgreSQL): data/ is a data folder that bugaboo serve --data-dir can start on (copy it first); sign-in.txt has one line per person (e-mail address, random password, role, name, the secret of the code app for the few people who have one, and the access key for the three who have one; the columns are separated by tabs, an empty column stays empty); dump.json is the canonical dump; sample.json marks the folder as made by the tool, so the next run may empty it and a folder with anything else in it is left alone. The passwords are random for every run and come from the operating system, never from the seed: no password is in the repository, and sign-in.txt is the only file that holds one (in target/, which Git ignores).
  • On PostgreSQL the program uses an empty database in the throwaway cluster of cargo xtask db (started and stopped by the command when needed). The address goes to the program in the environment variable BB_SAMPLE_DATABASE_URL, never on its command line.
  • People and organization: 50 fictional people with the mix of roles below, recorded in the plan (sample_people) and in the dump. After the people, bb_sample::Organization (the one filling of the extension point bb_sample::Later) makes the groups, the custom roles, the projects with their sub-projects and every row of Who has which role, as the first administrator, through the use cases of M2 (a change every second of the sample's clock, so the records come in the same order every time). Each person also chose a time zone and how dates and numbers are written, as they do in My settings, and a few have an access key. Names come from crates/bb-sample/data/names.toml, written for Bugaboo (no third-party name data); every address is under bugaboo.example. The people the demos name are the same whatever the seed: Ada Brandt (the administrator who runs the demo), Ana Moreno (a Contributor, on Website through the group External and nowhere else) and Ben Hale (a Team member for the whole organization, with No access on Android). The names of the groups, projects and custom roles are written once, in tools/dev/sample.json, which the program, xtask and the end-to-end tests read.
  • Issues of the sample (M3 WP-11): after the organization, bb_sample::Everything (the filling of the extension point that bb-sample runs) makes the issues of Projects below: the starting issue types and kinds of relation, how each project gives out its IDs, the own fields Severity, Platforms and Customer, the groups of labels and the labels, then every issue, sub-issue, tag, label, status change, relation and comment (some edited), and at the end one edit lock held and one draft waiting. All of it goes through the use cases, one change at a time, by the Administrators and Team members of the whole organization, each signed in on the working days they work (Monday to Friday, from nine, the clock of the sample running through eighteen months), so every date is a working day and every issue has a person who made it. The plan (crates/bb-sample/src/issues_plan.rs) has no database in it: it is worked out from the seed and the counts of tools/dev/sample.json (issues: the full count, the small count, the share of each type, of each project and place, the own fields, labels and tags, the numbers of relations and comments), and its words are in crates/bb-sample/data/issues.toml. --issues N scales every count to N issues (the full sample is issues.total, 10,000; --check and cargo xtask dev --sample make issues.smallTotal, 500). The readable IDs of the projects with Random IDs are the only thing that differs from run to run, and the dump leaves them out. No issue is restricted, and there are no releases. The history of every issue is read from the events at the end (what the daily job history.catch-up does), so the first page that shows one does not have to. The program is built with optimisations for this, as it runs about seventy thousand use cases: the full sample takes about six minutes on SQLite (the people and the organization, three seconds), the small one twenty seconds. Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (the dump of every --check run holds the numbers of the plan).
  • Using it in browser tests: cargo xtask dev --sample makes a fresh sample and starts the server on it (it prints where sign-in.txt is). A file of end-to-end tests that says test.use({ sample: true }) gets a server on a fresh copy of target/sample/data (one server per Playwright worker, ADR-0023 ports) and reads the people from samplePeople() (web/app/e2e/support/sample.ts). cargo xtask ci makes the sample before the browser tests; by hand, run cargo xtask dataset sample first. The M1 tests of setup and signing in still start from an empty data folder.
  • Working together (M4 WP-10): the same program goes on after the issues, in three parts, all through the use cases. (1) Before the issues the project OPS gets a workflow of its own, Operations, made the way the editor makes it (Create, the edit lock, Publish): the starting workflow with the status change Open to In progress asking for Assigned to (Ask for); every other place keeps the starter workflows Simple, Bug and Development of the first start. The walk of the status changes (Maker::status) supplies what a change asks for. (2) After the issues Maker::work_together (together.rs, together_files.rs) lets the people who are not on the team do their part (M3-F111): the Viewers follow issues (viewerFollows), the Contributors and Guests report issues of their own in the projects where they hold a role and comment under them (reports), the Contributors change the title and tags of what they reported (contributorChanges; a Contributor cannot change a status, so none is tried), the Team members change statuses under the workflows, many of them on followed issues (teamStatusChanges), and about five hundred small files are added to issues and comments (files: pictures as PNG or JPEG and one-page PDFs, generated so that no two are the same file, by bb_files::fixtures::varied_picture and varied_pdf). The files are kept in the files/ folder of the data folder, and the previews are made by the job runner (Ctx::run_due_jobs, with PreviewCommand::in_process), so every file has its preview when the sample is done. (3) At the end the notifications come from the sample's own changes (the reader of the outbox, run by the same run_due_jobs), and the Viewers, Guests and Contributors mark readPercent of theirs as read. The counts are those of issues.work in tools/dev/sample.json, scaled like the issues (WorkPlan::counts, the one place both the program and the judge read them). The dump has a part issues.work: the workflows (statuses, changes, changes that ask), the projects with a workflow of their own, the files (pictures, PDFs, on comments, previews), the notifications (by kind, by the role of the person, read, and the ones a Guest got about an issue they did not report: none), the reports by role, the status changes of the team, the changes of Contributors and the follows of Viewers. The dump lists the people an issue is assigned to by label, since the order of their random IDs is not part of the organization. Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (WorkPlan::judge in bb-dev-words, the tests m3_f111_…, att_04_…, wf_04_… of bb-sample).
  • The check: cargo xtask dataset sample --check makes the organization twice on SQLite and twice on PostgreSQL from one seed into target/sample-check/ and compares the canonical dumps. The dump leaves out what is random by design (IDs, password hashes, secrets and the hashes of the security log) and replaces each ID by a label that counts the records of a kind in the order they appear (person#3), so it still says which events and entries are about the same record. The run fails when two dumps differ, when an address is not under bugaboo.example, when a name is not a given name and a family name of the list, or when a password, secret or access key of sign-in.txt is found in any other file of a run (the database, the keys, the log files, the dump, what the program said). The dump also holds a part issues: for each project the issues of each type, status and priority, the sub-issues, the relations of each kind with the longest chain of blocks and the number of circles, tags, labels, the values of each own field, the comments (and how many were edited) and the locks and drafts left behind, and the run fails when they are not the plan of tools/dev/sample.json scaled to the issues asked for, within issues.tolerancePercent (IssuePlan::problems in bb-dev-words, which the tests of bb-sample ask as well). The dump also holds the groups with their members, the roles with how many people hold each, the projects with their leads, every row of Who has which role and the levels projects and custom roles set; the run fails when a group or project of this section is missing, when a role of the mix below is missing or held by another number of people, or when a project has no Project lead. The rules and their failing and passing examples are in xtask/src/checks/test_sample_data.rs and tools/checks/fixtures/TEST-SAMPLE-DATA/.

Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (cargo xtask ci runs it), ARCH-HTTP-EDGE (bb-sample is the second crate that may wire an adapter), SEC-SECRETS (no password in the repository).

People (50) and groups

  • 2 Administrators, 4 Project leads, 30 Team members, 8 Contributors, 4 Viewers, 2 Guests, plus 2 agents of one person (agents come with AI-30, M8).
  • Groups: Backend, Frontend, Mobile, QA, Support, Docs, Management, External. Every Team member is in one of the first six, every Viewer in Management and four Contributors (Ana is the first) in External.
  • Who has which role (made in M2, shown by Check access): the second Administrator and 18 of the 30 Team members for the whole organization; the other 12 Team members only through the groups Backend, Frontend, Mobile, QA and Docs (a group gives its role on its projects); the Viewers through Management for the whole organization; the Contributors in External on Website, the other four on Mobile app and Operations; the Guests one each on Website and Mobile app; one Project lead for each of the four projects; and one No access (Ben Hale on Android).
  • Two custom roles: Support agent (a Team member without Cost center, given to the group Support on Operations) and Security reviewer (needs two-step sign-in; the five people who have a code app hold it on Operations).
  • Cost center is hidden from Contributors, and Guests see no authors or mentions, on Mobile app; Website keeps the starting rules, so the M2 exit demo has something to change.
  • Generated names from a mixed international name list; e-mail addresses under the reserved domain bugaboo.example, so nothing can ever reach a real inbox.
  • Each person has a time zone, some have passkeys, two-step sign-in or access keys. Two people are already removed (Former user labels) to test GDPR flows.

What's inside

  • Issues over the last 18 months (dates are shifted at generation time, so the data always looks current): Bug 45 %, Task 30 %, Feature 20 %, Goal 5 %; realistic status ages, priorities and labels; own fields (Severity, Platforms, Customer); about 2 % restricted issues.
  • Sub-issues under goals, and about 3,000 relations of every kind, including chains deeper than four steps and one deliberate blocks circle (to test the warning).
  • Releases: three per project, one in the past, one current, one planned.
  • Comments: about 30,000, with mentions; some edited.
  • Files and documents: about 500 small generated attachments (images, PDFs), 60 pages and 20 files with several versions each.
  • Time: about 20,000 time entries with activities and cost centers, six months of working hours for every employee (including some broken working-time rules), and a few running timers.
  • Configuration: workflows for each issue type, field permissions (for example Cost center hidden from Contributors), Who sees people set for Guests, fields excluded from AI, saved searches, dashboards, two custom themes.
  • States worth testing: an edit lock held by someone, a pending conflict, a closed month, a person with a removal in progress.

The M2 exit demo on the sample

web/app/e2e/m2-exit-demo.spec.ts runs it in cargo xtask ci, on a phone and a computer, with axe in the four themes at every step; with BB_SCREENSHOT_DIR set the same run takes the pictures of the review page (M2/demo/<step>-<phone|computer>-<light|dark>.png). By hand, with cargo xtask dev --sample (it prints where sign-in.txt is; sign in as Ada Brandt, the first line):

  1. Organization settings › Roles & permissions: make the role Reviewer from a copy of Viewer and tick See how the server is doing.
  2. Website › Project settings › Field permissions: for Contributor set Cost center to Hidden. Mobile app has it hidden already; Shop and Blog show it hidden "from Website".
  3. Website › Project settings › Who sees people: for Guest set Assigned to to Hidden; the preview now says Someone.
  4. Website › Project settings › Check access: pick Ana Moreno and read why she is a Contributor (through the group External) and that Cost center is hidden from her. Pick Ben Hale in Android to read that No access wins over his role.
  5. Sign out; sign in as the Guest of Website (see dump.json, the row with the role Guest on WEB) and as Ana: the tree shows Website with its sub-projects only, and the settings pages and Mobile app are not found.

The M3 exit demo on the sample

web/app/e2e/m3-exit-demo.spec.ts (the steps are in web/app/e2e/support/demo-m3-*.ts) runs it in cargo xtask ci, on a phone and a computer, with axe in the four themes at every step; with BB_SCREENSHOT_DIR set the same run takes the pictures of the review page (M3/demo/<step>-<phone|computer>-<theme>.png, ten steps, four themes). It starts from two changes an administrator and a Project lead make through the API (the form of the Website gets Assigned to and an own field Cost center for everybody but Guests, because Cost center is a field of time entries until M6; Guests see no names of assigned people). By hand, with cargo xtask dev --sample:

  1. A Guest of the Website makes a bug with the short form (title and description, no priority, no person, no cost center).
  2. A Team member makes a bug with the full form: priority, Cost center, and a colleague assigned.
  3. The Team member relates that bug to two issues of the Website (blocks).
  4. The Team member takes the Guest's bug (assigns the colleague, writes the cost center); the Guest opens it and reads Someone for the colleague, with no Cost center. A Guest sees only the issues they made (the spec asserts it: the Team member's bug is not found by the Guest).
  5. The Team member edits the description; an administrator opens the same issue in a second browser and is told who is editing, presses Edit anyway and saves; the Team member's text is kept and offered with Compare and save.

The M4 exit demo on the sample

web/app/e2e/m4-exit-demo.spec.ts (the steps are in web/app/e2e/support/demo-m4-*.ts) runs it in cargo xtask ci, on a phone and a computer, with axe in the four themes at every step; with BB_SCREENSHOT_DIR set the same run takes the pictures of the review page (M4/demo/<step>-<phone|computer>-<theme>.png, seven pictures of six steps, four themes). It starts from what an administrator and the Guest do through the API: a mail server that takes the e-mail (BUGABOO_MAIL_BATCH_SECONDS is two, so the e-mail comes while the test waits), the Guest of the Website given a role in Operations, the field Customer and who is assigned hidden from Guests, and a bug the Guest reported in Operations, whose e-mail for what they follow is on. The workflow of Operations is the one the sample made (Open to In progress asks for Assigned to). By hand, with cargo xtask dev --sample:

  1. A Team member opens the Guest's bug in Operations: Open.
  2. Start working opens a small window that asks for who does the work; the Team member names a colleague and saves: In progress.
  3. The Team member pastes a screenshot onto the bug (the row and its preview), and writes the customer.
  4. Mark as done: Done.
  5. The Guest opens Notifications: the bug and its changes are there, without the customer, the colleague (the Guest reads someone) and the name of the Team member (the Guest reads Someone (Team member)).
  6. The e-mail has come to the Guest too, without the customer and without the names; its link opens the bug.

Speed on the sample

web/app/e2e/perf-issues.spec.ts (the Playwright project speed, which runs after every other project so nothing competes for the computer; by hand --project=speed --no-deps) measures the reads of an issue page (the issue, its relations, sub-issues, related issues, history, tags and labels, follow and followers, asked all at once as the browser does) and the first pages of every project's list on the ten thousand issues, then the same with ten people writing comments and one reading, and the preview of a move. PERF-01 is the 95th percentile under 100 ms, with the program the tests run against (BB_SERVER_BIN names another build); the numbers go to test-results/perf-*.json. On the sample, in a debug build: pages 17 ms, lists 17 ms, a comment with ten writers 53 ms (release: 8, 6 and 30 ms; the numbers of M3 were 38, 44 and 64 ms in a debug build and 18, 17 and 39 ms in a release build, before the role of a person was looked up only for a viewer who sees roles). M4 WP-10 adds three tests of the same kind, all against the budget, with the numbers of the 95th percentile in a debug build and a release build: perf_01_issue_page_with_files_… (the reads of the page and the files and what may be added to them, on 200 issues of which 40 got three more files: 48 ms in a debug build, 10 ms in a release build), perf_01_notifications_page_… (the number on the menu, the first page of 50 and the two after it, for ten Team members of the sample who have thousands of notifications each: 52, 39 and 70 ms in a debug build, 16, 13 and 24 ms in a release build; before the pages were read with one statement for each row and the rights of each different person, they were 139, 81 and 120 ms in a debug build and 48, 30 and 50 ms in a release build) and perf_01_a_status_change_through_the_judge_… (100 status changes, also the ones that ask for who does the work: 25 ms in a debug build, 9 ms in a release build). The notifications are held to the rule of perf_05_… too (perf_notifications.rs): a page of forty rows, and the number for forty unread, run as many statements as five, because the issues and the comments of a page are read in one statement each and the rights of a person are evaluated for their role only for a viewer who sees people by their role (M3-F113: what is left is one statement for each different person on a page). The reads of the issue page do not include mention-choices, which the page reads only while somebody types after an @. perf_05_… (bb-server, both databases) counts the statements a read runs (Database::statements_run) and fails when an issue with many comments, relations, sub-issues and tags runs more than one with two, or a page of forty issues more than a page of five. The project speed has one retry: on a busy computer run it alone (--project=speed --no-deps), because a speed test that other work competes with measures the other work. Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (the sample the speed is measured on).

Large dataset

cargo xtask dataset large [--issues N] [--database sqlite|postgres] [--check] makes the PERF-01 scale: 500 people, 500 projects (the sample's four with their sub-projects, the rest in families of up to five), 40 groups and a million issues, on both databases unless one is named. The kinds of things are the sample's; the scale and the shares are written once, in large of tools/dev/sample.json (LargePlan in bb-dev-words). The datasets are kept in .work/dataset/<database> (an older one of the database is thrown away first), and the data of PostgreSQL is in the database bblarge of the throwaway cluster.

  • How it is made. bb-sample --large makes the first start, the fifty people of the sample, the sample's organization and what the issues stand on (issue types, own fields, labels, the workflow Operations) through the use cases, as the sample does, and adds the own field Cost center, hidden from Contributors. The rest is written in big transactions without the use cases (large*.rs of bb-sample): about 450 more people in the mix of roles of the sample (they cannot sign in: their password is thrown away), the rest of the groups, projects and role rows, and every issue (one that a Contributor or a Guest reported is assigned to the team and goes on like the others, so the team's changes and comments tell the reporter) with its comments (English and German), followers, tags, labels, sub-issue, relation, own-field values and file record (no file bytes; a download is not found). Every record that the use cases would have written an event for has its event, built by the same functions as the use cases' (bb_app::event_members, in the order they happened), and the counters of the projects are set at the end. The history of every issue and the notifications are then read from the events by the code a server runs; notifications are made for the newest 2% of the events (the older ones count as read long ago). The only thing the store adds for this is the feature dataset of bb-store (Transaction::set_issue_counter), which only bb-sample switches on.
  • Same every time. Every issue is drawn from the seed and its own number, so a run gives the same data whatever the size of the transactions. The IDs of the fifty people of the use cases are random, so they are left out of the fingerprint.
  • The check. The program does not make the dump of the sample (it names the sample's four projects). It reads the database back and holds it against the rules of the sample that apply to the large dataset: every project that counts its issue IDs has a counter equal to its issues, the version of an issue is one more than the events that count a version up, every event about an issue has its row in the history of the issue, a Guest is told only about issues they reported, and neither Guests nor Contributors are told the value of Cost center. Every notification of a Guest or a Contributor that the check reads is held against the rules of what they are told. In a run of --check (the program is told --check) every event makes its notifications (checkNotifiedPercent) and the rules also fail when no notification of that kind of person was read, so they cannot pass without looking; a full build does not fail at 0. It prints a fingerprint of the issues, their comments (how many and their texts), their tags and their labels (of the issues that were held against their events). cargo xtask dataset large --check (a step of cargo xtask ci) makes 3,000 issues twice on each database with one start moment, and fails when a rule does not hold or the fingerprints differ. Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (the same rules as the sample's, for the large dataset).
  • Time and disk (this computer, release build, 1,000,000 issues): SQLite 18.7 minutes, 7.1 GB (the file and the keys); PostgreSQL 37.4 minutes, 9.0 GB (the database and the data folder). The check of the made dataset (20,000 issues held against their events) is part of those times.
  • The benchmarks. cargo xtask bench [--database …] starts a release server on the dataset of each database (a Node program, web/tooling/bench/main.ts, like cargo xtask load), signs in as the first Administrator, runs every scenario of web/tooling/bench/scenarios.ts 20 times as a warm-up and 200 times for the numbers, and writes p50, p95 and p99 of each to .work/bench/<date>.json, with how many runs were made (made) and how many were counted without one (skipped). A search that the server stops for taking too long (search.too-slow) counts as the time it really took (tooSlow says how many); once TOO_SLOW_IN_A_ROW runs in a row are too slow, the rest are not made and count as the slowest time seen, so a scenario that cannot finish shows plainly that it is far over its budget. The text index of a dataset is built once, before its first run (bugaboo search-index rebuild). A scenario is registered once, in scenarios.ts, with the name of its budget; the budgets are written once, in tools/checks/perf-bench.toml, and cargo xtask gen bench-budgets writes them as a TypeScript constant that the benchmarks and the speed tests (perf.ts) import. A run over a budget fails with the scenario, the number and the budget. Enforced by: PERF-BENCH (at commit time the file and the scenario list; every night the numbers).
  • The nightly run. cargo xtask nightly runs cargo xtask ci, then dataset large for a database whose dataset is missing or was made for another migration than the newest (dataset large writes the name of the newest migration into the file made-for in the folder of the dataset; names are compared, not file times, which a checkout changes), then bench, and writes one log to .work/nightly/. It waits while another full run is on the computer: ci, bench and nightly take a lock first, a local port (fullRunLock in tools/dev/ports.json) that the system gives to one program at a time and takes back when it ends. dataset large (without --check) takes it too. A waiting run says which port it waits for and gives up with an error after 6 hours, so the night cannot hang. The lock goes with the program that holds it: a killed xtask frees it while the programs it started (the server, the database, a dataset run) may still be running; kill those as well before you start another run. cargo xtask nightly --install registers the daily task (03:00, in the folder it is run in) with the scheduler of Windows; the task runs only while the user is logged on, and what it prints before the program has a log of its own (a failed build of xtask) is appended to .work/nightly/start.log; the lead runs it in bugaboo.win1 after the merge.

Speed on 1 M issues

The first numbers, on this computer, in a release build, at the 95th percentile (p50 and p99 in the file of the run), against the budget of 100 ms (PERF-01):

ScenarioSQLite p95PostgreSQL p95
issue-page: the eight reads of an issue page at once11.8 ms23.7 ms
list-big-project: the first page of the list of the big project (the first project of the sample, which the dataset ranks biggest; the benchmark fails when it has no more than one page)8.3 ms16.9 ms
list-small-project: the same for a small project (the one with the fewest issues among the last ten of the list, counted by reading its pages)8.2 ms13.0 ms
notifications-count: the number on the menu22.6 ms34.8 ms
notifications-page: the first page of 5020.2 ms30.3 ms
project-list: the list of projects (M3-F114)8.0 ms9.5 ms

The number on the menu was the read that cost most (M5 WP-03 fix round, on a dataset made with the final code: 1,000,000 issues, the biggest project APP with 133,505 issues and the smallest with 117). Before the fix it was 45.9 ms on SQLite and 88.0 ms on PostgreSQL (100.5 ms on the first dataset, over its budget), the page 35.7 and 62.6 ms. The statement for the rows is fast (0.8 ms on PostgreSQL, from the index notification_by_recipient); the time went into the rights: a page named the issues of a hundred notifications in many projects, and for each project the person's rows, roles and levels were read again (about fifteen statements) and the project on its own. They are now read once for all the projects of a page (Ctx::evaluate_projects, the same decision as Policy::evaluate_with), and the test perf_05_the_number_on_the_menu_runs_as_many_statements_for_twelve_projects_as_for_two holds it (183 statements against 53 before). After: 22.6 ms and 34.8 ms, the page 20.2 and 30.3 ms. The budget of the complex search (300 ms) has no scenario yet: the searches come with M5 WP-04 to WP-06, which add theirs to scenarios.ts.

Ten people at the same time

Concurrency is tested with 10 simulated people (an administrator and Team members of one project, made for the run), each in their own browser context (Playwright) or API client (cargo xtask load --people 10):

ScenarioWhat must hold
Three people try to edit the same descriptionOne gets the lock; the others see "… is editing"; Edit anyway moves the lock and keeps the first person's draft
Two people change the status of the same issue within a secondOne wins; the other sees the conflict message; nothing is half-saved
A lock holder's network dropsThe lock frees itself within a minute; their text is kept as a draft and offered with Compare and save
Ten people change different fields of one issueAll ten changes land (whoever was second presses Use mine); one event for each; the version counts up ten times
Ten people move issues through a workflow whose status change asks for who does the work (Ask for) and write an own field that Guests cannot see (M4 WP-10)Each status that was kept is the one the issue has; a change whose buttons were read before somebody moved the issue is refused, not half saved; the Guest, who reported one issue, is told only of that issue and no notification of theirs shows the hidden field
Ten people add files while others change the issueEvery file that was added is stored once on its issue, none is lost or doubled
Changing many issues while somebody edits one of themA lock covers only the long text, so the issue under edit changes too, and the editor's save lands afterwards with no conflict note (the status is another field); an issue whose text was saved after the preview is skipped and named, and the others change
Everyone drags cards on the same boardFinal board matches the event log; every person's screen shows the final state after refresh
Timers and working hours start and stop at the same timeNo double entries; working-time rules evaluated once per change
Searches while others change dataResults respect permissions at every moment; no errors; latency within budget

The load run and the invariants test run against both SQLite and PostgreSQL; the browser scenarios of ten Playwright contexts run on SQLite only, because each worker of the end-to-end tests starts its own server on its own data folder (ADR-0023) and a PostgreSQL database for each of them is not worth what it would add: the behaviour that differs between the databases (the conditional writes of the locks, the order of events) is what the load run and the invariants test cover on both. The short version (2 minutes) runs in CI; the long version (30 minutes, mixed workload) runs nightly and checks invariants afterwards: every change has an event, no lock outlives its lease, no text is lost.

The two ways to run them

  • Ten browsers (web/app/e2e/concurrent/): each person has a browser context of their own, signed in through the API (the sign-in has its own tests). The tests read what the people see (Saved, the "… is editing" note, Edit anyway, the conflict note with Use mine, Compare and save), never only timing, and wait for the answer of the server or for a note on the screen, not for a fixed time. The scenarios of the table above are iss_17_three_people_edit_one_description_and_the_first_text_is_kept, iss_17_a_lock_holders_network_drops_and_the_text_comes_back_with_compare_and_save, iss_17_two_people_change_one_status_within_a_second_and_one_of_them_is_told, iss_17_ten_people_change_ten_fields_of_one_issue_and_every_change_lands_once, iss_09_changing_many_issues_skips_the_one_changed_since_the_preview_and_names_it, which previews a change of status for four issues, lets one editor save the text of one of them, confirms the change and reads on the screen of the person that the issue is named and left alone while the others changed with one event each, and iss_09_changing_many_issues_changes_the_one_somebody_is_editing_and_their_text_is_saved_after, which previews the same kind of change, lets Ben hold the lock of the description with text that is not saved, confirms the change (all four issues change, Ben's too) and has Ben save: his text lands without Compare and save, and his issue has one status event and one text event (the preview and the change are previewManyChanges and applyManyChanges; web/app/e2e/support/many-changes.ts is the one place that knows their bodies). The scenario of the dropped network says which console lines it expects (tolerate) from the browser of the holder, and only while that browser is offline; every other console error, every uncaught error and every other browser stays checked. tolerate( may only be used in concurrent/locks.spec.ts and in mail-server.spec.ts and screenshots-notifications.spec.ts (where the one test of a wrong mail password, and the pictures of it, expect the 502 of mail.rejected, without cutting the network; TEST-CONCURRENT). The lock must free within the lease (60 seconds), plus the few seconds the page takes to look again; the time the test waits is made from leaseSeconds and heartbeatSeconds of the generated constants, never from a number of its own. The lock scenarios also run in the WebKit phone project.
  • cargo xtask load --people 10 [--minutes N | --nightly] [--database sqlite|postgres] (xtask/src/load/): the API at speed. xtask builds the program, starts the database of the run (the throwaway PostgreSQL for the second run) and runs the Node driver web/tooling/load/main.ts, which starts a server on the port loadTestServer and a data folder that xtask gave it, makes an organization (one project, six shared issues, Team members), lets the people change titles, edit descriptions under their locks (some editors vanish without letting go, some take the editing over), write comments and read, and writes what each person kept, was refused and read to a book (a JSON file). When the server has stopped, xtask runs bb-load-check on the book and the database of the run, which judges the invariants of the next section. The driver defines no invariant. Without --database it runs on both databases; tools/dev/load.json holds the defaults (ten people, two minutes, thirty for --nightly) and the name of the variable that carries the database address. cargo xtask ci runs it.
  • Against the database (test_concurrent_invariants_hold_after_a_run in bb-server, both databases in cargo test under cargo xtask db run): ten people change four issues together over HTTP while the clock of the test runs on until the last person is done, so leases really run out (a person who types for longer than the lease waits for the clock, not for real time), and then the invariants are read from the database by the same function the load run ends in.

Invariants after every run

They are written once, as the function check of the crate bb-load-check (judge.rs): the test of the server builds its book in memory and calls it, cargo xtask load calls it through the program bb-load-check with the book of the driver. Nothing else defines them (SSOT).

  1. Every change has an event: the events about each issue count each version from 2 up to its version once, one event for each change that was kept (events about a lock taken over or let go count no version), and there is one event for each comment.
  2. Versions only go up, one at a time: the versions of the kept changes of an issue are 2 up to its version, each once, and what one person reads of an issue never goes down.
  3. No lock outlives its lease: no lock row ends later than the lease (60 seconds) from now, nobody holds a lock when the leases are over (in a load run nobody starts to edit under a lock in the last 70 seconds), and after the purge no row of a lock is left. One definition, used while the people work (the test of the server) and at the end (both).
  4. No text is lost: a save that was refused (lock lost, taken over, text changed) is the draft of the person at once, the heartbeat draft of an editor who vanished is still there after the lease, and the description is the text of the last save that was kept.
  5. The title is what the last kept title change set (M3-F93), and the status what the last kept status change under the workflow set (WF-01); a change that is lost or half saved is found.
  6. The files of an issue are the ones that were added to it, none more and none fewer (ATT-01).
  7. No notification shows what its person cannot see (SEC-06): a Guest is told only of the issues they reported, and no notification of a Guest keeps a field that is hidden from Guests, neither a built-in one that the starting role hides nor the own field the run hid. The run has nine Team members and one Guest, a project with a workflow of its own that asks for Assigned to on Open to In progress, and the own field Internal note, which Guests cannot see.

Enforced by: TEST-CONCURRENT (the scenarios, the invariants test and the load step of cargo xtask ci are there and not switched off), TEST-EDIT-LOCKS (the browser scenarios of the locks).

Browser tests and the connections of the computer (M4 WP-03)

On Windows a computer that has no free ports or socket buffers left answers net::ERR_NO_BUFFER_SPACE, and a browser test that gets it fails (fixtures.ts counts every net::ERR_* as a defect, and no retry is added to hide it). A closed connection stays in TIME_WAIT for about two minutes, so what a run needs is the number of connections it closed in the last two minutes, not the number open. Three work folders that test at the same time share the computer.

What a run is measured by. The Playwright reporter web/tooling/connection-guard.ts looks at the connections of the computer during the run, one look after the other with a pause of a second between them (a look takes about 1.7 seconds on Windows; the next one is planned only when the one before has ended, the timer never keeps the process alive, and no look is made while the speed tests run, which measure on a computer that is otherwise idle; PowerShell's Get-NetTCPConnection on Windows, because netstat there prints the states in the language of the system; ss or netstat on Linux) and counts, for the ports of the workers' servers (e2eWorkersFrom to e2eWorkersTo of the folder's block), the connections in ESTABLISHED, TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT. At the end of the run it prints the peak, writes the second-by-second counts to test-results/connections.csv and fails the run when the most it saw in TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT at once is over MOST_LEFTOVER_CONNECTIONS (web/tooling/connections.ts, the one place that names the limit). The sentence names the peak, the limit, the server and the spec its worker ran last. The limit is 1,800: a run needs about 1,250, and the run before the work package peaked at 1,989, so a fall back to the old way of testing is seen. One work folder never came near the ports that Windows gives out for connections (16,384), so the failure of three merges of M3 most likely needed several folders testing at the same time, which is why the guard looks at what one run needs. The summary also says how many connections in TIME_WAIT the whole computer had (the ones with a local port of the dynamic range, from 49,152), for information; it never fails the run. Above BUSY_COMPUTER_TIME_WAIT (3,000) the summary adds "Other work is on this computer", and when a test fails with net::ERR_NO_BUFFER_SPACE the reporter prints the count of the whole computer next to what the run left over, so a reviewer sees whether it was the run or its neighbours (M4-F22). The run fails too when any look failed or none was made (PowerShell, or ss or netstat on Linux, not working), so that nobody believes a guard that did not look; the summary says how many looks failed. The pure part (reading the lists, judging) is tested in web/tooling/connections.test.ts. Enforced by: TEST-CONNECTIONS (the reporter is in the Playwright config and fails the run, the limit is one named number, the tests of the guard are not switched off, and tests are run again only in the speed project).

What was measured. The full end-to-end run (about 700 tests, 16 workers, one work folder testing):

RunPeak in TIME_WAITIn CLOSE_WAITOpen at mostWhere
Before (readiness probes, one request context for each session)1,989060WebKit phone
After the readiness wait and the shared connections of the sessions1,918054issues-new.spec.ts, WebKit phone
After WebKit runs two tests at a time1,248056issues-editing.spec.ts, WebKit phone

Most of the connections are from WebKit, not from the helpers of the tests. One spec file alone shows it: issues-new.spec.ts leaves 16 connections in TIME_WAIT in Chromium (6 tests) and 438 in WebKit (the same 6 tests), and the project webkit-phone (20 tests in four files) alone peaks at 1,689, almost all of the peak of the whole run. On Windows, WebKit opens a connection for about every request of a page and closes it again (27 requests of the sign-in page leave 29 connections behind, against 2 for Chromium); the server keeps its connections alive (curl reuses one, and so does a Node client), so the cause is not in the listener and crates/bb-api/src/listener.rs is not changed. The project therefore runs two WebKit tests at a time (WEBKIT_WORKERS), which takes the peak from 1,918 to 1,248 and the run from 5.7 to 7.2 minutes (7.4 to 7.7 in cargo xtask ci).

What each task changed.

  • Readiness (web/app/e2e/support/ready.ts): the wait for a server asks GET /health/live over HTTPS with pauses of 50, 100, 200 … 1,000 ms instead of a raw TCP connection every 100 ms. A question that is refused leaves no connection behind, and one that is answered leaves one. A test with a server that answers late (web/tooling/ready.test.ts) asks at most seven times and the server sees one connection. In the measured run this was too small to show in the peak (a start has one successful probe either way).
  • Shared connections for the sessions of the API (web/app/e2e/support/session-transport.ts): every ApiSession and useKey script of a server goes over one pool of keep-alive connections of that server (closed when the server stops) and keeps the cookies of its own in a jar, so two people never share a sign-in. Before, each session was a Playwright request context with connections of its own that were closed at dispose. A session that was opened for a helper call is now free (openSession and useKey are no longer async). A connection that nobody used for 20 seconds is closed by the pool before the server's header timeout (30 seconds) would close it, and a GET or HEAD that meets a connection the server closed is sent once more; a request that changes something is never sent again, because nobody can tell whether the server took it.
  • Fewer server starts is not done, and the measurement says why it would not help: a start leaves about one connection (its readiness question), a few hundred of the two thousand. A server that is reset instead of restarted needs a route that exists only in a test build, which is product code (bb-server, an architecture decision) and not part of this package; a fresh data folder on the same process is not possible, because the server holds its data folder open. What the package keeps is what the work package asks for first: a spec cannot see what an earlier spec left behind. A worker starts a server on an empty data folder for every file, and isolation.spec.ts proves it: it makes a project and an issue, asks the worker for the server of another file, and finds the same port with the setup code accepted again and no project in it.
  • The guard above, and No hiding: no retries are added (the speed project keeps its one), and fixtures.ts still counts every net::ERR_*.
  • Showcase pictures (M2C-F104): the browser of every window stands at the moment the sample was made (sampleStartMs()), so "3 days ago" is the same on every run, and the address of the invitation is fixed. The few screens that show what the server makes in every run (a date and time, how long it runs, the link of an invitation with its secret, the hash of the security log) have those places painted over in their pictures (support/showcase-masks.ts, M4-F24), the link of an invitation is written the same way before the picture (its secret wraps at other places, so the box around it was another height), and the pointer is out of the page: two runs of the 212 phone pictures are now the same bytes.

Reading the numbers again. Run the end-to-end tests with npm run test:e2e (or cargo xtask ci), and read the last lines: Connections of the tests: at most N left over at once …. The seconds-by-seconds counts are in test-results/connections.csv.

Browser tests wait for what they depend on (M4 WP-18)

A test that is right on a quiet computer can lose a race in the full run, where 16 workers share the processors. Two such races were found only by cargo xtask ci, so a browser test waits, with a web-first assertion (await expect(…)), for the state its next step depends on:

  • Before it stops the page's clock (page.clock.pauseAt, page.clock.setFixedTime), it waits until the screen it tests has drawn. The page reads its data on timers, and a stopped clock holds them back (access-key-day.spec.ts).
  • Before a second window reads, it waits until the first window shows that the change is stored, not only that the text is on screen (concurrent/locks.spec.ts: the watcher reloads only after Save mine is saved).

No retry and no longer timeout is added to hide a race; the fix is the missing wait.

Local ports (ADR-0023)

Your machine runs other Vite projects, so Bugaboo never uses default ports. All ports live in tools/dev/ports.json (single source); Vite, Playwright, the server and xtask read them from there, and every tool uses strictPort, so a busy port fails with a clear message instead of silently moving.

OffsetUsed by
0Bugaboo server in development (API + embedded app)
1Vite dev server (hot reload)
2Vite preview of a production build
3Server instance for end-to-end tests (fresh sample database)
4Vitest UI
10–29Parallel Playwright workers, one server and database each
30Load-test server
40Throwaway PostgreSQL for tests (cargo xtask db start)

The offsets are inside a block of 100 ports. Each work folder bugaboo.winN has its own block, starting at 47200 + (N − 1) · 100 (win1 47200–47299, win3 47400–47499, up to win9 48000–48099), so folders that build and test at the same time never share a port; any other folder uses block 1 and BUGABOO_PORT_BLOCK names another one. The table above shows block 1: the server of the first folder is on 47200, of the third on 47400.

The installed product asks for its port in the setup wizard (suggesting 8443 and checking that it's free); these development ports never appear in a customer installation.

Security: threat model and personal-data flows

Part of the security and data-flow documentation (COMP-07) for the CRA technical file and for customers' own risk assessments. It covers what is built so far and grows with every milestone: each milestone review checks that new entry points appear here.

The method is STRIDE per trust boundary (boundaries from Context). Every threat names the mitigation and what proves it: a check from the catalogue (tools/checks/catalog.toml), a test, or review when a person decides.

Scope (status: M4 built, M5 planned)

In scope nowComes later (own section then)
HTTPS and start-up config, security headers, sign-in (password, passkey, two-step codes), sessions, invitations, first-run setup code, rate limits, the security log, stored secrets, logs (M1); the permission engine (roles, groups, assignments, No access, field masks, Who sees people), projects and short names, access keys, two-step sign-in by role, settings in layers (M2); issues with their text, comments, tags and labels, own fields, layouts, edit locks and drafts, changing many issues and the background jobs that carry it (M3)Attachments, mail and workflows (M4; threats below), search and lists (M5; threats below, planned), MCP and the assistant (M8), Remove a person and exports (M9), webhooks (M12), the served model's control plane (M14)

Attack surface

flowchart LR
  browser(["Browser<br/>(untrusted)"])
  console(["Server console<br/>(operator)"])
  subgraph server["bugaboo process"]
    tls["HTTPS<br/>rustls"]
    hdr["Security headers<br/>rate limits"]
    api["/api/v1<br/>problem+json"]

  browser -- "1 · HTTPS" --> tls --> hdr --> api --> auth --> store --> db
  console -- "setup code<br/>bugaboo setup" --> server
  store --> keys
  tls --> cert
  server --> logs

Entry points in M1: the HTTPS listener (pages, assets, /api/v1, /health/*), the console and bugaboo.toml, and the data folder on disk. M2 adds no new listener: the new routes are below /api/v1, and scripts reach them with an access key (Authorization: Bearer bb_…) instead of a cookie. The sample-organization program (bb-sample) is a developer tool and is not shipped before OPS-12.

Permissions, projects and access keys (M2)

The model is ADR-0025 and §7, Authorization model. The trust boundary is the same (browser or script ↔ server); what is new is that the server now decides between people who are all signed in. The packages that build a row add its test when they merge; a name in the last column that does not exist yet is the test the package's plan asks for.

M3 stores text that people write and shows it to others, and lets several people edit one issue. Each row names the test that proves it (M3 plan).

Workflows, files and notifications (M4)

M4 takes files from people, sends mail out of the server for the first time, and lets workflows decide who may change a status. Each row names the check or test that proves it; the packages add the test names (M4 plan). A test named in a cell next to a check that holds a list of required tests must be in that list. Enforced by: DOC-PROVEN-BY.

TamperingThe text of a comment in a notification runs a script in the browserThe text comes as HTML that the server made with bb-markdown for this reader (NotificationEntry.html carries the mark x-safe-html), and the browser draws it only through MarkdownViewSEC-RICHTEXT; the table test of SAFE_HTML_PROPERTIES in bb-api; ntf_01_a_comment_on_an_issue_ana_follows_raises_her_count_open_lands_on_it_mark_as_read_lowers_it (WP-08)
Information disclosureThe page of the mail server shows, or its answer sends, the mail passwordThe page asks GET /api/v1/mail, which says only whether one is set (credential_set); the box for a new one is never filled; the password goes through PUT /api/v1/mail/password and is never read backsec_16_the_mail_password_is_stored_encrypted_and_never_sent_back, SEC-MATRIX (getMailServer), ntf_02_a_wrong_password_is_refused_in_words_and_the_button_then_waits (WP-08)

Elevation of privilegeA browser tab left open keeps a session alive for ever, because the number of unread notifications is asked for every 30 secondsThe poll and the check of versions (a POST that only reads, reads_by_post in the route table, set with route_reading) carry x-background-read, and the session check does not count such a request as use, so the idle time runs on (SEC-12); one function decides which requests may carry the mark (openapi::may_be_background_read)sec_12_a_background_count_does_not_keep_a_session_alive, sec_12_the_check_of_versions_in_a_tab_left_open_does_not_keep_a_session_alive (WP-08, WP-12)

Search and lists (M5)

M5 lets people type searches that become database queries, search the text of issues, and share saved searches. Each row names the check that proves it; the packages add the test names (M5 plan).

STRIDEThreatMitigationProven by
Information disclosureA search filters, sorts or groups by a field the person may not read, and the results or their order tell its valuesThe checker gets only the fields the person may read (ADR-0005, amendment M5); the server parses and checks every search again and never relies on the browserSEC-MATRIX (the search entry point, a hidden field used to filter, sort and group); the tests of WP-02 and WP-04
Information disclosureA hidden field gives another message, error code or time than an unknown field, so a person learns that it exists (QRY-05)One mistake for both, from one place in the checker; the same work is done for both before the answerthe tests of WP-02 (the same mistake) and WP-04 (no difference in time on the server)
Information disclosureA text search finds an issue through a comment, a file or a long-text field the reader may not seeEach indexed text is a row with its source; the compiled search leaves out every source the reader may not see, in the same statement as the visibility predicates (ADR-0016, amendment M5)SEC-MATRIX (search), ARCH-DB-PARITY; the tests of WP-05
Information disclosureA count, a group heading or a Tick all results tells how many hidden issues exist (PRIV-13)Counts and groups are computed on the issues the person sees, by the same compiled searchthe tests of WP-04 and WP-08
Information disclosureA shared saved search shows its receivers a hidden field, a hidden person or an issue they may not seeIt runs with the rights of the person who opens it; a receiver sees it only when its text checks cleanly against their own rights, otherwise its address answers like one that does not exist (ADR-0034)SEC-MATRIX (saved searches); qry_06_a_shared_search_runs_with_the_rights_of_the_person_who_opens_it, qry_06_a_shared_search_with_a_field_the_receiver_cannot_read_is_not_listed_and_its_address_is_not_found, qry_06_a_shared_search_with_a_hidden_person_group_or_project_in_its_text_is_not_found, qry_06_a_short_page_never_shows_that_searches_were_left_out, sec_06_a_hidden_saved_search_and_a_missing_one_run_the_same_reads
Elevation of privilegeA person shares a search with a project or a group they may not share with, or changes someone else's searchShare searches at the place of the share, being in the group, and only the maker changes it (ADR-0034, decisions 2 and 5)ARCH-PERMS, SEC-MATRIX; qry_06_only_the_maker_changes_a_saved_search, qry_06_sharing_needs_share_searches_at_the_place, qry_06_a_group_needs_being_in_it_or_manage_groups
TamperingA search text becomes SQLThe compiler builds parameterized statements through the query builder, never by joining text (SEC-17)SEC-PATTERNS, the tests of WP-04 (texts with quotes, comment marks and statement ends)
Denial of serviceA search with many conditions, deep chains of relations or a text that matches everything slows the server for everyoneAt most 2 seconds, 50 conditions, 5 steps, pages of 100, and 60 searches a minute per person (architecture §7, "Search limits")the tests of WP-02 and WP-04; PERF-BENCH
Information disclosureQuick search finds an issue, a project or a saved search the person may not seeIt asks the same search routes with the same rightsSEC-MATRIX (search); the tests of WP-09

STRIDEThreatMitigationProven by

RepudiationAn admin denies an action, or someone edits the security logAppend-only security log, hash-chained with an HMAC under a log key that is not in the database (keys/log.key, never rotated), so somebody who can only change the database cannot make a changed chain verify again; every append is also written to an append-only anchor file outside the database (logs/security-head.log), so cutting off or replacing the end is found; a verify command, and the status page shows the result. The command reads the whole log every time; the status page reads only the entries added since its last good check (and the whole log again once a day), and keeps its answer for a few seconds unless the server wrote an entry in between, so a long log does not make every visit slow (M1-F60)hash-chain property tests sec_15_any_changed_row_breaks_the_chain and sec_15_a_rewritten_tail_without_the_key_does_not_verify; security-log tests (WP-05); ops_08_the_status_page_checks_only_new_entries_and_the_command_checks_all (bb-store), ops_08_the_status_page_follows_the_log_and_reuses_its_answer_until_something_is_written
RepudiationSomebody who holds the host's key files (keys/log.key) and the anchor file rewrites the logNot stopped: this protects against attackers who reach the database only (SQL injection, a stolen database copy or backup), not against somebody with control of the host. The status page shows the head so an administrator can compare it with an earlier noteOut of scope for self-hosted installations (see the table of limits below); the served model keeps keys per customer (M14)

TamperingDatabase changes outside the defined schemaSchema and migrations defined once in Rust, refused on a newer schemaDATA-MIGRATIONS; ARCH-DB-PARITY
Elevation of privilegeMemory-safety bugsNo unsafe code unless an ADR allows itARCH-NO-UNSAFE

Accepted risks

RiskWhy acceptedRevisit
Somebody whom a share reaches and who holds the ID of a saved search can tell, by the time an answer takes or by a page of Shared with me that ends at the bound of names (a short page with the last search shown as its cursor, then an empty page), that a search shared with them exists and passes the check of its fields but fails on a name they cannot know (a person they are not shown by name, a group they are not in, an issue they do not read): resolving that name reads from the store, and a search that does not exist, does not reach them or fails an earlier check does notEvery one of these is the same answer: the status, the code and the body of not found. A search that does not exist, one that does not reach the person and one that fails the check of its fields run the same reads. The ID is random (80 bits) and is only known from a link or an event. What leaks is that a search that the person who shared it chose to share with them exists and fails on some name, never which name, and the receiver cannot choose the text (ADR-0034, decision 4 and item 8)sec_06_a_hidden_saved_search_and_a_missing_one_run_the_same_reads (the same reads), qry_06_a_search_that_does_not_check_for_the_receiver_is_not_there_for_any_call (the same answers); revisit when a search can be shared outside the organization
The preview of a file that is stored already shows as soon as the job of its attachment runs, while the preview of a new file is made first and takes longer, so somebody who watches when a preview appears can tell, a little, that the same content was stored beforeThe statuses and links in every answer are the same; the person already holds the content; a delay as long as the slowest preview would make every picture wait, so none is added (ADR-0032 §4)When files get rules of their own (M9, GDPR handling of file bytes)
Finishing a file that is stored already is a little faster than finishing a new one, so somebody who measures the time can tell that the same content was stored beforeThe answers are the same (no preview, no link, no status of the other attachment); the person already holds the content; equal time would mean reading and writing the file again for nothing (ADR-0032)When files get rules of their own (M9, GDPR handling of file bytes)
On Windows the child of a preview has a limit on its heap and none on its address spaceNo safe crate sets the memory limit of a job object and unsafe code is forbidden; the child is pure Rust and the allocator refuses what would pass 1 GiB (ADR-0032)When a safe way to set the limit exists
An administrator of the host machine can read the master keyAnyone with full control of the host can read process memory too; protection against them is out of scope for self-hosted installationsM14 (served model: keys per customer, operator without data access)
Somebody who controls the host (and so reads keys/log.key and can rewrite logs/security-head.log) can forge the security logThe log protects against attackers who reach only the database; the same control lets them read process memory and the master keyM14 (served model: keys per customer, operator without data access)
Somebody who keeps failing at an account can make it wait, up to 15 minutes at a time once the windows have grown (the limit counts failures and a success clears them, so it is never a lock for good)Any limit that stops guessing can be used to slow the person down; a permanent lock would be worse (SEC-14)When the settings registry takes the numbers (OPS-10)
A security-log entry that cannot be written (the anchor file or the database fails) is reported in the server log but does not undo or refuse the sign-in. The server counts the entries it could not write since it started, and the status page warns when the count is above zero (sec_15_the_status_page_warns_when_a_log_entry_could_not_be_written); the status page and bugaboo security-log verify also name a database that lacks the newest entries that the anchor file knows of (a restore from an older backup, lost writes or a cut-off end) and say what to check (sec_15_the_status_page_warns_when_the_anchor_is_ahead)A sign-in that fails because the log is full would let anybody who can fill the disk lock everybody outThe decision stays (M1-F40, done in M2 WP-04)
Check access tells a checker that a role comes from a project you can't see, so they learn that such a project exists above, never its name or anything in itA sentence that leaves the row out would explain a decision wrongly; only people who can check access at that place see it (ADR-0025, decision 12)When restricted projects need more (SEC-05, V1)
The version of a move preview is a digest of the tree, who has which role and the levels the roles set, so somebody who keeps asking for the preview of a project they see can tell that something changed in a project they cannot seeThe preview is what Show, then do needs and a stale one is refused; the digest is opaque and names nothing, no count and no place, and the person only learns that the preview is old (ADR-0025, decision 12)When restricted projects need more (SEC-05, V1)
People with Decide who has which role from above keep it on a project where they have No access, and see its name and short name thereOtherwise a project lead could shut the administrators out for good (ADR-0025, decision 6)—
The child that makes a preview holds the rights of the server account: protection is the separation of the process and the limits on memory, time and pixels, not a sandbox. A memory-safety bug in image, hayro or vello_cpu (they use unsafe inside, though our code does not) lets a crafted file run code in the child, which can then read the keys and the database of the server account and reach the networkThe libraries are pure Rust with only the gif, jpeg, png and webp decoders compiled in, and the child reads its input from standard input with limits; a sandbox needs system calls that code without unsafe cannot make today. The row of denial of service above says what the limits stop (crashes and bombs), not a compromise. On a small host, five previews at once may use 5 GiB of heapM4-F121 (landlock or seccomp on Linux, a separate user, a restricted token on Windows once a safe crate exists)
A person who may change their handle can learn once for each change whether one handle is taken (name.taken, or the handle of a group or a role), because a free handle is changed at once and starts the 7-day clock; a few refused tries are allowed firstHandles are made from names, so a guess is cheap, but the limits leave a person at most 20 answers taken in a day (TAKEN_ANSWERS_PER_DAY, counted per person, reserved in one step so parallel tries cannot pass the last one, after which every handle gets the same try again later) and, for each change, one more. The day is a fixed window from the first answer counted, so a person can get up to about 40 across the turn of a day; each server process counts for itself and a restart forgets the count, so with several processes the bound is 20 a day for each process; the refused tries of a minute only pace it. A person who never changed their handle has no 7-day clock, so the bound is 20 a day without end, for each account; the handle is shown wherever a mention is, and a mention follows Who sees peopleWhen a handle is judged apart from the rest of the person's data
While the list of domains for signing up is empty (open sign-up), a few networks can use up the cap on sign-up e-mails (ADDRESSES_PER_HOUR_MAX = 100 addresses an hour for the whole server): each network may make SIGN_UP_REQUESTS_PER_HOUR = 20 requests an hour, so five networks fill the cap, and real sign-up e-mails are then dropped without a word until the hour is overThe cap keeps strangers from receiving mail in bulk, and the server has to be cheaper to fill than to keep silent: the cap is the safer failure. The answer stays the same for every address; the cap counts only while anybody may sign up, so a list of approved domains (the first thing to set) takes the cap away; the moment the cap is reached is written once to the security log (sign_up.mail_capped); the request limit per network is held well under the cap by a const assertM4-F128 (review: a decision of the lead, a note for administrators when sign-up e-mails were capped, M9)
A plus tag (a+1@b.co) is another address to Bugaboo and often the same mailbox for the mail server, so one mailbox can be signed up several timesThe limit is 5 sign-up tries a minute for a network and the cap of the server; stripping tags would change addresses that are realWhen signing up is next changed
Whoever holds Change organization settings (or a stolen administrator session) can point mail.host and mail.port at the internal network and tell open ports apart from the answers of the test e-mailOne try in 10 seconds; changing the host deletes the stored password; the right is the one that sets the whole server upM4-F123 (ask for the password again before mail.* changes)
A Guest can mention a role and so e-mail everyone who holds itAt most 50 mentions in a text and one e-mail in 5 minutes for each issue; the mention follows the writer's rights and the recipient has to see the issueM4-F124 (review: a decision of the lead on mentions)
The editor of a workflow lists the names of all roles to a person who manages workflows, while the list of roles needs Manage roles or Decide who has which roleThe names are needed to choose Who can do it; it matters only for custom rolesM4-F125
Self-signed certificates show a browser warningSafer than plain HTTP; admins can provide a certificate, ACME comes in 1.0V1 (ACME)
A request with an access key takes a little different time depending on what is wrong with the key (not shaped like a key, unknown, ran out): only somebody who holds a whole secret can tell that it ran out, and the answer is the sameEqual time needs a dummy lookup and protects nothing against a person who already holds the secretM2-F51: when a measurement shows a difference that does not need a secret

No personal data leaves the server in M1: no mail, no AI, no outside fonts, scripts or analytics (PRIV-01).

Personal data in M2

M2 adds where people work (groups and roles), projects, access keys and each person's own settings. The marks below are decided here (ADR-0025); each package writes them on its entities, and cargo xtask gen privacy then lists them on the generated page docs/privacy/personal-data.md. Enforced by: DATA-MARKS.

A new category, organization: where a person works, meaning their groups and the roles they have, and where. Its legal basis is the contract (Art. 6(1)(b); for employees in Germany together with Art. 88 GDPR and § 26 BDSG): an organization cannot give people work in projects without recording who may do what.

flowchart LR
  admin(["Administrator or project lead"])
  person(["Person"])
  script(["Script or app<br/>with an access key"])
  subgraph bb["Bugaboo"]
    groups["Groups and members"]
    assign["Who has which role<br/>person or group, role or No access, project"]
    rules["Field levels and Who sees people<br/>(no personal data)"]
    keys["Access keys<br/>owner, name, hashed secret,<br/>last use (to the minute)"]
    mine["My settings<br/>time zone, region, appearance, shortcuts"]
    policy["bb-policy<br/>evaluation per request"]
    seclog["Security log"]
  end
  admin -- "manages" --> groups & assign & rules
  person -- "chooses" --> mine
  person -- "makes" --> keys
  script -- "Bearer key" --> keys --> policy
  groups & assign & rules --> policy
  groups & assign & rules & keys --> seclog

Personal data in M4

Decision records

Each record explains one decision: the situation, what we decided, what follows from it, what else we considered, and which checks enforce it.

ADR-0001: Modular monolith in one binary

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Bugaboo must be secure, fast and installable on Windows, Linux and WSL by people without operations experience. The scale target (500 people, 1 M issues) fits one machine.

Decision

Build one Rust binary containing the API, the embedded browser app, background jobs and the MCP server. Inside, use a hexagonal structure: a pure domain core (bb-core, bb-policy, bb-searchlang, bb-markdown), use cases (bb-app) that depend only on ports (traits), and adapters (bb-store, bb-files, bb-ai, bb-notify, bb-api, bb-mcp). Module boundaries are crates, and dependency rules are checked by cargo xtask check only ARCH-DEPS.

Consequences

  • One process, one security boundary, one thing to install, back up and update.
  • Use cases are testable with in-memory fakes; adapters are tested separately.
  • Scaling beyond one machine would need work later (accepted: not a 1.0 goal).

Alternatives considered

  • Microservices: more moving parts, more attack surface, harder installation. Rejected.
  • One big crate: faster to start, but boundaries erode and compile times grow. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-DEPS, ARCH-HTTP-EDGE, ARCH-MAP-SYNC, META-NEW-MODULE (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0002: HTTP stack: Tokio, axum, rustls

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

We need a mature async HTTP server with good middleware, HTTPS without system OpenSSL, and easy static builds for Windows and Linux.

Decision

Use tokio as the runtime, axum for routing and extractors, tower-http for compression, headers and limits, and rustls (with tokio-rustls) for TLS, using the ring crypto provider so static musl and Windows builds need no C toolchain beyond what Rust ships. instant-acme handles certificates from ACME.

Consequences

  • No OpenSSL dependency; memory-safe TLS.
  • axum extractors give one place to turn credentials into an actor.

Alternatives considered

  • actix-web: fine, but a smaller middleware ecosystem around tower.
  • aws-lc-rs provider: stronger FIPS story, but needs CMake/C for static builds; revisit if FIPS is ever required.

Enforced by

SEC-HEADERS, DEP-LICENSES (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0003: Databases: SQLite by default, PostgreSQL optional

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Installation must work with zero setup, but larger installations and the served model need a server database.

Decision

Support SQLite (bundled, WAL mode) and PostgreSQL 16+ through sqlx. Write queries with sea-query (bound through sea-query-sqlx) so one query definition produces both dialects. Define the schema and migrations once in Rust with the same query builder; both databases run the same migration list. Dialect-specific code is allowed only behind the bb-store port implementations and needs a comment explaining why.

Consequences

  • Every repository test runs against both databases in CI.
  • Some PostgreSQL features (for example row-level security) are not used in core paths; authorization stays in bb-policy anyway.
  • The served model uses PostgreSQL; self-hosted installations start with SQLite and can migrate with bugaboo migrate-to-postgres.

Alternatives considered

  • PostgreSQL only: simpler code, harder installation. Rejected for the default.
  • SeaORM: less control over generated SQL for permission predicates. Rejected.
  • Two hand-written migration folders: violates SSOT. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-SQL-EDGE, DATA-MIGRATIONS, ARCH-DB-PARITY (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0004: Authorization: one policy engine and Authorized

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04 · refined by ADR-0025

Context

Security is priority one. Permissions go down to single fields and single issues, and many entry points (UI, API, search, MCP, assistant, e-mail, webhooks, exports, live updates) must all obey them.

Decision

  • All decisions are made by bb-policy: permission catalogue, role assignments on the project tree with inheritance and explicit deny, field masks, visibility groups and token scopes.
  • Data leaves the domain only as Authorized<T>, whose constructor is private to bb-policy. It carries the field mask and applies it when serialized. Returning plain domain types from bb-app is a compile error at the API layer.
  • Searches get the actor's visibility predicates compiled into the same SQL query, and the parser only knows readable fields, so a hidden field looks exactly like an unknown one.
  • Outbound channels (notifications, webhooks, live updates, exports, assistant context) apply the receiver's mask.

Consequences

  • Forgetting a check is hard: the types don't line up.
  • A generated test matrix (roles × permissions × fields × entry points) runs on every build.
  • Per-request caching of evaluations keeps it fast.

Alternatives considered

  • Checks in each handler: easy to forget one. Rejected.
  • Database row-level security: PostgreSQL only, and field-level rules would still be needed in code. Rejected.
  • External policy engines (OPA, Cedar): another language and runtime to secure and ship; our model is fixed and well understood. Rejected for now; the catalogue could be exported to Cedar later.

Enforced by

ARCH-AUTHZ-ONLY, ARCH-API-OUT, ARCH-PERMS, SEC-MATRIX (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0005: Search language: one Rust crate, also in the browser

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

People need simple filter buttons and an advanced typed search, converting exactly into each other, with the same behavior in the browser and on the server, and without copying another vendor's language.

Decision

Write bb-searchlang: lexer, parser, syntax tree, canonical printer, checker and suggestions, with no I/O. Simple search edits the syntax tree; Advanced search edits text that parses into the same tree. Compile the crate to WebAssembly (bb-wasm) for instant highlighting, suggestions and error messages in the browser. The server compiles the tree to SQL in bb-store.

Consequences

  • One grammar (SSOT). Property test: parse(print(tree)) == tree.
  • WebAssembly adds download size; it's loaded only when search is first used, within its own WebAssembly budget in tools/checks/perf-bundle.toml (amendment M5, decision 7).

Alternatives considered

  • A grammar written twice (Rust and TypeScript): drifts. Rejected.
  • Parser generators (pest, lalrpop): fine, but hand-written recursive descent gives better plain-language error messages. Decision left to the milestone, as long as the crate stays I/O-free.

Amendment M5 (2026-10-25): the words, the limits and what crosses the wire

The M5 proposals (M5-Q7, Q10) were accepted. Decided:

  1. The parser is written by hand (recursive descent), for plain-language messages and a small WebAssembly module. No parser generator.
