For an actor and a place (the organization, or a project with its parents), bb-policy decides without I/O, from one port call that loads the actor's assignments for the place and its parents:

  1. Nobody signed in: only public routes. Signed in without an applicable assignment: nothing (default deny, SEC-01).
  2. Applicable are the actor's own and their groups' assignments for the whole organization, those on a parent of the project with This project and its sub-projects, and those on the project itself.
  3. Each applicable row has a rank: first the depth of its project (whole organization lowest), then the person's own row above a row of one of their groups.
  4. No access (M2-Q1): the highest-ranked No access row removes every role row of equal or lower rank. So it wins over roles given higher up, over a role of one of the person's groups on the same project, and over another group's role on the same project. A role given lower down (on a sub-project below the No access), or given to the person directly on the same project where a group has No access, still counts: the nearer, more personal row decides.
  5. The permissions are the union of the remaining roles, filtered by where it counts; then an access key narrows them (decision 8).
  6. The field mask and the Who sees people levels are worked out from the same remaining roles (decisions 10 and 11).

Evaluations are cached for one request and never across requests, so a role taken away counts from the next request. Enforced by: review (the cache is a field of the request context, which a reviewer sees in the diff), backed by the tests sec_03_no_access_on_a_sub_project_wins_over_a_role_from_above, sec_03_a_role_taken_away_counts_from_the_next_request and the property tests of WP-05 (a new role never takes a permission away; No access never adds one), and SEC-MATRIX.

4. Starting roles are editable copies
  • One Rust definition in bb-policy holds the six starting roles of SEC-08 and M2-Q5 (Administrator, Project lead, Team member, Contributor, Viewer, Guest): their permissions, field levels, Who sees people levels and order (architecture §7). A system use case makes editable copies from it once, at the first start, with events and security-log entries (never in a migration). After that the definition is read only by Reset to the starting permissions, which a copy keeps through a starting mark that renaming does not remove.
  • A starting role can be renamed, changed and deleted like any other role; the last-administrator rule (decision 6) still holds. Enforced by: the tests sec_08_starting_roles_are_made_once_and_can_be_changed_and_reset and sec_08_a_changed_starting_role_can_be_reset.
  • The order of roles (the starting order, then new roles where an administrator puts them) decides the label of a person shown as Role only when they hold several roles: the first in the order.
5. The administrator flag becomes the Administrator role
  • Migration m0003 keeps the list of M1 administrators. In the same change that makes the starting roles at the first start, each of them gets the Administrator role for the whole organization, with its event and security-log entry; afterwards the flag no longer exists in the database, the API (/auth/me answers the person's organization permissions instead) or the browser app. Enforced by: the test sec_08_m1_administrators_become_administrators_and_nobody_else_does (both databases).
  • Setup (AUTH-09) stays open while nobody can manage roles for the whole organization (decision 6 makes that the state of a fresh installation only). Making the first administrator makes the starting roles if they do not exist yet and gives the person the Administrator role for the whole organization, in one change.
6. Nobody locks the organization out, and nobody gives what they do not have
  • The last administrator: a change that would leave no person who holds both Manage roles and Decide who has which role for the whole organization (through their own row or a group) is refused, with a sentence that says why. This covers removing a row, taking a person out of a group, deleting a group or role, and taking a permission out of a role. Enforced by: the test sec_08_nobody_can_remove_the_last_way_to_manage_roles.
  • No access never locks out the people above: Decide who has which role on a project is kept for a person who holds it through a row that the project's No access removed, only when that row is strictly above the No access (a parent project, or the whole organization). A row at the depth of a No access that removes it, such as a role of the person's group next to their own No access on the same project, is removed as a whole: otherwise a person could lift their own No access. They see the project's name and short name in Who has which role and can take the No access away again; they see nothing in the project. Enforced by: the tests sec_03_no_access_cannot_lock_out_the_people_who_decide_roles_above and sec_03_decide_roles_is_kept_only_from_rows_strictly_above_the_no_access (engine), and sec_03_decide_roles_is_not_kept_from_a_row_at_the_same_depth_as_the_no_access (both databases).
  • No escalation: a person can add a permission to a role, or give a role, only when they hold every permission of it at that place themselves (organization permissions are left out of this comparison for a role given on a project, because they count nowhere there). A role given with its sub-projects reaches the sub-projects made later as well as those that exist, so the giver holds it through rows that reach sub-projects themselves (their rows for the project alone do not count) and in every sub-project that exists (a lead for one project only cannot make themselves lead of everything below it, now or when a sub-project is made). Putting a person into a group gives them every role of the group, so the same holds for each row of the group. The check runs inside the change, after the policy lock (making a project takes the lock too), so two changes cannot both pass on what was stored before; the same holds for adding to a role and for resetting one, which read the role and what the person holds there. A level is held to the same rule: taking a project's setting away is setting the level that then applies there (the nearest parent's, else the role's own). Enforced by: the tests sec_08_nobody_adds_a_permission_they_do_not_hold_to_a_role, sec_02_nobody_gives_a_role_with_more_than_they_hold_there, sec_02_nobody_gives_a_role_with_sub_projects_they_do_not_hold_there, sec_02_a_role_with_sub_projects_needs_a_row_that_reaches_sub_projects, sec_02_a_group_with_a_role_for_sub_projects_is_not_joined_by_a_lead_of_one_project and sec_04_nobody_raises_a_level_by_taking_an_override_away.
  • Manage groups does not lift a No access: taking a person out of a group, or deleting a group, that has No access rows takes those rows away for them, so it needs Decide who has which role at each project where the group has one, like taking the row away itself. Giving, adding to a group, taking out of a group and deleting a group are the four ways a person's rights change through a group. Enforced by: the test sec_02_manage_groups_does_not_lift_a_no_access_of_the_group.
7. Two-step sign-in is a switch on the role
  • A role has a switch Two-step sign-in for everyone with this role (AUTH-03, M1-F45), stored with the role; the text setting security.two-step-required-roles is removed with its stored values (WP-05). security.two-step-required stays: it asks it of everybody.
  • A person needs a second step when the organization switch is on or any role they hold anywhere (own row or group, any place) has the switch on. It takes effect at the next request: until the person has a code app or a passkey, their session can only set one up. Enforced by: the test auth_03_a_role_that_requires_two_step_sign_in_makes_its_people_set_it_up_first (WP-09).
  • Access keys follow it (M2-F46): while a person is asked for a second step, the keys they made are refused too, with 403 auth.second-step-required and an entry in the security log, and work again as soon as they have set one up. Without this, an old key of a person who is asked for a second step would still work and could even switch the requirement off for its owner. Enforced by: the tests auth_03_a_key_made_before_the_switch_is_refused_until_its_owner_sets_up_a_second_step and auth_03_a_key_cannot_switch_off_the_requirement_of_its_owner (WP-09).
8. Access keys can only narrow
  • What it may do (M2-Q6) is one of three choices: See only (permissions of kind See, every field at most Can see), See and change (See and Change), Everything I can do (all kinds); under More options, single permissions instead. Optionally a list of projects: the key then counts only in them and their sub-projects (by project ID, so a move does not change it) and gives nothing for the whole organization.
  • At every use the key's permissions are the owner's evaluation at that place intersected with the key's choice and projects; a key never widens anything, and follows its owner's roles at once (AUTH-07). No key reaches the owner's own sign-in data (password, passkeys, two-step, sessions, access keys), and a key is refused while its owner is asked for a second step (decision 7).
  • What no key holds (decision): whatever its choice, even Everything I can do and single permissions, a key never keeps Invite people, Manage people, Manage groups, Manage roles, Decide who has which role, Decide what roles see and Change organization settings (lead decision of 2026-10-06, so that a key cannot switch off the two-step requirement, open signing up or change how long sessions last). Later decisions added five: Edit anyway (ADR-0019), Manage issue types, kinds of relation and layouts, the permission to create, change and retire fields, Manage labels and tags (M3-Q6), and Manage workflows (ADR-0031), so the list in the code has twelve entries. They stay in the app, where the person is signed in, so a stolen key cannot invite an administrator, take roles away or change the settings of the organization. The list is defined once beside the kinds, in bb-policy (NOT_FOR_KEYS); narrowing removes them, the key form does not offer them and the server refuses a key made with one. Enforced by: the tests auth_07_a_key_never_invites_people_or_changes_roles_whatever_its_choice (it also tries the settings of the organization), auth_07_single_permissions_of_a_key_never_include_those_a_key_never_holds and the property test auth_07_a_key_can_do_only_what_its_owner_can_and_its_scopes_allow (WP-09).
  • Keys end with Sign out everywhere (decision): the person's keys are deleted in the same change, each one with an entry in the security log. A password change ends the other sessions and leaves the keys. Enforced by: the test auth_07_sign_out_everywhere_ends_the_keys_and_a_password_change_leaves_them (WP-09).
  • Every key runs out: 90 days unless the person picks another date, never later than the organization's longest time (an organization setting, default and most 365 days). The key ends at a moment, now plus a number of days, and every day the screen shows is the calendar day of a moment in the person's region zone: the day filled in is the day of now plus the default (or the longest time, if that is shorter), the latest day the day of now plus the longest time, and a picked day is sent as the end of that day or the longest time from now, whichever comes first. The server refuses a moment later than the longest time, except that one at most five minutes later (a device clock a little fast) is cut to the longest time. The settings are declared in the registry by WP-09. Enforced by: the tests auth_07_a_key_can_do_only_what_its_owner_can_and_its_scopes_allow (property test), auth_07_a_moment_a_little_after_the_longest_time_is_cut_to_it_for_a_clock_that_is_fast, auth_07_a_moment_later_than_the_slack_or_not_in_the_future_is_refused, the Vitest file expiry-day.test.ts, auth_07_a_key_follows_its_owner_losing_a_role_at_once and auth_07_a_key_cannot_change_the_owners_sign_in_data, and SEC-MATRIX (an access key with See only, and one for another project).
9. Every permission change is in the security log

Every change of roles (permissions, two-step switch, name, reset), groups (made, renamed, deleted, members), assignments (including No access), field levels, Who sees people levels, project moves and short names, and access keys (made, deleted, refused) writes its domain event and a security-log entry in the same change (SEC-15). Enforced by: ARCH-EVENTS, and the generated test sec_15_every_change_of_permissions_is_in_the_security_log that runs every management use case (WP-05).

10. Field masks
  • The field catalogue (built-in fields of M2-Q7) is declared once in bb-core; own fields join in M3 (CF-06). Each field has a level per role: Hidden < Can see < Can change. The organization level is the role's own level; a project can set another level for a role, which its sub-projects inherit until one of them sets its own.
  • The mask is the highest level of the remaining roles (decision 3), capped at Can see for a See only key. Authorized<T> carries it and leaves hidden fields out when it is serialized; a hidden field and an unknown one are refused alike. Enforced by: ARCH-AUTHZ-ONLY, ARCH-API-OUT, SEC-MATRIX, and the test sec_06_a_hidden_field_is_not_in_the_answer_and_asking_for_it_fails_like_an_unknown_field.
11. People: PersonRef and the kinds of people information
  • Who sees people (ADR-0022) is set per role and per kind of people information; M2 adds the kind Project members (M2-Q3): member lists of a project. Levels are inherited like field levels; the viewer's level is the most open of their remaining roles (Names > Role only > Hidden).
  • People who manage see names (M2-Q3): in Organization settings, Who has which role and Check access, a viewer who holds Manage people, Manage groups, Manage roles or Decide who has which role at that place always sees names; everybody else sees the people there by the kind Project members. E-mail addresses are part of no PersonRef: only Manage people and the person themselves see them.
  • PersonRef resolves for the viewer, the kind and the place into a name, a role label, Someone, or a random Former user label (PRIV-13); the viewer always sees their own name. A role label and Someone carry no ID of the person. Enforced by: ARCH-PERSON-REF, SEC-MATRIX (people rows), and the tests priv_12_people_are_shown_by_name_role_or_someone_as_the_rules_say and priv_13_former_user_labels_are_random_and_unique.
12. Check access answers with reasons

Check access is a query use case: for a person and a place it lists every permission that counts there with yes or no, every field with its level and every kind of people information with its level, each with its reasons as data (the row, the person or group, the role, the project it is on, whether it is inherited, a No access that decided, or that no role gives it). The browser turns the reasons into sentences from message keys. A reason never names a project the checker cannot see: it says the row is on a project you can't see. Enforced by: the property test sec_03_check_access_explains_every_result_with_the_chain_of_reasons (the decision equals the engine's and the reasons lead to it) and sec_03_check_access_names_no_project_the_checker_cannot_see.

13. Projects and short names
  • A short name (M2-Q4) is 2 to 10 capital letters or digits and starts with a letter (WEB, APP2); it is unique in the organization, old short names included, and can be changed. An old short name stays with its project, so its addresses keep working (project_alias, like issue_alias in ADR-0021); only that project can take it back. One definition, ShortName in bb-core. Enforced by: the tests prj_01_a_short_name_breaks_no_rule_of_m2_q4 and prj_01_an_old_short_name_redirects.
  • Hidden projects stay hidden: a project the person cannot see answers resource.not-found like a missing one, by address and by short name; a visible sub-project of a hidden project is shown at the top and never names its parent. A short name that is taken is told only to people who may create projects at that place, with the same sentence whether the project is hidden or not. Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX, the tests prj_01_a_hidden_project_answers_not_found_like_a_missing_one, prj_01_a_visible_sub_project_of_a_hidden_project_does_not_name_it and prj_01_a_taken_short_name_is_told_only_to_people_who_may_create_projects.
14. Who may change a setting

The registry's changed_by (ADR-0018) maps to the catalogue: Administrators → Change organization settings; Project leads → Change project settings on that project; Each person → only their own value. Enforced by: ARCH-SETTINGS, and the test cfg_06_only_administrators_change_organization_values_and_each_person_only_their_own (WP-07).

Consequences

  • WP-05 builds the engine from this record and architecture §7; WP-08, WP-09, WP-11 and WP-12 put screens and routes on it; SEC-MATRIX (WP-10) runs every route for every starting role, a role on a parent and on a sibling project, No access and two access keys.
  • The deny rule has one exception (decision 6), so administrators cannot be shut out of a sub-project for good; the people above see that the project exists, but not what is in it.
  • Group membership and role assignments are personal data of a new category, organization (where a person works); access keys and the person's own settings are personal data too. The marks are listed in 12-security.md and come from the code into the generated personal-data page when WP-05, WP-07, WP-08 and WP-09 add the entities. Enforced by: DATA-MARKS.
  • Check access tells a checker that a role comes from a project you can't see, so a hidden parent's existence (never its name) shows there.
  • Removing the M1 flag touches every place that read administrator, in Rust and in the browser app (WP-05).

Alternatives considered

  • No access that wins in its whole subtree, even over roles given lower down: simpler, but an organization could then not hide a big project from a group except for one sub-project. Rejected; the nearer row decides, as for field levels.
  • No access only for the people it names, never over a group's role at the same project: a person could not be taken out of one project without leaving their group. Rejected (M2-Q1).
  • Hard-coded roles: SEC-08 asks for editable copies. Rejected.
  • Reading the starting definition at every evaluation (roles as overrides of the definition): a change of the definition in an update would silently change every organization's roles. Rejected; copies are made once.
  • Access keys with their own role: keys could then hold more than their owner. Rejected (AUTH-07: keys only narrow).
  • The deny as a role (No access is a role with no permissions): a role adds, it cannot take away. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-PERMS, ARCH-AUTHZ-ONLY, ARCH-API-OUT, ARCH-PERSON-REF, ARCH-NO-COUNTERS, ARCH-EVENTS, ARCH-SETTINGS, DATA-MARKS and SEC-MATRIX (see tools/checks/catalog.toml), backed by the named tests of WP-05, WP-08, WP-09, WP-11 and WP-12; the per-request cache by review.

ADR-0026: One theme file for everything about how the app looks

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-08 · replaces the styling part of ADR-0010

Context

Requirement (M2C): all UI theming lives in one theming file, the way the sister project the sister project keeps its complete look in defaults/theme.kdl. ADR-0010 made design/tokens.json the source of colors, fonts, sizes, radii and shadows, but let every component keep its own CSS Module. The audit of M2C (section D) found what that costs:

  • 55 CSS modules with 3,261 lines; values that have no token (font-weight: 700 57 times, line heights 38 times, about 50 1px solid borders, a z-index chosen per file, opacities, keyframes);
  • the same rule copied into many modules (the focus ring 22 times, the muted text, .stack, .row), the skip link twice, and forced-colors handling in ten components;
  • the theme list written in tokens.json and again in the settings registry in Rust, held together by a test (M2C-F64);
  • theme names and the data-look attribute written by hand in TypeScript and in the browser tests.

the sister project compiles its theme to CSS in the browser and injects it as a style element. Bugaboo cannot do that: the content security policy is style-src 'self' (SEC-11), so nothing may put a style on the page at run time.

Decision

  1. One file, design/theme.kdl (KDL, like the sister project; decision M2C-Q1). It holds everything: the themes, the choices that change token values, every token with its variants per mode, the contrast rules, the mixins, the keyframes and the rules of every component. Comments are allowed, and each token is one line. It replaces design/tokens.json. Only cargo xtask gen theme reads it (with the kdl crate, pinned like the sister project's); the server and the browser never parse KDL.

  2. Values are tokens, with their variants per mode on the line of the token. A token has a kind (color, font, size, number, duration, easing, shadow, weight, line-height, border-width, layer, opacity) and, besides its value:

    • <theme>= for each of the four themes (colors and shadows), with kind="light" or "dark" on the theme;
    • <theme>-more= for a device that asks for more contrast (prefers-contrast: more);
    • forced= while forced colors are on (forced-colors: active);
    • <choice>= while a choice of the person is on: compact spacing, larger-text, less-motion (which the device can switch on too).

    Every token of ADR-0010 keeps its value; the file adds font weight, line height, border width, layers (z-index), opacity, easing, the brightness of a pressed primary button, and forced colors as a mode. The focus ring is two tokens (ring-width, ring-offset) and one mixin (ring) that every rule uses.

  3. Rules are part rules that use tokens only. part "button[variant=primary]:hover" { background "$accent" } styles every element that says data-part="button" and data-variant="primary". A value is a word, 0, a percentage, or $token (written var(--token) in the output); a length, color, duration, weight, line height, layer or opacity written out is a finding of LINT-CSS and STY-TOKENS. base rules style the page frame (html, body); mixin, keyframes and forced { … }, more-contrast { … }, media "…" { … } blocks complete the language.

  4. Components carry no style values and no class names. They emit data-part, data-state and data-variant, through partOf(part.button, { variants: […], states: […] }) of @bugaboo/ui. The names of the parts and the words a part may have (partWords) are generated into tokens.ts from the rules, so a misspelled part or word is a type error. React Aria's own data-* state attributes (data-hovered, data-pressed, data-selected, data-focus-visible, data-entering, …) are allowed and used: a rule names them as button[hovered].

  5. The file is compiled at build time into one static style sheet, web/packages/ui/src/theme.css (committed, with a copy for the design pages at docs/design/theme.css). The content security policy stays style-src 'self'; no style element or attribute is made at run time. This is where Bugaboo differs from the sister project. Neither file is edited by hand: DOC-GENERATED compares them with the output of cargo xtask gen theme.

  6. The list of themes is written once. The four built-in themes (Daylight, Paper, Dusk, Midnight) and the two that start are defined in the file. gen theme writes them to TypeScript (tokens.ts: themeIds, lightThemeIds, darkThemeIds, the defaults) and to Rust (crates/bb-core/src/settings/themes.rs: the choices of the settings Light theme and Dark theme and their defaults, which catalog.rs names). The reader of the settings registry follows those names, so the browser's generated choices and defaults come from the same file. There is no hand-kept list in catalog.rs and no test that holds two lists together (closes M2C-F64).

  7. Custom themes, later, store token values only: names from the generated token list, values checked by the kind of the token. They never add a rule, a selector or CSS text. How the values reach the page without breaking the policy is decided when the theme editor is built.

  8. Contrast is checked per theme and per mode (STY-CONTRAST), the way the sister project's theme_contrast does: every text color on every background in each theme, and with <theme>-more= the 7:1 and 3:1 rules of ADR-0010. The rules for it are the contrast and distinct lines of the same file.

  9. The design pages are generated too. docs/design/components.css, docpage.css, ux-design.css and mockup.css style the documents and mockups in docs/, not the app (the last two hold what the UX page and the mockup had in a <style> block, and the classes that replaced their style= attributes). They are written in the same file as docs blocks: rule lines with plain CSS selectors (the pages use class names and elements, which parts must not) that use tokens only, and the tokens of the pages themselves (doc-…), which go to docs/design/theme.css and not to the app's sheet. gen theme writes both sheets, LINT-CSS reads them like the parts, and DOC-GENERATED compares them (M2C-F93, done in C-06). The motion of the pages follows the motion tokens, so there is no reduced-motion rule with !important. THEME-ONLY reads the pages of docs/ too: no <style> element and no style attribute in the markup, unless the page's own script builds its value (a position or a color it computes, which is a style of the run time, M2C-F105).

  10. Moving was done in two steps. M2C C-01 built the engine and moved the primitives of packages/ui. M2C C-06 moved every app feature, the shell and the other components (M2C-F90): there is no CSS Module, no cx and no exemption any more, and THEME-ONLY passes with nothing exempt. What several features said the same way is one part (stack, text, muted, row, list, item, facts, hint, …, M2C-F65), and the focus ring, the skip link and the forced-colors outline of the marked item (marked) are written once.

  11. The names of the page frame are written once. The attributes of <html> that the sheets and the code use (data-look, data-theme, data-preview-look) are the frame line of the file. gen theme writes them to the sheets, to tokens.ts (pageAttributes), which theme.ts, the theme sample and the end-to-end specs read, and to docs/design/frame.js (bugabooFrame), which the scripts of the design pages read (M2C-F91). The choices (data-spacing, data-text, data-motion) are read from variants the same way.

Update 2026-10-16 (M3 WP-16, the new look)

  • Choices of the device. A variant may have only media= (no attribute on the page): touch ((pointer: coarse), (width < $bp-tablet)) gives a token its finger value (size-control 36 becomes 44, size-row 44 becomes 64), phone gives text 16. A media query may name a $token with a plain value.
  • Container queries. A rule may hold container "(min-width: $bp-window-side)" { … }, written as @container: a window follows its own width, not the screen's (UX §6.3).
  • One run-time style. The size a person drags a window to is two variables of the theme file (window-width, window-height). THEME-ONLY allows exactly element.style.setProperty(variableOf("…"), value): variableOf only takes the name of a token, and nothing else may set a style from code.
  • The pictures use the parts. cargo xtask gen theme also writes docs/design/parts.css, the rules of the parts without the tokens, so the pictures of the UX design are drawn with the same data-part markup as the app and cannot differ from it.
  • Several distinct rules. The hovered and the selected row must differ from the tint of a status group as well as from the plain surfaces, so the file has one distinct rule for the plain surfaces and one for each tint.

Consequences

  • A change of look is a change in one file, and the generated sheet shows it in the diff. A rule exists once: the focus ring, the muted text, the field label.
  • Writing a component needs no CSS file and no class name. A style that the person's choices (spacing, text size, motion, contrast) cannot reach cannot be written.
  • cargo xtask gen theme is part of the build of the browser app and of DOC-GENERATED. The generated sheet is committed, so the server's embedded app needs no extra build step.
  • Specificity is that of attribute selectors, so the order in the file is the order in the sheet: a rule for a state is written after the rules for the variants it must win over. Enforced by: review (the order is seen in the diff of the file; the screenshots of the showcase show a change of look).
  • Rules for forced colors move to tokens (forced=) where one system color serves everywhere; a part keeps a forced { … } block where its own colors differ (a disabled button, a link).

Alternatives considered

  • Keep JSON (design/theme.json): no new dependency, but no comments, long, and the variants of a value would not sit on one line. The maintainer chose KDL.
  • the sister project's way, compiling in the browser: needs a style element or adoptedStyleSheets from a string, which style-src 'self' forbids. Rejected.
  • Keep CSS Modules next to the token file: the situation of the audit. Rejected.
  • A hand-written style sheet with the same data attributes: the values and the rules would again be in two places that no tool joins, and the theme list could not be generated from it.
  • Tailwind CSS and CSS-in-JS at run time: rejected in ADR-0010 and still.

Enforced by

THEME-ONLY (no style=, no className, no CSS file but the generated one), STY-TOKENS (no color written out), STY-PARTS (every part a rule names is a part some component has), LINT-CSS (the compiled rules use token variables only), STY-CONTRAST (every theme and mode), DOC-GENERATED (the sheet, the names and the theme choices are the output of the file).

ADR-0027: Layouts, rules per issue type and the starting workflow

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-09

Context

M3 brings issue types (ISS-02), layouts for the issue page and the new-issue form (CFG-01), field levels per issue type (SEC-04, UX §5.2 More options), kinds of relation (ISS-04) and own fields (CF-03). All of these are set for the whole organization or a project, and some also for one issue type. The settings registry (ADR-0018) has the layers default → organization → nearest project → person, but no issue type, and a layout is a structure, not a value. Workflows come in M4, yet every issue needs a status from the start.

Decision

  1. Own tables, settings-like lookup. Layouts, field levels per issue type and kinds of relation live in their own tables, not in the settings registry. Each row names its place (the organization or a project) and optionally an issue type.
  2. One lookup order, defined once: for a project and an issue type, the nearest place with a row wins (the project, then its parents, then the organization); at one place, a row for the issue type wins over a row for all types. The lookup is one function in bb-core, used by layouts and by field levels; a sub-project uses its parent's layout until it gets its own.
  3. Field levels per issue type join the evaluation of architecture §7 (step 7) through that lookup; a level for a type is set under More options on the field-permission page.
  4. Layouts never widen permissions. A layout decides where a field shows and for which roles; a field shows only if the layout lists it for one of the person's roles and the field level lets them see it (to fill it in on the new-issue form: change it).
  5. The starting workflow (decision M3-Q1): one workflow, defined once in bb-core, with Open (status group Not started), In progress (In progress) and Done (Done); every status can follow every other; entering a status of the Done group sets the closed date and leaving it clears it. Every issue type uses it until M4, whose workflow editor makes it the first workflow of the organization; stored statuses keep their IDs.
  6. Editors lock. The layout editor takes an edit lock (ADR-0019) while open, like the workflow and theme editors.

Consequences

  • Own fields, layouts and per-type levels follow one inheritance rule people learn once.
  • The settings registry stays a registry of single values; structures have their own tables and migrations.
  • M4 replaces the starting workflow without a data migration of issues.

Amendment, M3 WP-05: field levels per issue type

The lookup of decision 2 is bb_core::lookup::nearest_row: the one function that finds the row for a place and an issue type. The levels of fields per issue type use it today (bb_policy::nearest_typed_rule, which nearest_rule for the plain levels also calls); layouts (WP-09) use the same function.

  • Storage. A level for one issue type is a row in role_type_field_level (the role's own) or project_type_field_level (set for a project), next to the tables of the levels for all types. The rows join the evaluation as LevelRules::typed; they are read together with the other levels of the roles at a place.
  • Reading. Evaluation::field_level_for(issue_type, field) is the level of a field on an item of that type, field_mask_for the mask. A view that holds its issue type (#[masked(item_type)]) is masked with the mask of that type; a view that does not say its type gets, for each field, the lowest level the field has in any type, so a field that is hidden for some type is never shown by a view that does not say which type it is for.
  • Setting. The route of the field permissions takes ?issue_type=; taking a level for a type away is allowed at the organization too (the role's own level for all types always exists).
  • Names of own fields. A screen that names fields (Field permissions, Check access, the move preview) lists an own field, and prints its name, only for a viewer who may know the field: they may see it in some issue type (any level above Hidden), or they have Manage fields, because whoever manages fields reads every definition on the Fields settings page anyway. For every other viewer the field's name, its ID and its rows are left out of the answer. Values are another matter: a value follows the level of its field, and Manage fields gives no right to read one. The rule is may_know in bb-app (fields/catalogue.rs); the move preview applies it per project of a row, so a field for a sub-project keeps its name for a viewer who may know it there.
  • Naming people in a field. One rule, may_name in bb-app (access/candidates.rs), decides whether a person can be put into Assigned to or into an own field of people, and which people the list to choose from offers: the person exists, the viewer is shown people by name (Assigned to and Project members both show names, ADR-0022) or names themselves, and the person may see the item. A viewer who is shown others only as a role has no ID to name them by, so the ID of somebody else sent in a request is refused alike for a person who is there and one who is not. A value the field holds already, or that Undo puts back, skips only the access of the person named; the person still has to exist.
  • Names of tags. The settings list of tags (Organization settings › Labels & tags) follows the same rule as the names of own fields and projects: a tag is listed, and can be changed, renamed or combined, only for a person who may know the tag: it has no limit, or it is limited to a project they see, or it is used in one. A tag only projects they cannot see know is not there for them (resource.not-found), and the answer never says that a hidden limit exists: a tag with limits only to hidden projects reads as for every project. Saving the projects of a tag replaces only the limits on projects the person sees; the limits on projects they cannot see stay, so a person never drops a limit they cannot see, and an empty list from such a person never makes a tag that is limited to hidden projects a tag for the whole organization. The rule is known_tags in bb-app (tags/manage.rs); the tests are tag_01_the_settings_list_leaves_out_a_tag_only_a_hidden_project_knows, tag_01_saving_the_projects_keeps_the_limits_on_projects_the_person_cannot_see and tag_01_an_empty_list_from_such_a_person_does_not_create_the_tag_organization_wide.

Amendment, M3 WP-09: layouts

  • Storage. layout (where it is set: a project or the organization, an issue type or all, and the form: new-issue or issue-page), layout_section, layout_field and layout_field_role (migration 12). A layout is saved as a whole on the version the editor looked at.
  • Lookup. bb_core::layout::find is nearest_row, the same walk as for field levels. Until somebody customizes a form no row exists and LayoutContent::starting counts. Customize makes a row as a copy of the layout in force.
  • Reading. form_layout applies the layout to the roles of the person and to the levels of the fields: the rule is layouts::effective, which asks the mask and the own-field functions of the field use cases (changeable_own_fields, visible_own_fields) and restates no level. A required own field stays on the new-issue form for everybody who can fill it in.
  • Editing. The editor needs Manage issue types, kinds of relation and layouts at the place, holds an edit lock on the layout (part layout), and saves through save_text, so a lost lock or an old version keeps the sections as a draft. Own fields the editor may not know are left out of the editor and kept on save (may_know).
  • Drafts. The draft a refused save keeps holds only what the editor sent, never the own fields that were put back for it (may_know), so a draft cannot show the ID of a field the person may not know. The event and the write hold the whole layout.
  • Size. A layout holds at most PLACED_MAX fields: the most own fields (own_fields::FIELDS_MAX) plus the most built-in fields of a form, so the starting layout of any organization can be stored. Customize checks the copy like a save does.
  • Roles in the editor. Role names, the per-role marks "field permissions win" and the tick boxes need Decide what roles see at the place (the permission the Field permissions page needs); somebody with only Manage issue types, kinds of relation and layouts gets the editor with choose_roles: false, no role names and no marks. Their save does not change roles: a field that is on the layout keeps its roles, and a field that is added is shown to every role, unless it was on the layout before and was taken off: a field taken off keeps its roles (table layout_off_field, migration 19, one row for each field of the layout that is off the form, its roles still in layout_field_role), so putting it back shows it to the same roles (M4 WP-09, M3-F107). The list of roles is cut at ROLES_MAX (100) like the table of field permissions.
  • Taking a layout away. Refused with edit.in-progress while somebody else holds its edit lock (the page names who, with the people levels of the reader, from the lock); a lock of the person's own is let go in the same change.
  • Required. One function, must_be_asked_for (required and without a default), decides for the server (a new issue without a value is refused), for the form a person gets and for the "required" mark in the editor.

Amendment, M4 WP-11: issue types and groups of labels per project

  • Where something is offered is data. A row of offer (migration 18) says, for one issue type or one group of labels and one place (a project, or the whole organization), whether it is offered there. One definition of the answer, bb_core::offer::is_offered, uses bb_core::lookup::nearest_row (the walk of layouts and workflows): the nearest place with a row wins, and a project follows its parent until it has a row of its own. No row means offered everywhere, so an upgraded database offers what it offered before.
  • Where it was created. An issue type and a group of labels get the project they were created in (none for the whole organization; the ones that were there keep none). A subject created in a project is offered there and below until a row below it says otherwise; a row above it, or for the whole organization, is no part of the answer.
  • Who manages what is judged at a place. Manage issue types, kinds of relation and layouts and Manage labels and tags are judged where the type or the group was created (creating, renaming, retiring, and the labels in a group), and a row of the offers where the row is for. A Project lead therefore manages what they created in their projects, and can switch a type or a group of the whole organization off in their own projects and below, and nowhere else. A subject created in a project takes rows for that project and below only. Combining two labels needs the permission for both groups. A key never holds either permission.
  • One change of the offers is made whole or not at all, inside one change that counts the version of the subject up, so a person who looked at an old state is told (edit.version-changed). It takes the lock of the workflows alone (lock_workflows), and so does retiring an issue type; creating, changing and moving an issue, and putting a label on one, take it shared (lock_chain_in, then ensure_type_takes_issues_in or group_offers_in judge the offers again), so no issue gets a type or a label that a change of the offers has taken away meanwhile. The order of the locks is LockClass in bb-store (ARCH-LOCK-ORDER).
  • A Project lead of P changes what the projects under P are offered, and may switch a type of the organization back on. A row for a project is judged at that project, and a person who holds the permission in P holds it in every project below P, also in one where they have No access for everything else (the permission to look after types and labels is not a right to see issues). So a lead of P can switch a type off or on for a sub-project of P that they cannot see, and can switch an organization type that an administrator switched off for the whole organization back on in their own projects (a row at P is nearer than the row for the organization). That is the decision, confirmed in the review of WP-11. Two leads who change the rows of one type at the same moment are told by the version of the type (edit.version-changed): the second one looks again.
  • Who may know a subject. The name of a type or a group created in a project is not told to everybody who is signed in. One rule (offers/known.rs) decides it for the lists, the rows of the offers, Check access and every use case that takes a type or a group by its ID: a subject created for the whole organization is known to everyone; one created in a project is known to a person who may know that project (the one definition of the policy, Evaluation::knows_project: they see it or decide who has which role there) or who sees a project inside it (a visible sub-project under a hidden parent is told what the parent created and what reaches it), or when it is used on an issue they read (for a group of labels: on an issue whose labels their role lets them see, as for a tag, SEC-06). Anything else is resource.not-found, exactly like one that is not there. A key sees what its project narrows it to. A label is known with its group. A list about a project (?project=) holds only the subjects that can reach it (bb_core::offer::reaches). The editors of layouts and workflows, the catalogue of fields and an issue written with a type apply the same rule; the types of an issue the person reads are known by use. The lists of labels and of groups of labels are lists like the others: paged, with fields= and a page-size cap (GET /api/v1/labels and GET /api/v1/label-groups).
  • Names. A name is unique among the subjects that can meet in one project: those created for the whole organization, and those created in the same chain of projects (the project, the projects above it and those below it); siblings may use one name. A subject of the organization stays unique against all subjects. A clash with a subject the person may not know still answers name.taken; that is accepted, and it reaches only the person's own chain (bb_core::offer::can_meet; migration 18 takes the unique key of the names of groups away, the program judges it inside the change). The name of a label is unique in its group.
  • Limits are counted for each place. A place has at most ISSUE_TYPES_MAX types, LABEL_GROUPS_MAX groups and LABELS_MAX labels of the groups created there (the labels in no group, and the organization's, are the organization's); a project that is full does not use up the room of another.
  • A rename that reaches other projects. A label stays on an issue that moved out of the project of its group. Renaming or combining such a label rewrites those issues, so a person who does not hold Manage labels and tags for the whole organization is refused (access.forbidden, without a number) when an issue of a project they do not look after has the label.
  • The rows a reader gets leave out places they may not know, and the event of a change of the offers names only the places that were changed.
  • Issues keep what they have. A new issue, and a change of the type of an issue, refuse a type that is retired (issue.type-retired) or that the project does not offer (issue.type-not-offered); a label of a group the project does not offer is not put on an issue (label.not-offered). An issue that has a type or a label keeps it. Moving an issue never counts a retired or an unused type as missing (M3-F124): the preview names it ("{type} is not used in {project}"), no run is skipped for type-missing any more (the word stays readable in runs that were stored), and label-not-here is the reason for a label put on an issue by a change to many issues.
  • Check access per issue type (M3-F44). Evaluation::explain_level_for and report_for give the level of a field for one issue type with the reason of each role, found the way field_level_for finds it. The answer says differs_by_type (some type has a level for some field that the all-types answer does not, among the fields the reader may know), and the screen asks Which issue type? only then.

Alternatives considered

  • Layouts as settings values (JSON in the registry): no issue-type dimension, no typed validation, and every reader would parse JSON. Rejected.
  • Fixed statuses with no workflow model: M4 would have to migrate every issue. Rejected.

Enforced by

Review (the lookup function is the one place; its property test cfg_01_a_layout_never_shows_a_field_the_role_cannot_see lives in WP-09) and SEC-MATRIX for the levels per issue type.

ADR-0028: The message catalog is split into parts; the first page loads one

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-13

Context

messages/en.json is the one source of every word (UX-07). The browser got all of it as one object, so every text of every screen was in the first page, and each new screen made the first page bigger: the catalog was about 22 KB of the 250 KB the first page may have (PERF-04, ADR-0009). The next package in line already pushed the first page over the budget through new texts alone.

Decision

  1. en.json stays the one source, and the generator writes the parts. cargo xtask gen messages writes one TypeScript file per part into web/packages/messages/src/generated/: shared.ts (the first page) and one file per folder of web/app/src/features/, plus types.ts (the type of every key, with no text in it) and all.ts (every part, for tests).
  2. One rule says where a key goes, and nobody keeps a list of keys. Code names a key when it writes it as a string, or builds it from a template (`issue-field.${code}` or "issue-field." + code): a template names every key that starts with its text. Comments do not count. A key goes to the part of a feature when that feature is the only code that names it (the same reading TXT-CATALOG uses for "used"). It goes to shared when code outside the features names it, when two features do, and when no code names it: the server sends such a key, or a word of an enum makes it, and then any page may show it. The keys that the words of the enums make (error codes, issue-field., starting-role., permissions and so on, from one list that the generator and TXT-CATALOG share) are always shared, whatever the code says: the server sends them by key and shared code looks them up at run time. The one table in the generator lists the parts (shared and the feature folders); it stays a table, because the paths of generated files are known without reading the folders (META-COVERAGE counts them). A test and TXT-CATALOG compare it with the folders, so a new feature cannot be forgotten (its texts would stay on the first page until it is added). A new key therefore starts on the first page and moves to its area as soon as the area's code names it; the diff of the generated files shows it.
  3. t() stays synchronous and keeps its types. Every part registers its texts when its file is loaded (registry.ts). The entry of a feature (index.ts) imports its part as its first import, so the part lands in the chunk of that feature and is evaluated before the feature runs. Routes load a feature with import() before they render it, so the texts are there; a screen that sits behind OnlyWith has a route loader (loadsScreen) that loads it first, because the router cannot see a lazy component inside another one. isMessageKey is true for loaded keys only, which is why the code that looks keys up by a string lives in the area whose part holds them, or the keys are on the first page. A text that is not loaded is a defect of the build, and a person never sees a key. While the app is built for development (import.meta.env.DEV, which vitest sets too) t() throws with the key in the message, so the defect is found at once. In production t() writes console.error once per key, naming the key, and returns an empty text, so the rest of the page keeps working. The end-to-end tests fail a test on any console.error of the app (the shared fixture; the browser's own "Failed to load resource" lines for refused requests do not count), so the defect is still found before release. The vitest tests cannot find a part that an area forgot to import, because they load every part; TXT-CATALOG finds it.
  4. Outside the browser app everything is loaded. @bugaboo/messages resolves to an entry that loads every part for Node (unit tests and end-to-end tests); the browser build resolves to the plain entry.
  5. Precompiling the messages at build time is not done now. It would let the first page drop the ICU parser (about 57 KB of source, some 8 KB after Brotli), but it needs the ICU syntax tree written by the generator and an alias of the parser in the build and not in the tests. Splitting the catalog gives the room that was asked for; the parser can go later, as its own decision.

Consequences

  • The first page carries the texts of the shell, sign-in, setup and errors shown anywhere, plus the texts of the features that the first page itself loads. A feature that is loaded lazily brings its texts in its own chunk; the texts of the rest of M3 and beyond land there too.
  • cargo xtask gen messages now reads the code of web/ as well as the catalog. DOC-GENERATED fails when a change of code moves a key, and gen messages fixes it.
  • A feature that the first page loads statically (today account, shell, sign-in, home) keeps its texts on the first page. Making such a feature lazy moves its texts with it.
  • A text that two lazy features show is on the first page. That is cheap for common words and a reason to name such a text once in shared code.

Alternatives considered

  • A table from the first part of a key (its area) to a part. Simple, but a key shown by two areas (a projects. text that the issues screens also show) cannot be placed, and the table drifts from the code.
  • Load a part asynchronously from t(). Makes t() asynchronous at every call site. Rejected.
  • One chunk per area chosen by hand in the build configuration. A second list of areas that nothing checks. Rejected.

Enforced by

DOC-GENERATED (the parts are the output of the catalog and the code), TXT-CATALOG (every feature folder has a part, the entry of every feature with texts imports its part as its first import statement, in code and not in a comment, and nothing else does), the end-to-end fixture (a console.error of the app fails the test), PERF-BUNDLE (the first page stays within its budget), LINT-TYPES (every key keeps its type), and the tests in web/packages/messages (every key is in exactly one part, a key is found once its part is loaded, a missing text fails).

ADR-0029: AI agents: apps that act for a person, and agents that work on their own

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-16 · refines ADR-0013 and ADR-0025

Context

M8 plans the MCP server (AI-20…AI-23): an outside AI app signs in as a person and does what that person may do (AI-04). Decision: this stays, and agents should also be able to work on their own, with a person's permission, on chosen issues. Bugaboo does not run agents, now or in the foreseeable future: they run outside (coding agents in a developer's tools, a company's own agents) and connect through MCP.

An agent works on an issue differently from a person:

PersonAgent
The issueA reminder and a conversation; much of the context is in people's headsThe whole job: it knows nothing that is not written there or linked from it
MemoryRemembers yesterdayStarts fresh each time; what it learned must be stored
How work goesSteady, with a comment now and thenIn attempts: plan, work, result or failure, try again; several at once
When stuckAsks someoneAsks through the issue and waits, or guesses
Done"Looks fine to me"Checkable: tests pass, what Done when says is true
What it leavesA comment, a new statusA branch, a pull request, a test report, a log, its time and cost
TrustEarned over yearsEvery result is reviewed by a person
PaceOne issue at a timeHundreds of reads and changes in minutes, often unattended

One person may also drive several agents at the same time, each on its own issues.

Decision

1. Two ways in, one policy engine
  • An AI app acting for a person (AI-04, AI-22, AI-23, unchanged): the app signs in as the person through OAuth or an access key, does at most what the person may do, narrowed by the key's choice, and the history says "Ada Brandt via Claude Code". This is the way for "give all my open issues in Website to Lea".
  • An agent working on its own (AI-30): an account of its own that is not a person. It can do nothing until a person gives it work (decision 3).
  • Both go through bb-policy and the one tool registry of ADR-0013; there is no second rule set. Enforced by: ARCH-AI-TOOLS and SEC-MATRIX (rows for the actor kinds person via app and agent).
2. Agents
  • Every agent has one responsible person, normally the person who made it; handing an agent to another person needs that person's acceptance. Creating agents takes the new permission Create agents that work for you (organization, kind Change; at the start Administrator, Project lead and Team member have it). Administrators see every agent of the organization in Organization settings › Agents and can stop any of them; an administrator can switch agents off for the organization or a project, like AI itself (AI-02). Enforced by: the tests ai_30_an_agent_needs_a_responsible_person and ai_30_an_administrator_stops_any_agent (M8).
  • What an agent can do at a place is at most what its responsible person can do there, narrowed by its work (decision 3) and its limits (decision 9). When the person loses that access, is switched off or leaves, the agent loses it at the next request, and its open work becomes Stopped. Enforced by: the tests ai_30_an_agent_never_does_more_than_its_person and ai_30_an_agent_stops_when_its_person_loses_access (M8).
  • An agent is not a member: it has no role, is in no group, never appears in Who has which role, and is never Assigned to an issue. The issue keeps its person; while an agent works on it the issue shows "worked on by Fixer". This keeps a person answerable for every issue and keeps COMP-10 simple. Enforced by: the tests ai_30_an_agent_cannot_be_assigned and ai_30_an_agent_has_no_role (M8).
  • Shown as its name with an agent mark and its person: "Fixer, agent of Ada Brandt". Its own name is always shown (it is not a person); its person follows Who sees people for the viewer ("agent of Someone (Team member)").
  • An agent signs in with its own agent key (an access key that belongs to the agent and always runs out) or with OAuth for its app. Agent keys are listed with the agent and can be renewed or taken back there.
  • One person, several agents: a person may have several agents, and each agent may work on several issues at once, within its limits. My agents (decision 8) shows all of them together, with what waits for the person first.
3. Giving an agent work: hand over, or a standing rule

There are two ways, and no third one (a project-wide permission would be a standing rule without a filter).

  • Hand over (AI-31): a person hands one or several issues, by their IDs, to one of their agents in the Hand over to an agent window. They choose:

    • the agent;
    • the brief: taken from the issue (description, Steps to reproduce, Done when), plus a note; the window says what is missing ("No steps to reproduce") but does not stop the hand-over;
    • what the agent may do in Bugaboo: always read the issue and what it links to, comment, report its work, log its time, attach results and link related issues; ticked on request: change named fields, change the status, make sub-issues;
    • a budget: attempts, time, and the cost the agent reports;
    • whether its plan needs approval before it starts.

    The hand-over ends at Accept, Throw away, Stop, or when it runs out (14 days unless set otherwise). The person handing over needs Change issues (or Change the issues they reported) on each issue. Enforced by: the tests ai_31_a_handed_over_agent_sees_only_its_issues and ai_31_a_hand_over_ends_at_accept (M8).

  • Standing rule (AI-32): a person lets one of their agents work on everything a saved search finds, for example "every new bug in Website". Because anybody who changes an issue so that it matches gives the agent that issue, a standing rule is narrower than a hand-over:

    • it may propose (default: nothing changes until a person clicks Apply, as with the assistant), or change only the fields named in the rule from a short list (Labels, Tags, Type, Duplicate of, Found in release); it may create issues in one named project when the rule says so (for an agent that reports failing tests);
    • it never changes a field that holds people (Assigned to, Followers, Reported by) and never the status; Enforced by: the test ai_32_a_standing_rule_never_changes_people_fields (M8), and COMP-10 in review;
    • it runs out after 30 days unless set otherwise (at most 90) and is renewed with one click;
    • every issue that newly comes under the rule is written down, so the person sees what the agent saw.

  • Never given to an agent: the permissions of kind Manage (people, roles, settings, fields) and Take over text someone else is editing. Enforced by: the test ai_30_an_agent_never_holds_a_manage_permission (M8).

4. Agent work: the record of what the agent does on an issue
  • Agent work (AI-33) is a record of its own on the issue, apart from the comments, so the conversation stays readable for people. It holds the brief, the attempts (each with the agent's plan, its steps, its results as links such as a branch, a pull request or a test report, and the time and cost the agent reports, marked as reported by the agent), the questions and their answers, and the review.
  • States, shown on the issue page, as a mark on list rows (the row keeps its status color) and searchable (agent:Fixer, agent-state:waiting-for-you): Waiting for the agent, Agent working, Waiting for you (a question or a plan to approve), Ready for review, Agent gave up, Stopped.
  • When an attempt is ready, one short comment marked Written by an agent says so and links to the agent work.
  • The issue's own status is not an agent state. It moves only through the review (decision 6).
5. Questions back, instead of guessing
  • An agent that is stuck asks (MCP tool ask). Its work waits as Waiting for you; the responsible person and the person who handed it over get a notification (NTF-01). The answer is stored in the brief, so the next attempt and any other agent read it. Enforced by: the test ai_34_a_question_waits_for_an_answer_and_the_answer_joins_the_brief (M8).
  • With Plan needs approval, the first step of each attempt is the plan, and the agent waits for Approve plan or a note.
6. Review
  • At Ready for review a person chooses Accept (the hand-over ends; the status moves to the one the reviewer picks, proposed by the workflow), Send back with a note (a new attempt with the note in the brief) or Throw away (everything the attempts changed in Bugaboo is undone in one step; results outside Bugaboo, such as a branch, are the agent's business, and the window says so).
  • A project can allow Accept by itself when its checks pass for handed-over issues (off at the start). Issues accepted that way are listed under Accepted by itself in My agents until a person has looked at them. Enforced by: the test ai_35_accept_by_itself_is_off_at_the_start (M8).
7. Runs: everything an app or an agent did, undone together
  • Every session of an AI app acting for a person, and every attempt of an agent, is one run (AI-38), built on the store of changes to many issues (change_run, its events and its Stopped state). A run is shown as the list of its changes and can be undone in one step; a change that somebody changed again afterwards is skipped and named, as in Change many issues. Enforced by: the test ai_38_a_run_is_undone_in_one_step_and_skips_later_changes (M8).
  • Text written through MCP is marked Written by an AI app or Written by an agent, stored with the text like Written with the assistant (COMP-08, COMP-09).
8. My agents: one person, several agents
  • My agents (AI-37) lists the person's agents and all their work at once. On top is what waits for the person (questions, plans to approve, results to review, standing rules about to run out), then the work in progress per agent, then the standing rules. Each agent can be paused or stopped, and Stop all my agents stops every one in one step.
  • On a phone, My agents shows Waiting for you first, so questions and reviews can be answered on the way.
9. Built for agents: tools, limits, safety
  • MCP tools for agents (AI-36), in the one tool registry: take an issue that is handed over (all or nothing, with the issue's version, so two agents never start the same work), report a step, ask, attach a result, give up with a reason, and changes since (what changed in the issues it may see since a mark it got before). Every write tool takes preview and then answers what would happen, from the same one evaluation as the preview of Change many issues. Each tool says whether it only reads or changes something. Enforced by: ARCH-AI-TOOLS (every tool declares read or change and has a preview test).
  • Long texts: agents never hold an edit lock for longer than one save and never take over a person's text; a save against an older version is refused with the newer text, as for people (Compare and save). Enforced by: the test ai_36_an_agent_never_takes_over_a_lock (M8).
  • Limits per agent and per key: changes per minute, issues at once, attempts per issue. Reaching a limit pauses the agent with a sentence; it never drops a change halfway.
  • Untrusted text: tool answers mark every text with who wrote it (someone in the project, a Guest, someone outside, an agent), so the agent's own safeguards can treat it as data, not as instructions (AI-05). The prompt-injection test set covers agents and standing rules.
  • COMP-10: no tool ranks, evaluates or picks people. An app acting for a person may assign issues because the person told it to; an agent working on its own never changes a field that holds people (decision 3).
10. Agents of the organization (V1)
  • AUTH-08 (V1, M12) becomes agents of the organization: the same model, with the organization as the responsible party and a role instead of a person's rights, for webhooks (NTF-03) and imports. It is built on this decision, not beside it.

Consequences

  • One new kind of actor in bb-policy (agent), evaluated as the intersection of its person's rights, its work and its limits. The access-key narrowing of ADR-0025, decision 8, is reused for agent keys.
  • New records: agents, hand-overs, standing rules, agent work with attempts, questions and reviews. Runs reuse change_run.
  • New words in the glossary (Agent, Hand over, Brief, Done when, Standing rule, Agent work, Attempt, the agent states, Accept / Send back / Throw away, My agents, Agent key, Written by an AI app / an agent); Bot account gives way to Agent, and the assistant's entry no longer forbids the word agent.
  • M8 grows by AI-30…AI-38 and the new permission; its demo shows a hand-over, a question, a review and Throw away.
  • The UX design gains the hand-over window, agent work on the issue page, My agents and its phone form (UX concept, 2026-10-16).

Alternatives considered

  • Agents as ordinary members with roles: an agent could hold more than the person who set it up, and nobody would clearly answer for it. Rejected.
  • Assigning issues to agents: blurs who answers for the issue, and makes AI part of who-does-what decisions about people. Rejected; worked on by shows the agent instead.
  • Access by saved search only: anybody who edits an issue so that it matches gives the agent that issue, Guests included. Kept only for standing rules with narrow powers; real work goes through a hand-over by ID.
  • Agent progress as comments: buries the conversation between people under logs. Rejected; agent work is its own record with one summary comment.
  • Bugaboo running agents: needs heavy machines and access to code, and is out of scope.

Enforced by

ARCH-AI-TOOLS, ARCH-PERMS, SEC-MATRIX (see tools/checks/catalog.toml), and the tests named above, which the M8 work packages add.

ADR-0030: Planning with people: who works on a bar, work times, time factors and plan warnings

Status: Accepted · amended the same day (work hours and shares; the person's own estimate) · refines PLAN-01…05 and ADR-0022; bounded by PRIV-09 and COMP-10

Context

Requirement: the timeline shows three more things: the person who works on each issue; a factor per issue and person, because people need more or less time for some tasks; and away times (holidays, other absences) per person, with Bugaboo saying where they clash with the plan or delay it.

Asked how other planning tools handle different paces, the lead found five ways: time per person (hours per day, a share per project, a calendar; nearly every tool), the person doing the work estimates it (LiquidPlanner, Scrum), the pace of the whole team (Jira Plans and other sprint tools), skill levels to find people but not to set dates (Primavera P6, Planview, Kantata), and paces learned from past work. The first two were taken.

All three are about employees, so they meet the rules we already have: working time and performance are sensitive employee data (PRIV-09), there are no performance scores and no ranking of people (COMP-10), and people are shown only as Who sees people allows (PRIV-12). In Germany, a tool that records how fast employees work is also a matter for the works council (Works Constitution Act, §87 (1) no. 6), and the reason for an absence can be health data (GDPR Art. 9).

Decision

1. The person on the bar
  • Each bar shows the picture and first name of the person it is Assigned to, at its end (PLAN-10); Group by person gives one row per person, so overlapping work is visible. Both follow Who sees people for the viewer: Role only shows "Someone (Team member)" and offers no grouping by person, Hidden shows nobody. Enforced by: the test plan_10_the_timeline_shows_people_only_as_who_sees_people_allows (M7).
2. Work times: when and how much a person works
  • Away is a stretch of whole or half days on which a person does not work (PLAN-11). A person enters their own; people with the new permission Enter work times for others (organization, kind Manage; at the start only Administrator) enter them for others, and the person gets a notification.
  • No reason is stored: Bugaboo does not know whether it is a holiday, a course or an illness. Others only ever see Away. A note is possible and only the person sees it. Enforced by: review (the record has no reason field, which a reviewer sees in the migration), backed by the test plan_11_others_see_only_away.
  • Usual work days per person (for example Monday to Thursday) and public holidays per region (presets per country and, for Germany, per federal state; the person picks their region) say when a person normally works.
  • Work hours per usual work day (PLAN-15; for example 6 hours on Monday to Thursday; at the start 8) say how much. They come from the work contract, so the person or someone with Enter work times for others enters them, never Bugaboo.
  • Share in the project (PLAN-15): how much of a person's work hours belong to one project, for example 60 % for Mobile app. A Project lead sets it on Project members; at the start 100 %. When the shares of one person add up to more than 100 %, the person and the leads of those projects see that, without seeing the other projects' names unless they may.
  • Usual work days, work hours, shares and away times are a new kind of people information in Who sees people (Work times: Names / Role only / Hidden; at the start Names for Team member and above, Hidden for Guests). Away times are deleted one year after they end; work hours and shares when the person leaves the organization (keep and delete rules, PRIV-05).
3. Plan by effort
  • A timeline can plan by effort (PLAN-12): an issue with Estimated time (TIME-03) and a person gets as many of that person's work days as the estimate, times its time factor, needs: each day counts with the person's work hours times their share in the project, skipping away days, days off and public holidays. A person with 6 hours and a 50 % share gives an issue of 9 hours three days. Away days inside a bar are shown as a hatched gap, so the bar gets longer instead of hiding the gap. An issue with a fixed due date keeps it and gets a warning when the days don't fit.
  • Without an estimate, or with planning by effort off, bars keep the dates people set (PLAN-01).
4. The time factor: the person's own estimate for this issue
  • Time factor (PLAN-14) is a value on the issue, for the person it is assigned to: ×1.5 means "this issue will take this person half again as long as the estimate". It is a field with field permissions (at the start Can change for Project lead and Team member, Hidden for Guests), but the assigned person may always change it on their own issues, also where the field permissions would not allow it: they know best how long it will take them. They can enter it as a time ("Takes me 10 days"), and Bugaboo works out the factor. The issue shows who set it: "Lea's own estimate" or "set by Ada Brandt"; the assigned person always sees it and is notified when someone else changes it.
  • It belongs to the issue and goes back to ×1 when the issue is given to another person. Bugaboo keeps no factor per person, no default per person or per kind of task, no totals, averages or reports of factors, and never sets or proposes a factor itself, with AI or otherwise. Without these limits it would be a stored judgement of how fast an employee works: a performance score (PRIV-09) that also needs the works council. Enforced by: review against COMP-10 and PRIV-09, backed by the tests plan_14_the_time_factor_resets_when_the_person_changes and plan_14_no_report_or_search_sorts_by_time_factor.
5. Plan warnings
  • Bugaboo checks the plan and lists plan warnings (PLAN-13), each on the bar and in a list with what can be done:
    • Away: "Lea is away 26–30 Oct, while WEB-280 is planned for her";
    • Not enough days: "WEB-280 needs 6 work days, there are 3 before its due date";
    • Delay: "WEB-280 now ends 2 days later, and WEB-284 after it moves too" (along dependencies; the full chain to the end date with Deadline drivers, PLAN-05); Enforced by: the test plan_13_a_delay_moves_along_dependencies (M7);
    • Too much at once: "Lea has 9 hours planned on 27 Oct in Mobile app; her share there is 3.6 hours" (work hours times share, PLAN-15).
  • The way out is always a person's choice: Move it after, Make it longer, Give it to someone else… (opens the usual person picker, with no suggestion of whom, COMP-10), or Keep and accept. Accepted warnings stay visible in a faded form.
  • Warnings appear only for issues and people the viewer may see; a hidden person's away time shows at most as "the assigned person is away".

Consequences

  • New records: away times, usual work days, work hours per day, a share per person and project, a region per person, public-holiday calendars; a field Time factor in the field catalogue, with who set it; a kind Work times in Who sees people; the permission Enter work times for others.
  • The timeline gains a picture per bar, rows per person, hatched away days, planning by effort and a warnings list. PLAN-07 (L) keeps baselines and export; the workload rows of PLAN-07 are now the rows per person here.
  • The UX concept's timeline shows all of it.

Alternatives considered

  • A factor per person and kind of task ("Lea is slower at testing"), also as an option an organization switches on: a performance profile of an employee. Not taken (PRIV-09, COMP-10, and the works council where there is one). The person's own estimate on an issue gives the same plans without a profile.
  • Paces learned from past work (estimate compared with time spent, per person): a hidden speed rating. Rejected (PRIV-09, COMP-10).
  • Only the pace of the whole team (sprint velocity): fits sprint teams, but says nothing about away times or who is busy when. Not taken.
  • Storing the kind of absence (holiday, illness, training): health data and not needed for planning. Rejected.
  • Moving bars by themselves around away times: surprises people and breaks dates someone promised. Rejected; dates move only when planning by effort is on, and fixed due dates never move by themselves.

Enforced by

ARCH-PERSON-REF (people on bars come as PersonRef), SEC-MATRIX (rows for away times), the tests named above (M7), and review against PRIV-09 and COMP-10.

ADR-0031: Workflows: statuses as data, one judge for a status change

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-16 · refines WF-01…WF-06 and ADR-0027 decision 5; owner's answers M4-Q1, M4-Q2

Context

Until M4 every issue type uses the starting workflow, a fixed enum in bb-core (Status: open, in-progress, done) in which any status may follow any other. The browser knows the same three words from the generated client. M4 lets an organization and its projects make their own workflows (WF-01), with rules on each status change (WF-03, WF-04), an editor (WF-02) and starter workflows (WF-06). ADR-0027 promised that this happens without a migration of stored issues.

Decision

1. A workflow is data
  • A workflow has statuses and status changes.
    • Status: a name, a status group, a position and a stored key.
    • Status change: a from-status, a to-status, the button text in words (Start working), and its rules.
  • Workflows live in their own tables (migration of M4 WP-04). The key of a status is stable: renaming a status changes its name, never its key, so stored issues and history keep working.
  • The three statuses of the starting workflow keep their keys open, in-progress and done. The starting workflow becomes the organization's Simple workflow, so no stored issue changes. Enforced by: a migration test on a database written by M3's code (M4 WP-04).
  • The API sends a status as key, name and group. The browser keeps no list of statuses; it shows what the API sends. Enforced by: TXT-TERMS and review (no statusWords left in the client).
2. Which workflow counts
  • A project and an issue type find their workflow like a layout: the nearest place with a row wins (the project, then its parents, then the organization); at one place, a row for the issue type wins over a row for all types (bb_core::lookup::nearest_row, ADR-0027 decision 2). There is no second lookup.
  • A project may change the workflow it inherited; its sub-projects inherit the change (M4-Q2).
3. One judge for a status change
  • One function in bb-core decides, for an issue, a person and a status change, whether the person may make it now and what it needs. Its answer is one of:
    • allowed;
    • needs these fields (Ask for, Must be filled in; enforced by: TEST-WORKFLOWS);
    • not allowed, because …, with a sentence.
  • The issue page, the status button, Change many issues and its preview, the workflow editor's Try it, the API and later the assistant, apps and agents all use it. Enforced by: TEST-WORKFLOWS (M4 WP-04) and review (no second place that decides a status change).
  • The rules:
    • Who can do it: roles, groups, the person assigned, the person who reported it.
    • Only if …: conditions on fields, in the same words as Must be filled in. Enforced by: TEST-WORKFLOWS.
    • Must be filled in: fields that need a value before the change. Enforced by: TEST-WORKFLOWS.
    • Ask for: fields shown in a small form during the change.
  • The rules can only narrow what Change issues or Change own issues already allow; they never give a right. A field the person may not see is never asked for: then the change is not allowed with a sentence that names no hidden field. Enforced by: TEST-WORKFLOWS and SEC-MATRIX.
  • Then automatically … (WF-05) and versions of workflows (WF-07) are V1.
4. Changing a workflow
  • The editor works on a draft under the edit lock (ADR-0019). Publish makes it count.
  • When a published workflow drops a status that issues still have, Publish asks where those issues go, and moves them as a run of many changes (ADR-0017), with history.
  • The permission Manage workflows (organization or project; Admin everywhere, Project lead in their projects) is needed to change a workflow (M4-Q2). An access key may never hold it.
5. Starter workflows (M4-Q1)
WorkflowStatuses (status group)Used by
SimpleOpen (Not started), In progress (In progress), Done (Done)Task, Goal, and every issue type that exists at the upgrade
BugOpen, In progress, Testing (In progress), Done, Won't fix (Done)Bug, on a new organization
DevelopmentOpen, In progress, In review (In progress), Testing (In progress), DoneFeature, on a new organization
  • They are made once, from one definition in bb-core, as editable copies for the organization.
  • An organization that ran M3 keeps Simple for every type until someone changes it, so nobody's issues move by themselves.
  • The closed date still follows the Done group (ADR-0027 decision 5).

Consequences

  • Every place that knew the three statuses (the Status enum, closed_after, the DTO enums, statusChoices in the browser) changes to the data and the judge. That is most of M4 WP-04 and WP-07.
  • Change many issues may now skip issues whose workflow does not allow the change, and its preview says so (UX §4.2).

Alternatives considered

  • A workflow as a column on the issue type: simpler, but projects could not change it, and it would be a second lookup next to layouts. Rejected.
